`MatrixProvider` exposes Matrix-specific methods (`getClient`, `getEnrichmentCapabilities`) not present on `IChatProvider`. These are only called from Matrix-specific paths gated on a runtime `instanceof` narrowing:

```ts
const matrixProvider: MatrixProvider | undefined = (() => {
  const p = providers.get("matrix");
  return p instanceof MatrixProvider ? p : undefined;
})();
```

This narrowing is the **single** `instanceof` check site. Matrix-only subsystems that still gate on `matrixProvider` being non-null: initial backfill, gap backfetch, message backfetch, redecryption sweeper, and enrichment capabilities. When `matrixProvider` is `undefined` (no Matrix in the registry), those subsystems are silently absent; the rest of the runtime operates normally.

The 11 channel-scoped tools and `set_profile` use the `IChatProvider.channelClient()` / `IChatProvider.setProfile?()` abstraction through the generic provider registry rather than gating on `matrixProvider`. The channel context/label resolver and user_activity membership roster similarly dispatch through the generic `channelClient` path.

### buildMatrixHost — cast site documentation

`buildMatrixHost()` (inner function in `startMikuAgent`) is the **single documented as-cast site** for Matrix-specific event payload narrowings (two casts total, annotated "Cast 1/2 of 2"):

- **Cast 1** — `ProviderLifecycleEvent` (= `unknown`) → `Exclude<MatrixNativeEvent, inbound|reaction>` in `onNativeEvent`
- **Cast 2** — `unknown` → `ReturnType<MatrixNativeClient["start"]>` in `onDiagnostics`

The reaction path is cast-free: `MatrixProvider.poll()` adapts native reaction events to the generic `ReactionStreamEvent` via `adaptMatrixReactionEvent` before invoking `host.onReaction`.

These casts are safe because `MatrixProvider.start()` ONLY calls these callbacks with the corresponding Matrix-specific types. A runtime provider-id guard at the start call (only `"matrix"` providers receive this host) provides defence in depth.

### Per-provider capability wiring

At startup, enrichment capabilities are wired for every registered provider using `IChatProvider.enrichment()` (not the Matrix-specific `getEnrichmentCapabilities`):

```ts
for (const p of providers.values()) {
  for (const accountId of p.accountIds()) {
    const caps = p.enrichment(accountId);
    if (caps) enrichmentPool.options.providerCapabilities.set(`${p.id}:${accountId}`, caps);
  }
}
```

Capability keys are `<provider-id>:<account-id>` (e.g. `"matrix:acct1"`). This loop runs automatically for all registered providers without Matrix-specific branching.

### Canonical event model

All providers normalize events to `CanonicalChatEvent`:

- Identity: `id`, `externalId`, `timelineKey`, `provider`, `agentSessionId`
- Content: `role` (user | assistant), `sender` (`SenderInfo` with `id`, `displayName`, `username`, `isSelf`), `body`, `htmlBody`
- Timing: `timestamp` (event time), `receivedAt` (ingestion time)
- Metadata: `attachments` (`AttachmentMeta[]`), `replyTo` (`ReplyContext`), `linkPreviews` (`LinkPreviewMeta[]`), `mentions`, `reactions`, `threadId`
- Trigger: optional `TriggerInfo` with type, reason, hold timing, grouped event IDs
- Encryption: optional `undecryptable` (`{ sessionId?, reason? }`) — set when the event could not be decrypted (UTD). The renderer keys off this field (not the body) to show a human-client-style "🔒 unable to decrypt" placeholder, so `body` stays empty and never leaks. Cleared by the re-decryption sweeper when keys arrive (see section 6a — Undecryptable events).

At normalization time, `attachments` are stubs (metadata only, no `localPath`), `replyTo` has only `externalId` (no resolved body/sender), and `linkPreviews` is empty. All of these are populated later by the enrichment pipeline and hydrated at context-build time from the enrichment tables (see section 7a).

---

## 6. Matrix Integration

### Rust native core

The Rust NAPI module (`native/crates/matrix-core/`) wraps `matrix-sdk` for:

- Sync loop (long-running tokio task, `sync_once` in a loop with 30s timeout)
- E2E encryption and device verification. At startup `restore_recovery` imports the account's secrets (cross-signing + the key-backup decryption key) from secret storage using the configured recovery key, and the client is built with `BackupDownloadStrategy::AfterDecryptionFailure` (the matrix-sdk default) plus `auto_enable_backups: true`. On each decryption failure the SDK fetches that one missing megolm session from the server-side key backup (paginated, per-session, retried on every UTD), so history encrypted before this device existed becomes decryptable as it is re-attempted — provided an earlier session backed its keys up. Stored UTD rows are driven back through decryption (and thus trigger these per-session fetches) by the re-decryption sweeper (section 6a). `BackupDownloadStrategy::OneShot` is deliberately **not** used: it attempts a single unpaginated bulk `download_all_room_keys` only at the one startup that first enables the backup — which "doesn't work for any sizeable account" (matrix-sdk's own note), swallows the failure, never retries, and installs no per-UTD fallback handler, leaving all pre-device history permanently UTD.
- Media download/upload (with decryption)
- Link preview resolution via Synapse `/_matrix/media/v3/preview_url` — for **generic** URLs only. X/Twitter status URLs never reach this path: they are partitioned out and enriched in the TS layer via the FxTwitter API (§7a "X.com enrichment via FxTwitter"). (The Rust module contains a leftover FxTwitter resolver from the ported system, but it is unreachable dead code — no production path ever enabled it; deleting it is a maintainer-discretion follow-up since it requires a native rebuild.)
- Message sending with Matrix reply/thread relations, custom emoji rendering (shortcode→mxc URL resolution from usage catalog), and outbound mention pills (`@user:server` text → `matrix.to` link + `m.mentions`)
- Reactions with shortcode resolution (custom emoji catalog lookup, unicode shortcode fallback)
- Custom emoji usage catalog (frequency-ranked, room-boosted, time-decayed scoring)
- Inbound event normalization (extracting mentions, media, reply/thread relations; surfacing `m.replace` edits with their target id and replacement content — see "Message edits"; stripping rich-reply fallbacks — see "Rich-reply fallback stripping")
- Undecryptable (UTD) event surfacing — both live sync and backward paging emit a placeholder rather than dropping the event (see section 6a)

Most NAPI methods are async (`#[napi] pub async fn`) — the Rust side runs on a Tokio runtime and returns `JsPromise`s, avoiding blocking the Node.js event loop. This includes `download_media`, `message_summary`, `resolve_link_previews`, and `member_info` which are used by enrichment workers. NAPI methods exchange JSON strings; the TS layer handles typed serialization.

The same NAPI module also exports the **GLM tokenizer** (`NativeTokenizer`, `native/crates/matrix-core/src/tokenizer.rs`) — the Hugging Face `tokenizers` Rust crate (inference only, `onig` regex backend for pretokenizer parity) loaded from a `tokenizer.json` and surfaced as the `glm` `Tokenizer` (§9 "Tokenization"). It exposes sync `encode` / `decode` / `countTokens` (`add_special_tokens = false`, so per-string counts carry no BOS/`[gMASK]`/`<sop>` overhead) plus `encodeAsync` on the libuv threadpool, and a `fromFileAsync` factory that parses the asset on the threadpool too (seconds for a GLM-size vocabulary; startup overlaps it with opening storage, and falls back to the sync `fromFile` on an artifact that predates it). The re-export list in `npm/index.js` and the TS declarations in `src/context/tokenizer/native-binding.ts` are hand-maintained (the crate does not enable napi's `typedef` feature, so `napi build` regenerates neither). **Build caveat:** `build:native` builds the debug/dev profile, where an un-optimized BPE loop runs 10–30× slower and could end up slower than the JS it replaces; `native/Cargo.toml` carries `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 3` to optimize all dependencies (incl. `tokenizers`) under that profile while leaving the workspace crate at default for fast iteration. The `test/tok-bench.ts` perf gate confirms the override took effect.

### Inbound processing

The TS Matrix layer (`src/matrix/inbound.ts`) normalizes native events via `normalizeMatrixInboundEvent()` — a pure field-mapping function with **no I/O**. It produces a `CanonicalChatEvent` with:

- `body`, `htmlBody`: always available from the native event (already fallback-stripped for replies — see "Rich-reply fallback stripping")
- `attachments`: stubs with `id`, `filename`, `mimeType`, `mediaType`, `sizeBytes` — no `localPath` (downloads happen later in enrichment). Each native media descriptor is mapped by the shared `mediaToAttachment(eventId, media)` helper, which the initial-backfill converter (`classifySummary`) also uses so live and backfilled attachments are byte-for-byte identical (see "Initial backfill").
- `replyTo`: `{ externalId }` only — no resolved body, sender, or attachments
- `linkPreviews`: empty (fetched later in enrichment)
- `undecryptable`: set when the native event carries `undecryptable: true` (a UTD placeholder). The normalizer copies the `sessionId` and, critically, forces `trigger` to `undefined` — a UTD event never triggers the bot (a human client wouldn't act on a message it can't read), even in a DM or with a mention.
- `edit`: set when the native event carries `relatesTo: { relType: "m.replace", eventId }` (an edit). The normalizer surfaces `inbound.edit = { targetExternalId }` and forces `trigger` to `undefined` — an edit updates content in place and must not re-fire a session (see "Message edits").

All enrichment (attachment downloads, reply resolution, link preview fetching) is handled post-persistence by the enrichment worker pool (see section 7a). The Matrix provider exposes an `EnrichmentCapabilities` interface that the enrichment workers use for provider-specific operations (media download, message summary, link preview resolution via Synapse for generic URLs, member info lookup). `resolveLinkPreviews` is optional on the interface; providers that do not implement it cause the worker to fall back to `DirectLinkPreviewClient` (og:/twitter: meta scraping). These NAPI bindings are async (returning `Promise`s backed by Tokio tasks) so they don't block the Node.js event loop.

### Message edits

A Matrix edit (`m.replace`) is **applied to its target message in place** — the original row's body/attachments are updated — rather than dropped (the old live behavior) or stored as a standalone message. This mirrors what a human client shows.

- **Native** (`events::normalize_inbound_event`, `events::summarize_timeline_event`): the replacement message lives under `m.new_content`; the top-level `body` is only the `* fallback` and is **not** used. Normalization reads the body / formatted body / media / mentions from `m.new_content`, and surfaces the edit via `relates_to: { rel_type: "m.replace", event_id: <target> }` on both `MatrixInboundEvent` (live) and `MatrixMessageSummary` (re-fetch). The reply/thread relations continue to surface via the dedicated `reply_to_id` / `thread_root_id` fields; `relates_to` is reserved for the `m.replace` signal on the inbound type.
- **TS normalizer** (`inbound.ts`): `relatesTo.relType === "m.replace"` → `inbound.edit = { targetExternalId }`, `trigger` forced to `undefined`. `event.body`/`event.attachments` already carry the replacement.
- **Store primitive** (`Storage.applyEditToTarget` / `TimelineStore.applyEdit`, on the single-writer queue): locates the target by `(provider, externalId, timelineKey)` — **scoped by `timeline_key`** so that in a multi-account shared room (the same Matrix event stored once per bot account, rows differing only by canonical `id`) the edit lands on the right account's row, not an arbitrary one. An edit is always same-room/account as its target, so the caller's `timelineKey` is the correct scope. If found, it updates `body` + `attachments` in place via `applyEditToCanonical`, and `mentions` when the edit carries them (the provider's normalization of the new content: Matrix `m.new_content["m.mentions"]`, Discord's resolved mentions; late input reads mention changes off the stored row; a parked edit replays body and attachments only) (identity, timestamps, sender, role, thread/reply placement preserved) and recomputes `enrichment_status` via `editStatus(updated, timelineState)` — the same inactive-timeline gating as the re-decryption path (an edit landing on an **inactive** timeline keeps `'inactive'` and nudges no pool; otherwise `needsEnrichment` → `'pending'`/`'skipped'`). If the target is **not** found, the resolved replacement is **parked** in `pending_edits` (see "Edit-before-target replay" below) and the result is `{ applied: false, pending: true }`; the edit is never inserted as a standalone row. Repeated edits to a stored target are **latest-by-`origin_server_ts` wins** (issue #3): the row tracks `last_edit_timestamp` (the timestamp of the most recently applied edit), and an incoming edit older than it is a **no-op** (it returns the already-stored event/status, so the caller — e.g. the re-decryption sweeper — still retires its placeholder but re-arms no pool for a stale edit). This guards against out-of-order delivery — notably a re-decrypted older edit arriving after a newer live edit across the live/re-decryption boundary — and mirrors the `pending_edits` `>=` guard so the applied and parked paths agree (equal-timestamp re-applications still apply, harmlessly).
- **Live path** (`app.ts` `handleInbound` → `applyEdit`): an `inbound.edit` is routed to the store primitive before the echo/activation branches (so it's handled uniformly for any sender and any timeline state), and never appended. Enrichment/captions are re-armed only per the stored status (pending → enrich; attachments + non-inactive → captions). A missing target logs `edit_target_missing_parked` (the edit is parked, not dropped).
- **Re-decryption path** (`redecryption/#applyDecryptedEdit`): edits can arrive UTD in E2EE rooms. When a decrypted UTD probe's summary is an `m.replace`, the sweeper first **resolves the target's actual timeline key** (issue #4) before scoping the edit: a UTD placeholder always lands on the room/DM key (its thread relation was megolm-encrypted at store time), but the decrypted target original may live on a thread key (`…:thread:<root>`). `store.resolveEditTargetTimelineKey(provider, externalId, roomKey)` matches `(provider, external_id)` across the room key and any `<roomKey>:thread:%` keys (the room base embeds `matrix:<account>:room:<roomId>`, so multi-account scoping is preserved), preferring the exact room-key match; it falls back to the placeholder's room key when no target is stored (so a missing target still parks under a key the room-target replay path can match). Without this, a thread target was missed, the edit parked under the room key, and replay (keyed by the target's own thread key) never matched — silent, permanent edit loss. The sweeper then applies the edit via the same store primitive, then **deletes the placeholder row** (`deleteUndecrypted`, guarded on `is_undecryptable = 1`) so no standalone duplicate remains. If the target is missing, the replacement is parked in `pending_edits` (logged `redecryption_edit_target_missing_parked`) and the placeholder is still deleted (the edit fallback is not a renderable standalone message). This mirrors the §6a non-message retirement; `decryptedCanonical` no longer needs to handle `m.replace` (edits never reach it).
- **Edit-before-target replay** (`pending_edits` table, issue #12): an edit received/decrypted **before** its target is stored (plausible during backfill or out-of-order sync) is no longer dropped. `applyEditToTarget` parks the resolved replacement (post-edit `body` + serialized attachments) keyed by `(provider, target_external_id, timeline_key)`; if several edits target the same not-yet-stored message, **latest wins** by edit origin timestamp (an upsert that only overwrites when the incoming `edit_timestamp >= ` the parked one). The **append path** (`TimelineStore.appendIfMissing`, used by live routing, backfill, and UTD placeholder insertion) checks for a matching pending edit after a successful insert — scoped by the same `(provider, externalId, timeline_key)` — and, in the **same write transaction**, merges it onto the just-stored event, recomputes `enrichment_status` with the identical inactive-timeline gating (`editStatus`), and deletes the pending row. So the target never renders its pre-edit body, and the replay is account-scoped (a pending edit on one account's timeline never bleeds onto another account's row).
- **Deletions** (Discord deletions, §6c "Deletes"; Matrix redactions, below) arrive as an edit with `edit.deleted = true`, carrying no content. `applyEdit` never applies one as an edit: it records a **deletion marker** on the stored message (`TimelineStore.markDeleted` → `Storage.markTimelineEventDeleted`, on the single-writer queue, located by `(provider, externalId, timelineKey)` like an edit target): `event_json.deleted = { at, by? }`, `at` the deletion's own timestamp (the redaction's `origin_server_ts`; Discord gives none, so its receipt time) and `by` the deleter when the provider says (`edit.deletedBy`: a Matrix redaction's sender; absent for Discord). Nothing else changes: not the body, attachments or mentions, no column (not even `updated_at`; no trigger watches `event_json`), no quote, no `pending_edits` row. It is idempotent: a repeated deletion keeps the first marker and does nothing else (logged `message_deletion_observed {stored, marked}`). A deletion of a message the store does not have yet is not dropped: a message still held by the startup gap backfetch (a buffered live event or a fetched gap message not committed yet, §7c) is marked in that buffer (`GapBackfetchCoordinator.markBufferedDeleted`, in place on the buffered event, so a commit already appending from its snapshot of the buffer stores it marked), so it is stored already marked; otherwise the deletion is **parked** in memory (`PendingDeletions`, `src/timeline/pending-deletions.ts`, keyed by provider, external id and room, so two accounts sharing a room each park their own) and the insert's transaction sets the marker when the message lands in that room or one of its threads (`appendIfMissing`, and for the agent's own messages both sides of the send/echo race, `ingestAssistantSend` and `ingestAssistantEcho`, whether they insert or merge) (`message_deletion_observed {stored: false, buffered | parked}`). Both happen inside the write that found nothing (`markTimelineEventDeleted`'s `onMissing`), so an append queued behind the lookup cannot miss it. A parking expires after 10 minutes and at most 1000 are kept (the oldest go first), so the deletion of something that is never stored (a reaction, a state event) does not accumulate; a restart loses them with the in-flight events themselves, and history fetched again never returns a deleted message. A message stored marked this way reaches late input like any marked message: a trigger is dropped on delivery (`inputWithdrawn`) and a session registered later replays the marker (§8 "Late input", "Deletions before launch"). None of the edit path's follow-up work runs for a deletion: no chat-search reconcile, no summarization reconcile or threshold re-evaluation, no enrichment or caption re-arm, no quote refresh. So search keeps indexing the message as it was (§9e), and summaries are never remade or invalidated: a summary that already covers the message stays as written. What a deletion changes is what the recent tiers show (§9 "Deleted messages"): the message renders as a placeholder there, as clients show it. It also corrects a request still being answered (§8 "Late input"; only on its first marking). The old path, which stored a deletion as an empty edit and wiped the row, is gone; the rows it wiped are marked by the v30→v31 migration, repaired by v31→v32, and a sibling agent's copies marked by v32→v33 (§7).
- **Redactions** (`matrixRedactionDeletion` in `inbound.ts`): the native layer forwards every `m.room.redaction` on the reaction stream as a `remove` of the redacted id (§9f), since it cannot tell a reaction's redaction from a message's. The provider passes it to `onReaction` (the reaction store no-ops on unknown ids) and also emits it as a message deletion: `edit = { targetExternalId: <redacted id>, deleted: true, deletedBy: <redacting user>, lookupTimelineKeys: [<room key>, <DM key>] }`, an empty body, the redaction's own `origin_server_ts` as the time and the redacting user as the sender. `applyEdit` resolves the target in those timelines with their threads (inside the marking write) and marks a stored message; otherwise the deletion is parked for those timelines like any deletion of a message not stored yet (above), and a reaction's or a state event's redaction simply expires there. An encrypted room needs nothing more: the redaction itself is never encrypted, and a target still UTD is a stored placeholder that takes the marker like any row. Only a redaction by the message's own sender withdraws it for late input (§8 "Late input"); a moderator's redaction only marks the message (and the placeholder names the moderator). An event that arrives already redacted (`unsigned.redacted_because`: live, initial backfill, gap backfetch, a re-decryption re-fetch) is never stored: the live handlers and `summarize_message_value` drop it, and a UTD placeholder carries no content in the first place (a redacted one never decrypts, so the sweeper never fills it in). A message redacted before redactions were routed keeps its stored content, unmarked.
- **Rendering**: the edited target renders normally with its updated body (no `(edited)` annotation).
- **By-id lookups and quotes**: a provider fetch of a message by id (Matrix `messageSummary` → `load_or_fetch_event`) returns the **original** event, since an edit is a separate event that never rewrites its target. `Storage.getEditedBody(timelineKey, externalId)` returns the stored post-edit body of a message that has an applied edit (`last_edit_timestamp` set), scoped to the room of `timelineKey` together with its threads (the lookup may come from a different sub-timeline than the target, mirroring `resolveEditTargetTimelineKey`; an exact room-key row wins). Reply-context enrichment (§7a) and `read_messages` with `message_id` (§10) replace the provider summary's body with it. `applyEditToTarget` also refreshes existing quotes: in the same transaction it sets `reply_contexts.body` to the post-edit body for every row quoting the target (`reply_external_id`, indexed by `idx_reply_contexts_reply_external_id`) whose quoting event lives in the target's room or its threads, so a reply stored before the edit renders the current text, the way a client's reply preview does. Another account's rows in a shared room are never touched, and a body-less stub (the provider could not quote the target, possibly because it was redacted) stays a stub. Quotes stored before this behavior were repaired once by the v19→v20 migration.
- **Initial backfill** (`classifySummary` in `src/backfill/index.ts`, issue #1): `m.replace` summaries are **not dropped**. matrix-sdk's `room.messages()` does not fold edits into their originals (the original keeps its pre-edit body; the edit is a separate event), so dropping edits would leave the backfilled original rendering a stale body. Each `m.replace` is routed through the same `TimelineStore.applyEdit` primitive the live and re-decryption paths use — applied in place if the target is already stored, otherwise parked in `pending_edits` and replayed by `appendIfMissing` when the target lands in a later backward page. An edit is never a standalone row, never counts toward the stored cap, and never advances the consecutive-UTD halt; `editStatus` preserves `'inactive'` on the edited target so the activation bulk-flip still governs enrichment.

### Rich-reply fallback stripping

A Matrix rich reply carries a **legacy fallback** in its content (Matrix spec, "Fallbacks for rich replies"): the plain `body` is prefixed with the quoted original (`> <@user:server> …` lines plus a blank separator line), and `formatted_body` wraps the quote in an `<mx-reply>` block. The spec requires clients to strip both before display — without stripping, every reply's body duplicates the quoted original alongside the structured `replyTo` context, polluting the rendered context, the FTS index, summaries, and link-preview extraction (a URL inside the quote would be fetched as if the replier posted it).

Stripping happens in the **native layer**, so every consumer downstream of normalization sees a clean body:

- **Live path** (`events::normalize_inbound_event`): `strip_reply_fallback` removes the leading `>`-prefixed lines and the blank separator from `body`; `strip_mx_reply` removes `<mx-reply>…</mx-reply>` from `formatted_body` (dropping the formatted body entirely if nothing remains).
- **Summary path** (`events::summarize_message_value` via `readable_body`, used by `messageSummary` — and therefore reply-context enrichment — plus initial backfill and the re-decryption sweeper): the same plain-body strip, and `render_formatted_body_text` removes `<mx-reply>` blocks **before** tag-stripping (otherwise the quoted text would survive as plain text).
- **Gating**: the plain-body strip is applied only when the event carries a **genuine** reply relation — `Relation::Reply`, or a thread relation with `in_reply_to` and `is_falling_back: false`. A thread `is_falling_back` shim and a non-reply message have no fallback; a leading `> ` there is a legitimate markdown quote and is preserved. `<mx-reply>` removal is unconditional (the element exists only as the reply fallback). A body that is *only* fallback (the user quoted without adding text) resolves to the empty string.
- **Shape gating**: even on a genuine reply, `strip_reply_fallback` strips only a **spec-shaped** fallback — the first line must name the quoted sender in angle brackets (`> <@user:server> …`, or `> * <@user:server> …` for emotes). Reply fallbacks are deprecated (Matrix 1.3) and clients such as Cinny and Element X send replies without one; there, a reply body starting with `> `/`>` is the user's own markdown quote and passes through untouched. (Before this gate, any leading `>` run on a reply was eaten — a whole-quote reply persisted as an empty body; the v2→v3 storage migration repairs the affected rows from their surviving `htmlBody` blockquote, see §7.)

### Custom emoji pipeline

Custom emoji resolution is handled entirely by the native Rust layer:

- **Inbound observation** (`src/matrix/emoji-resolve.ts`): on each inbound message with `formattedBody`, extracts `<img data-mx-emoticon>` tags and records shortcode+mxc URL pairs via `recordCustomEmojiUsage()`. This feeds the native catalog.
- **Outbound resolution** (native `build_message_content`): when `send_message` or the runner's final delivery sends plain text (no explicit HTML), the native layer calls `mentions::render_message_html`, which resolves `:shortcode:` patterns to proper `<img>` HTML with real mxc URLs from the catalog (falling back to unicode for known unicode shortcodes) **and** turns bare MXID text into mention pills (see "Outbound mentions" below). A body with neither an emoji nor a mention short-circuits through `emoji::render_text_with_custom_emoji` unchanged, sending as plain `m.text`.
- **Reaction resolution** (native `react_message_internal`): `reactMessage` resolves the key through `resolve_reaction_key_info` — custom emoji shortcodes become mxc URLs, unicode shortcodes become emoji characters, plain emoji pass through.
- **Inbound reaction surfacing** (native reaction/redaction handler): the same `m.reaction` handler that feeds the catalog now also pushes *every* inbound reaction (unicode, custom, text) onto the poll queue, and an `m.room.redaction` branch pushes removals. This is the passive-perception path (the agent "sees" reactions on messages without a tool call); the inbound direction uses `resolve_inbound_reaction_key_info` (the key gives kind/normalization, the `m.relates_to` metadata gives the shortcode). See **§9f Reaction surfacing**.
- **Catalog ranking**: entries are scored by global message count (30-day decay) plus room-local message count (14-day decay, 1.5x boost). `listKnownShortcodes` returns deduplicated shortcodes in ranked order.

### Outbound mentions

Plain `@user:server` text in an outgoing body is **not** a Matrix mention: clients only pill-render and notify on a `matrix.to` link in `formatted_body` **plus** the target in the event's `m.mentions.user_ids` (intentional mentions, spec §"User and room mentions"). The bot writes exact MXIDs in prose, so without conversion its `@`-references never notified anyone. The native `mentions` module (`native/crates/matrix-core/src/mentions/mod.rs`) closes both halves, entirely in the send/edit path (`build_message_content`, `build_message_edit_content`):

- **Detection** (`detect_mentions`): a regex finds MXID-shaped tokens (`@localpart:server[:port]`); each candidate is validated with ruma's `UserId::parse` (grammar-correct, no room-membership lookup). Because the server-name character class greedily swallows a trailing `.`/`-` — most often a sentence-ending dot, which ruma actually **accepts** as a root-FQDN server name — trailing `.`/`-` are trimmed *before* parsing so the pill covers exactly the intended MXID (`…ping @a:matrix.org.` pills `@a:matrix.org`, dot left outside). Non-conforming captures stay plain text.
- **Rendering** (`render_message_html`): interleaves mention pills with the emoji renderer in one escaping pass — gap segments between pills go through `emoji::append_shortcode_rendered` (the shared per-segment helper factored out of `render_text_with_custom_emoji`), so a body can carry both pills and `:shortcode:` emoji. The pill's anchor text is the **exact MXID the author wrote**, keeping `body`/`formatted_body` consistent (Element renders the pill from the link regardless). Returns the `formatted_body` plus the distinct mentioned user ids.
- **`m.mentions`**: the collected ids are attached via `RoomMessageEventContent::add_mentions`. The bot's **own** user id is dropped (the spec forbids self-notification). On the reply path the ids are added to the base content *before* `make_reply_event`, which **merges** (adds the replied-to sender) rather than overwriting — so pills and the auto-reply-mention coexist.
- **Custom-HTML path**: when the caller supplies its own `html`, that formatted body is kept verbatim, but `m.mentions` is still derived from the plain-text body (`detect_user_ids`) so referenced users are notified.

Mirrors the inbound side, which already surfaces `m.mentions.userIds` (see "Trigger detection" — a structured mention of the bot's own id is what fires the `mention` trigger).

### Trigger detection

Three trigger types are actively produced:

- **`dm`** — any message in a direct room from someone other than self (`detectTrigger`, `src/matrix/inbound.ts`)
- **`mention`** — structured Matrix mention (not plain-text `@name`); requires `mentions.userIds` to include the bot's user ID (`detectTrigger`)
- **`reply`** — a reply to one of the bot's *own* messages (one stored with an `agent_session_id`), always, like a mention (spec SESSION-RECORDS §6.1; it once required reply-resume to be enabled, spec RESUMABLE-SESSIONS §5). Unlike `dm`/`mention`, this is **not** produced by `detectTrigger`; it is resolved one step later, *inside the trigger hold* (`emitWithTriggerHold` → the `resolveReplyTrigger` callback wired in `app.ts`), so a bare group reply that `detectTrigger` left untriggered can still enter the pipeline. The provider stays resume-unaware — the callback (owning the timeline lookup) only answers "is this a reply to a message I sent?"; what the reply gets (a fresh session given that message's session record, §8i, or a resume where enabled) is decided downstream (§8 "Resumable sessions"). DMs already trigger as `dm`, so in practice the resolver only ever fires for groups (it runs only when `!inbound.trigger`); self-replies are excluded.

Self-sent messages never trigger. The `TriggerInfo` type also defines `timer` and `manual` types for future use.

### Trigger hold

When a trigger fires, a hold of `trigger_hold_ms` (default 250 ms; at most 500 ms while late input is on, §8 "Late input") starts. During this window, **every** further message from the **same sender in the same timeline** is grouped into the held trigger via `groupedEventIds` — **whether or not it carries its own trigger**. A non-triggering follow-up rides the existing timer; a **trigger-bearing** follow-up additionally **debounces** the hold, resetting it to a fresh `trigger_hold_ms` but never past `holdStartedAt + trigger_hold_ms × TRIGGER_HOLD_MAX_MULTIPLIER` (the first message's start, ×4 — a code constant, not config), so a steady drip can't hold a trigger open indefinitely. This catches both the common text+image pattern (a user sends "@miku look at this" then an image in a separate message — Matrix clients don't support mixed text+media) **and** a same-sender burst of several *independently-triggering* messages — most importantly consecutive **replies to the bot**, which each carry an auto-mention trigger because Matrix adds the replied-to user to `m.mentions`. Previously only non-triggering follow-ups grouped; a trigger-bearing one flushed the held trigger early and started its own hold, so each message in such a burst spawned a **separate session** (the duplicate-session incident). Grouping here is the upstream collapse to one trigger → one session; co-target coalescing (§8) remains the *cross-sender* / out-of-window backstop. A held trigger is now flushed only by its (possibly debounce-extended) timer — there is no early flush.

The hold owns the **pre-launch** regime; **follow-up folding** (§8 "Follow-up folding") owns the **post-launch tail**. The two partition the timeline cleanly: a same-sender follow-up landing inside the 2 s hold is grouped into turn 1 (the watch isn't armed until the session launches, after the hold flushes), and one landing after the session launched is folded (steered / parked, or a fresh session given the owner's record once the owner completed) instead.

**Deferred fold-immediacy when a burst overlaps an armed watch.** Because the hold now *groups* a trigger-bearing follow-up rather than flushing it, a *new* same-sender trigger burst that lands while a *prior* session's watch is still armed reaches `foldFollowUp` as a single **lead** trigger (the rest of the burst riding as its `groupedEventIds`); the fold steers (or, owner settled, launches a fresh session for) the lead, and the grouped tail messages surface on the next context rebuild rather than each being steered in live. Single-consumption still holds (the tail is never double-delivered) and nothing is lost (each tail message is ingested as a normal timeline event) — only the *liveness* of the fold for those tail messages is deferred. This is an uncommon shape and the intended trade-off of the group-don't-flush hold, not a regression.

**Reply-as-trigger resolve (first, before the raw emit).** At the top of `emitWithTriggerHold`, an *untriggered* reply to another sender's message is offered to the `resolveReplyTrigger` callback (spec RESUMABLE-SESSIONS §5, SESSION-RECORDS §6.1: any reply to a stored bot message, whether or not resume is on; see "Trigger detection"). If the callback returns a `TriggerInfo`, `inbound.trigger` is set to it **before** the strip/hold below — so a resolved `reply` rides the exact same hold + same-sender grouping as a native `dm`/`mention`, rather than being synthesized late in the app (the now-deleted `maybeSynthesizeReplyTrigger`). This is what makes a bare group reply earn exactly one held, grouped trigger-bearing delivery (and not be handled twice). Self-replies (`event.sender.isSelf`) are skipped.

**Invariant:** Every event is emitted immediately to the timeline with `trigger: undefined` — the timeline always gets the raw event for storage regardless of the hold (the reply-resolve above only sets the in-memory trigger; the raw emit is still stripped). The hold only delays the trigger callback, not ingestion. If a new trigger from the same sender arrives during a hold, the pending trigger is flushed immediately.

**Consequence — a trigger-bearing event reaches `handleInbound` twice:** once on the immediate `trigger: undefined` emit and once on the post-hold emit with the trigger populated (same `event.id`). Every `handleInbound` step on this path is idempotent except steering: a reply to an active session (DM replies are *always* triggers; a bare group reply to a bot message is *now* one too, via the resolver) would otherwise be injected into the session twice. `steerReplyToActiveSession` therefore dedups by `event.id` (bounded FIFO of recently-steered ids) — it steers at most once per event but still returns `true` on the redundant delivery so the reply never falls through to the spawn path. The dedup runs **before** the target-is-active check, because the trigger-bearing twin can land after the session that read the raw steer has settled: such a twin is consumed (`reply_twin_consumed`) rather than spawning a second session for the same reply. A twin whose raw steer the settled session did **not** read takes the native path, so the reply is still answered (§8i "The turn").

### Outbound

Messages with both text and attachments are sent as separate Matrix messages: the text goes first as its own message (preserving long text), then each attachment is uploaded separately. The text event is the primary delivery receipt.

### Room-label resolution

The Matrix client exposes `channelContext({ roomId })` (`src/matrix/native-client.ts`), which resolves both a human room label (`displayName ?? canonicalAlias ?? roomId`, suffixed ` (parentSpaceName)` when the room has a name-resolvable parent space) and the room's DM flag from a single `channelInfo` call; `channelLabel({ roomId })` is a thin wrapper keeping only the label. This is a homeserver-backed call. Three consumers map a per-room timeline key → account + room id → that account's client:

- The **diary header** (§9c), which needs a label per job — via the shared `resolveChannelLabel` resolver in `app.ts`.
- The **`<runtime_state>` channel descriptor** (§ "Satellite block and final user turn"), via the builder's injected `resolveChannelContext` hook in `app.ts` (label + DM flag, never-throws, null on an unresolvable timeline).
- **`RoomLabelCache`** (`src/matrix/room-label-cache.ts`), which caches resolved labels in `room_metadata` so the observability console room list shows real names. Because resolution is network-backed it must never block the inbound hot path: `ensureLabel(timelineKey)` — called for every non-edit inbound event in `handleInbound` — does a cheap synchronous freshness check (is a label cached and younger than the 6-hour TTL?) and, only when a re-resolve is due and not already in flight, kicks off the resolve + persist in the background. Concurrent calls for the same timeline coalesce via an in-flight set; a failed resolve is logged and leaves the prior label (or the room-id fallback) in place. To stop a persistently-failing room from firing one homeserver call per inbound message, failures are recorded in an in-memory negative cache and the freshness gate (in both `ensureLabel` and `backfillAll`) skips a re-resolve until a `failureCooldownMs` cooldown elapses (default 5 minutes); a later success clears the entry. A resolve that returns an empty/whitespace label is treated the same as a failure — not persisted (the store assumes non-empty labels: `room_metadata.display_name` is NOT NULL but does not reject `''`, and `listConsoleRooms` only falls back to the room id on NULL) and it engages the same backoff. At startup, after `provider.start()`, a throttled `backfillAll()` (fire-and-forget, spaced to avoid a homeserver thundering herd) resolves labels for already-known — possibly idle — rooms so they get names without waiting for their next message.

---

## 6a. Undecryptable (UTD) events

Encrypted events whose room keys haven't arrived can't be decrypted. Rather than dropping them, the system surfaces them like a human Matrix client does — a "🔒 unable to decrypt" placeholder showing sender + timestamp but no body — everywhere (live sync and backfill), and replaces them with the real event once keys arrive.

Keys arrive two ways: shared live by other devices (the common case for momentarily-late keys), and **fetched per-session from the server-side key backup on decryption failure** — the client is built with `BackupDownloadStrategy::AfterDecryptionFailure`, and `restore_recovery` imports the backup decryption key from secret storage on every start (see section 6, "Rust native core"), so each UTD event triggers a paginated fetch of just its megolm session from the backup; any session that previously backed up its keys thus makes that history decryptable on this device as the event (live, or a stored UTD row re-driven by the sweeper) is re-attempted. A key "never arrives" only for events whose megolm session was never backed up by any of the account's sessions (e.g. history from before the account joined the room).

### Native surfacing

The native module uses raw matrix-sdk callbacks + `room.messages()` (not the `matrix-sdk-ui` Timeline), so there is no automatic re-decryption signal. UTD is surfaced at two points:

- **Backfill / `messageSummary`** (`events::summarize_timeline_event`): when `event.kind.is_utd()`, it returns a `MatrixMessageSummary` with `body=""`, `undecryptable=Some(true)`, `session_id` from the SDK's UTD info, a `utd_reason` code (see below), and event_id/sender/ts from the raw `m.room.encrypted` envelope — instead of `None`. This covers `read_messages`, pinned events, and `message_summary`.
- **Live sync** (`client/mod.rs` raw `Raw<AnySyncTimelineEvent>` handler): the SDK re-injects decrypted events under their decrypted type, so an event still typed `m.room.encrypted` in the raw handler is a live UTD. It is pushed as a `MatrixInboundEvent` placeholder via `normalize_utd_inbound_event`. `last_successful_decryption_at` is **not** bumped (no decryption happened). `utd_reason` is **always `None`** here — the raw handler receives only the encrypted envelope, not the SDK's structured `UnableToDecryptInfo`; the reason becomes available only when the sweeper later re-fetches the event through the summary path.

Both `MatrixMessageSummary` and `MatrixInboundEvent` carry `undecryptable: Option<bool>` + `session_id: Option<String>` + `utd_reason: Option<String>` (camelCase `utdReason` over the JSON bridge), mirrored in `src/matrix/native-types.ts`. A UTD event has empty body and empty media. `utd_reason` is a stable lowercase code mapped from the SDK `UnableToDecryptReason` (`missing_megolm_session`, `unknown_megolm_message_index`, `malformed_encrypted_event`, `megolm_decryption_failure`, `payload_deserialization_failure`, `mismatched_identity_keys`, `sender_identity_not_trusted`, `unknown`); diagnostic only, surfaced into the canonical `undecryptable.reason` by both the live (`inbound.ts`) and backfill (`classifySummary`) producers.

### Storage & rendering

UTD events are stored through the normal path with `enrichment_status='skipped'` (nothing to enrich — no body/media). The canonical `undecryptable` field rides inside `event_json`. A generated column `is_undecryptable` (VIRTUAL, from `json_extract(event_json, '$.undecryptable')`) with a partial index makes UTD rows cheap to find for the sweeper without scanning JSON (it persists across restarts, unlike an in-memory set).

A UTD event's thread/edit relation is megolm-encrypted at store time (`relatesTo` is undefined), so it can't be filtered by thread membership. During **initial backfill** of a thread timeline, `classifySummary` therefore lands UTD events on the **room** timeline rather than dropping them (issue #5) — mirroring the live UTD path (which always stores UTD on the room/DM key) — so the re-decryption sweeper can recover and re-home them to the thread once keys arrive. The UTD's canonical id (`matrix:<account>:<eventId>`) is independent of the timeline key, so dedup against any later live/backfill arrival still holds. The canonical id format is injected via `CommonContext.buildId: (externalId) => string` (§11.3 provider-agnostic classify.ts) — Matrix callers pass `(id) => \`matrix:${accountId}:${id}\`` — so `classifyForTimeline`/`classifyForRoom` do not hardcode the `matrix:` prefix.

The renderer (`src/context/renderer.ts`) has a UTD branch in **both** `renderCompactMessage` and `renderRichMessage` that emits the lock placeholder with sender + timestamp, ignoring body/attachments — so a UTD event reaching the model looks exactly like what a human client shows, and the body can never leak. Because summarization input is assembled by the same context builder over the same stored rows (`getTimelineEventsBetween`), UTD placeholders automatically appear in summary **input** for any range they fall in (they need not appear in the summary output).

### Re-decryption sweeper (`src/redecryption/`)

A background loop (wired in `app.ts`, started after the provider, stopped first on drain) periodically retries stored UTD events. Each tick:

1. `TimelineStore.getUndecrypted(limit)` returns due UTD rows (oldest first), each paired with its persisted `redecrypt_attempts` count, filtered by a per-event exponential backoff (1 min base, capped at 1 h) so events whose keys may never arrive don't hammer the homeserver. **RC8 gate:** `#probe` checks `event.provider !== "matrix"` first — non-Matrix providers have no megolm concept, so their events must never reach `retireUndecrypted`; the sweeper logs `redecryption_skipped_non_matrix` and returns early, leaving the row in place for a future provider-specific path. **Give-up ceiling:** the query excludes rows whose `redecrypt_attempts` have reached `MAX_REDECRYPT_ATTEMPTS` (and the `REDECRYPT_RETIRED` sentinel), so permanently-dead UTD rows (sent before the bot joined → keys will never arrive) leave the oldest-first candidate window and can't starve newer, decryptable rows. Each failed probe persists an attempt (`recordRedecryptFailure`); the in-memory backoff map is pruned every tick to the ids still in rotation so it stays bounded, and on a cold start the backoff is reseeded from the persisted attempt count so a long-dead row isn't probed immediately on boot.
2. For each, it re-fetches the summary via the native `messageSummary` primitive (which re-runs `load_or_fetch_event` + summarize) — resolving the room id from the event's timeline key. A UTD row with no resolvable room/event id can never be re-fetched, so it is **retired** (`retireUndecryptedEvent` stamps the sentinel) and leaves rotation in the DB rather than sitting front-of-queue forever. Across multiple bot accounts sharing a room, `resolveMultiAccountRetry` tries every account and prefers a decrypted result (a megolm key one account lacks may be known to another), falling back to a still-UTD summary only when none decrypts; if every account throws (room unknown / fetch failure) it rethrows so the failure is treated as transient (not collapsed to a non-message signal).
3. The probe outcome is one of four:
   - **decrypted `m.replace` edit** (`summary.relatesTo.relType === "m.replace"`) → the decrypted UTD is an edit (edits can arrive UTD in E2EE rooms). Rather than convert the placeholder into a standalone message, `#applyDecryptedEdit` applies the replacement to the target via the shared `TimelineStore.applyEdit` primitive (same path as the live edit — see section 6, "Message edits") and then **deletes the placeholder row** (`deleteUndecrypted`) so no standalone duplicate lingers. If the target is missing, the replacement is **parked** in `pending_edits` for replay when the target lands (issue #12), and the placeholder is still deleted. Enrichment/captions are re-armed only per the stored status, with the same inactive-timeline gating. (Handled before the normal decrypted-summary branch, so `decryptedCanonical` never sees an `m.replace`.)
   - **decrypted, non-UTD summary** → the megolm session is now known: `TimelineStore.replaceUndecrypted(eventId, updater, computeStatus)` rewrites `body`/`event_json` with the decrypted content (flag cleared, real attachments) and sets `enrichment_status` to the value `computeStatus` returns. The status mirrors the live append path and respects the timeline lifecycle (`postDecryptStatus`): for an **inactive** timeline it is `'inactive'` (decryption still happens, but enrichment/captioning is deferred to the activation bulk-flip — neither pool is nudged, per spec §3); otherwise it is `needsEnrichment(updated) ? 'pending' : 'skipped'`. `replaceUndecryptedEvent` reads the (possibly re-homed) timeline's live `timeline_state` inside the same write transaction and returns the chosen `status`, so the sweeper's notify decisions match exactly what was stored — `notifyEnrichment` only when `'pending'`, captions only when the decrypted event has attachments **and** the timeline isn't inactive. The `updater` (`decryptedCanonical`) also recovers the now-decrypted **relation** from `summary.relatesTo`, mirroring the backfill `classifySummary`: a bare in-reply-to (no `relType`) sets `replyTo`; an `m.thread` relation sets `threadId` **and re-homes the row** to the thread timeline key (`matrix:<acct>:room:<roomId>:thread:<root>`) — a stored UTD always lands on the room timeline because its relation was encrypted at store time, so the true placement is only knowable after decryption. (`m.replace` edits are handled by the branch above, so they never reach this merge.) `replaceUndecryptedEvent` persists the new `timeline_key`/`threadId` (the canonical id — the dedup key — never changes) and a re-home is logged as `redecryption_rehomed_to_thread`.
   - **`null` return** (the native primitive returned `Ok(None)` — fetched & decrypted, but a non-renderable message: sticker/poll/reaction) → the live append path never stores these, so the placeholder is **deleted** (`deleteUndecryptedEvent`, guarded to act only while the row is still UTD) to match live parity. The row leaves rotation; no enrichment/caption nudge.
   - **still-UTD summary** (`undecryptable === true`) **or a thrown fetch failure** → a transient miss: persist an attempt and back off. (A still-UTD summary is distinct from a `null` return — the native UTD path always yields a summary with `undecryptable: true`, never `None`, so `null` is an unambiguous "decrypted non-message" signal.)
   - `replaceUndecryptedEvent` returns `{ event, replaced, status }`. When the row is already non-UTD (the sweeper raced backfill or a `message_summary` touch that decrypted it first), it writes nothing and reports `replaced: false`; the sweeper then skips re-arming enrichment/captions and the `redecryption_replaced` log.

**Residual limitation:** a thread message that *never* re-decrypts (its room keys never arrive) stays permanently on the **room** timeline, since its `m.thread` relation is forever encrypted and the sweeper can never learn it belongs to a thread. Only re-decryptable thread UTDs are re-homed.

Configured under `[timeline]`: `redecryption_sweep_interval_ms` (default 60000; 0 disables the sweeper) and `redecryption_sweep_batch` (default 50; max UTD events probed per tick).

## 6b. User Identity Store

Some providers (Discord) use stable internal user IDs that are not human-readable, and users can change their visible name over time. The user identity store tracks the current username and display name for each `(provider, user_id)` pair, as well as a bounded history of prior usernames, so the system can render events under the sender's current name and expand retrieval queries to also search under aliases.

### Tables

Two tables form the identity store (defined in `USER_IDENTITIES_SCHEMA`, included as a sub-constant of `SCHEMA`; added by the **v4→v5** migration `addUserIdentityTables` for existing databases):

- **`user_identities`** — `WITHOUT ROWID`, primary key `(provider, user_id)`. Columns: `username` (current), `display_name` (nullable), `first_seen` / `last_seen` / `updated_at` (all unix ms). Indexed on `(provider, updated_at DESC)`. One row per user, mutated in place on each upsert.
- **`user_identity_aliases`** — prior username values. `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` (never reuses rowids, so "delete lowest rowid" always evicts the genuinely oldest alias). Columns: `provider`, `user_id`, `username` (the previous name), `display_name` (snapshot at rename), `recorded_at`. Indexed on `(provider, user_id, rowid)`. Bounded at `USER_IDENTITY_ALIAS_BOUND = 16` rows per user; the oldest (lowest rowid) are deleted when the count exceeds the bound.

### Upsert rule (`Storage.upsertUserIdentity`)

Called from the shared ingest path in `app.ts` (`handleInbound`) immediately after `router.route()`, inside a fire-and-forget promise chain (never blocks the hot path; errors are logged as warnings and swallowed). The hook runs only when `inbound.event.sender.username` is truthy — **Matrix events never set `sender.username`**, so the hook is never called for Matrix, guaranteeing zero writes for the current sole Matrix deployment.

Three cases, all executed inside a single `write()` call:

1. **First sighting** — no existing row: insert `user_identities` with `first_seen = last_seen = updated_at = observedAt`.
2. **Username unchanged** — existing row with same `username`: update `last_seen` and (if changed) `display_name` only. No alias row is created.
3. **Username changed** — existing row with a different `username`: insert the old `(username, display_name)` into `user_identity_aliases` with `recorded_at = observedAt` (the timestamp of the event that first observed the rename), then update `user_identities` with the new name and `updated_at = observedAt`. After inserting, evict any aliases beyond `USER_IDENTITY_ALIAS_BOUND` by deleting the rows with the lowest rowids for that user.

`isSelf` senders are included — the bot's own identity is tracked the same as any other sender.

### Render-time current-identity resolution (`ContextBuilder`)

Before the context window is handed to the renderer, `ContextBuilder` runs a batch identity lookup over all events in `compactionInput` and `triggerEvents`:

1. `buildIdentityMap` collects distinct `(provider, sender.id)` pairs from the combined event list and calls `Storage.getUserIdentityMap`, which does a single parameterized `SELECT` scoped to those PKs (returning a `Map<"provider:userId", CurrentIdentity>`).
2. If the map is non-empty, `applyIdentityOverrides` shallow-copies each array, patching `event.sender` with `username: current.username ?? event.sender.username` and `displayName` from the stored value (a stored `null` becomes `undefined` to match `SenderInfo.displayName?: string`).
3. **If the map is empty** (which it always is for a Matrix-only database), neither array is touched — the output is byte-identical to what it would have been without this code. (The map lookup itself still runs: one empty-table PK SELECT per distinct sender, nanosecond-class; only the override pass is skipped.)

This means old events are always rendered under the sender's current name: if a user renamed from `alice` to `xoxo_alice`, messages stored under the old name surface as `xoxo_alice` in the LLM context.

### Retrieval alias expansion (`ContextBuilder.buildTriggerUsers`)

The user lane of the retrieval query (`src/context/builder.ts`, `buildTriggerUsers`) collects the set of names to match against the embedding/FTS index. For any trigger-window sender that has a `username`, the builder fetches up to 4 prior alias usernames via `Storage.getUserIdentityAliases(provider, userId, 4)` and adds them to the names set alongside the current `username`. This means a renamed user's older messages (indexed under a prior name) are still found. The maximum expansion is **current name + 4 aliases = 5 names per user**. Matrix senders (no `username`) contribute only their `displayName` to the names set, which is the pre-existing behaviour.

### Matrix zero-write guarantee

Matrix events never carry `sender.username` (the `SenderInfo` field is absent for the Matrix normalizer). The ingest hook gates on `sender.username` being truthy, so for a Matrix-only deployment:
- `upsertUserIdentity` is never called → both tables remain empty
- `getUserIdentityMap` returns an empty map → `buildIdentityMap` returns an empty map → `applyIdentityOverrides` is skipped entirely
- `getUserIdentityAliases` returns `[]` → no extra names are added to the retrieval query

The resulting context and retrieval output are byte-identical to what they would have been before this feature was added.

### Cross-channel query methods

Three additional `Storage` methods support the cross-channel messaging tools (§10 Cross-channel messaging):

- **`searchUserIdentities(query, opts?)`** — fuzzy LIKE search over `user_identities`. Matches the query substring against both `username` and `display_name` (case-insensitive via SQLite's `LIKE`). Optional `opts.provider` narrows to one provider; `opts.limit` caps results (default 10). Returns `Array<{ provider, userId, username, displayName, lastSeen }>`. Used by `send_dm` to resolve display names to stable user IDs.
- **`findDmTimelineKeysForUser(userId, opts?)`** — returns timeline keys for DM channels where `userId` has posted (i.e. rows in `timeline_events` whose `sender` matches and whose timeline key contains `:dm:`). `opts.provider` filters by provider. Used by `read_messages` to accept a bare user ID in place of a DM timeline key.
- **`getLastAssistantEvent(timelineKey)`** — returns the most recent `timeline_events` row with `role = "assistant"` for the given timeline. Used by `read_messages` with `anchor: "last_self"` to centre the history window on the bot's most recent message in a channel.

### DM opt-out table

**`dm_optouts`** — added by the **v16→v17** migration. Primary key `(provider, user_id)`. Columns: `created_at` (unix ms), `origin_timeline_key` (the channel where the opt-out was recorded). Row present = user has opted out of agent-initiated DMs. Methods: `getDmOptout(provider, userId)`, `setDmOptout(provider, userId, originTimelineKey)`, `clearDmOptout(provider, userId)`. The `dm_optout` tool writes/deletes these rows; the `send_dm` tool and the proactive scheduler check them. IRC user ids are stored lowercase (case-insensitive canonicalization applied at all write and read sites).

**`dm_peers`** — added by the **v17→v18** migration. Primary key `(provider, account_id, dm_channel_id)`. Column: `peer_user_id`. Records the known non-self peer for each DM channel. Written on two occasions: (a) every inbound non-self message in a dm-kind timeline (`handleInbound` in `app.ts`); (b) after a successful `send_dm` `openDm()` call. Methods: `setDmPeer(provider, accountId, dmChannelId, peerUserId)` (upsert; last writer wins — peer ids are stable), `getDmPeer(provider, accountId, dmChannelId)` (returns `undefined` when the peer is unknown). `dmTimelineKeysForPeer(provider, accountId, userId)` (the duplicate check's `send_dm` target, §8j): the account's DMs with the user, the recorded peers (`idx_dm_peers_peer`) and the DMs the user posted in (the partial `idx_timeline_events_dm_sender` over DM rows: `(sender_id, timeline_key, timestamp) where instr(timeline_key, ':dm:') > 0`, also serving `findDmTimelineKeysForUser`), newest last message first; indexed reads only, since it runs on every judged `send_dm`. Both indexes are in `SCHEMA`, so an existing database gets them at its next open. The proactive scheduler's DM opt-out gate first scans recent events for the peer; if absent, it falls back to this table; if neither yields a peer, the scheduler **skips the channel** (`skip_dm_unknown_peer` decision) rather than posting without consent verification (fail-closed).

**`workspace_seed_ledger`** — added by the **v18→v19** migration. Composite primary key `(agent_name, rel_path)`, declared `WITHOUT ROWID` for clustered key access. Columns: `source` (`"workspace"` | `"feature:<name>"`), `origin` (`"seeded"` | `"adopted"` | `"updated"`), `template_hash` (SHA-256 hex of the source template at last write), `created_at` / `updated_at` (unix ms). Tracks per-agent, per-file template provenance for the reconcile engine (§4b). One row per file that has ever been touched by the engine: absent row = never seeded by this engine (crash-window file → adopt). `origin='seeded'` = written from template on first encounter; `origin='adopted'` = pre-existing file taken in without content change; `origin='updated'` = auto-overwritten when local was unmodified and template changed. A row whose local file has since been deleted is a **tombstone** (row present, file absent — no flag column needed) and is never re-seeded. Methods: `getSeedLedgerRow(agentName, relPath)` (sync read; returns `undefined` when absent), `listSeedLedgerRows(agentName)` (sync read; all rows for one agent), `upsertSeedLedgerRow(row)` (async write through single-writer queue, `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`). `app.ts` wraps these in the `SeedLedgerOps` adapter; `seed.ts` never imports Storage directly.

## 6c. Discord Provider

`src/discord/` implements the Discord gateway provider using discord.js v14. It splits into a pure normalizer module (`normalizer.ts`) and the live provider class (`provider.ts`).

### Normalizer (`src/discord/normalizer.ts`)

A pure-function module with no live discord.js Client references. The provider extracts plain data from discord.js objects and passes them here, making all normalization logic unit-testable without a gateway connection.

**Key shapes** (spec §4.1):

| Context | Timeline key |
|---|---|
| Guild text channel | `discord:<accountId>:room:<channelId>` |
| DM channel | `discord:<accountId>:dm:<channelId>` |
| Thread / forum post | `discord:<accountId>:room:<parentChannelId>:thread:<threadId>` |

Thread detection uses `THREAD_CHANNEL_TYPES = {10 (AnnouncementThread), 11 (PublicThread), 12 (PrivateThread), 15 (Forum)}`. Forum post-channels appear as type-15 parent channels with thread children; their posts are therefore routed as `room:<parentId>:thread:<postId>` — identical to ordinary thread routing.

Event id grammar: `discord:<accountId>:<messageSnowflake>`.

`buildDiscordTimelineKey(accountId, channelId, channelType, parentChannelId?)` and `buildDiscordEventId(accountId, messageId)` are the canonical factories; all other code imports them rather than constructing keys inline.

**Markup translation** — `translateDiscordMarkup(content, {users, roles, channels})`:

| Discord token | Rendered as |
|---|---|
| `<@id>` / `<@!id>` | `@username` / `@displayName` (nick form for `!`) |
| `<#id>` | `#channel-name` |
| `<@&id>` | `@role-name` |
| `<:name:id>` / `<a:name:id>` | `:name:` (static / animated custom emoji) |

Unresolvable IDs (not in the passed maps) pass through verbatim so no information is destroyed.

**Attachment normalisation**: `attachmentToMeta` maps `DiscordAttachmentData` to `AttachmentMeta`, inferring `mediaType` from MIME prefix and setting `asVoice`/`durationMs` when `isVoiceMessage=true` (Discord `IS_VOICE_MESSAGE` message flag 8192). Stickers are converted via `stickerToAttachment`, which maps the `StickerFormatType` enum (set by the provider in `extractMessageData`) to MIME type and filename extension: PNG (1) / APNG (2) → `image/png` / `.png`; GIF (4) → `image/gif` / `.gif`; Lottie (3) → `application/json` / `.json` with `mediaType: "file"` so the captioning worker (which only captions `image|video|audio`) skips it.

**Embed → link previews** — `embedsToLinkPreviews(embeds)`: only embeds with a URL are converted. The same trailing-punctuation strip used by `DirectLinkPreviewClient` (`.replace(/[.,;:!?)"'\]}>]+$/, "")`) is applied so embed URL exclusion matching works correctly at enrichment time. Result `sourceKind` is `"discord_embed"` so the enrichment worker can skip re-scraping those URLs.

**Trigger detection** — `detectDiscordTrigger(msg, ctx, isSelf)`:
- DM channel (type 1) → `{ type: "dm" }`
- Direct user mention of the bot snowflake → `{ type: "mention" }`
- Role mentions and @everyone/here do NOT trigger
- Own messages (`isSelf`) → `undefined`
- Reply-to-bot trigger is resolved separately by the provider via `host.resolveReplyTrigger` after storing the event

**Poll fallback**: when `msg.poll` is present and body content is empty, body is set to `[poll] <question> — <answer1>, <answer2>, ...`.

**Reply context**: `buildReplyContext(ref)` populates `replyTo` fully at ingest time from the `referenced_message` payload included in the gateway event. Reply enrichment via REST is not needed for Discord (unlike Matrix where the SDK doesn't include it): the provider omits `messageSummary`, and the enrichment worker resolves the `reply_contexts` row from this ingest snapshot (falling back to the stored target event on a message-cache miss) — see §7a step 2.

**Emoji observations** — `extractEmojiObservations(content)`: captures `<:name:id>` and `<a:name:id>` pairs from the raw content string, deduplicated by id, and returned as `{name, id, animated}` triples. The provider calls `runtime.emojiCatalog.observeEmoji(obs.id, obs.name, obs.animated)` for each triple at ingest time.

**`DiscordNormalizeResult`** is the return type of `normalizeDiscordMessage`: `{ inbound: InboundChatEvent, emojiObservations }`. Embeds delivered inside the MESSAGE_CREATE payload are attached to `inbound.event.linkPreviews` (`sourceKind: "discord_embed"`).

### Provider (`src/discord/provider.ts`)

`DiscordProvider` implements `IChatProvider`. One discord.js `Client` instance is created per configured account at `start()` time; reconnect and WebSocket resume are managed by discord.js.

**Capabilities**:

| Capability | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `maxMessageChars` | 2000 | Discord API limit |
| `maxAttachmentsPerMessage` | 10 | Discord API limit |
| `formatting` | `"markdown"` | |
| `typing` | `true` | |
| `reactions` | `true` | `messageReactionAdd/Remove/RemoveAll/RemoveEmoji` gateway events routed to `host.onReaction`/`host.onBulkReactionClear` |
| `reactionKinds` | `["unicode","custom"]` | No text-shortcode reactions on Discord |
| `customEmojiScoped` | `true` | Guild-scoped sendability |
| `edits` | `true` | |
| `deletes` | `true` | |
| `threads` | `true` | |
| `pins` | `true` | |
| `pollCreate` | `true` | `DiscordChannelClient.createPoll` |
| `pollVote` | `false` | No bot vote endpoint in Discord API |
| `history` | `true` | `DiscordHistoryClient` returned by `history()` |
| `threadHistory` | `"separate"` | Each thread is its own channel with its own `/messages` history; gap backfetch (§7c) pages every thread as its own unit |
| `mediaUpload` | `false` | Local-file attach is the upload path; no Matrix-style MXC |
| `encrypted` | `false` | |
| `linkPreviews` | `"none"` | Embeds are handled at ingest, not via provider API |
| `singleAttachmentPerMessage` | `false` | Discord allows up to 10 per message |
| `membershipRoster` | computed | `true` iff any account has `member_intent = true` in config |
| `voiceMessages` | `true` | ogg/opus send via ffmpeg + 256-sample waveform; `as_voice` wired in `send()` |

**`accountIds()`** returns `Object.keys(this.config.accounts ?? {})` — config keys, not the runtime map — so it works correctly before `start()` is called (e.g. for enrichment pool registration).

**`ownsUserId(id)`**: `/^\d+$/.test(id)` — any all-digit string is treated as a Discord snowflake. Used by the budget predicate `isUserIdentity`.

**`channelClient(target)`**: returns a `DiscordChannelClient` when the target resolves to a running account. Resolves `guildId` from the discord.js channel cache (`runtime.client.channels.cache`), with a fallback guild-cache scan. Returns `undefined` for foreign targets (unknown accountId, channel not resolvable).

**`enrichment(accountId)`**: returns an `EnrichmentCapabilities` object when the account is running. `downloadMedia` throws (Discord attachments always have `remoteUrl`, so the enrichment worker never calls this path). `messageSummary` is **omitted** (reply context is fully populated at ingest from `referenced_message`; the worker resolves the target from the event's `replyTo` snapshot, then from the stored timeline event — §7a step 2 — so no REST lookup is made and a target that is quoted in the payload or already stored never degrades to a stub). `resolveLinkPreviews` is absent (triggers `DirectLinkPreviewClient` fallback in the worker — see §7a). `memberInfo` performs a live lookup against the guild member cache: iterates allowed guilds, calls `guild.members.cache.get(userId)`, and returns `nickname ?? globalName ?? username`; returns `{ displayName: undefined }` on cache miss.

**`history(target)`**: returns a `DiscordHistoryClient` for the resolved channel. Used by both `read_messages` (via `DiscordChannelClient.readMessages`, which delegates to the same client) and the initial-activation backfill (`runInitialBackfill` in `app.ts` calls `provider.history?.(target)` for non-Matrix providers).

**Gateway intents**: `Guilds`, `GuildMessages`, `DirectMessages`, `MessageContent`, `GuildMessageReactions`, `DirectMessageReactions`, `GuildExpressions`; plus `GuildMembers` iff any account has `member_intent = true`.

**Cache limits** (discord.js `makeCache`): `MessageManager / GuildMessageManager / DMMessageManager: {maxSize: 50}`, `GuildMemberManager: {maxSize: member_intent ? 200 : 0}`, `GuildEmojiManager: {maxSize: 500}`, `ThreadManager: {maxSize: 200}`. The timeline store is the source of truth for history; the client cache only needs what thread-parent resolution, member lookup, and emoji resolution require.

**Inbound pipeline** (spec §8):

1. `messageCreate` → `handleMessageCreate` → `extractMessageData` → `normalizeDiscordMessage` → `host.onEvent`. Embeds already present in the payload ride on `inbound.event.linkPreviews`; the timeline store (`Storage.insertIngestLinkPreviews`, called from `appendIfMissing` / `appendTimelineEvent`) writes them as `discord_embed` `link_previews` rows **in the same write transaction as the event row**. This is what satisfies the `link_previews.event_id → timeline_events(id)` FK: the pipeline's `handleInbound` yields to the activation gate before it enqueues the event insert, so any preview write enqueued separately by the provider right after `host.onEvent` returned would land on the single-writer queue ahead of the event row and fail with `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed` (the pre-fix behaviour on active timelines).
2. Trigger-hold (spec §8.4): the Matrix provider's hold (§6 "Trigger hold"), same semantics (`applyTriggerHold`). The reply-to-bot trigger is resolved first, so a reply trigger takes the hold too. With `trigger_hold_ms > 0` every message is emitted at once without its trigger, so it is stored as it arrives (its ingest embeds with it, on `event.linkPreviews`); a trigger opens a hold keyed by timeline **and sender**, and every further message of that sender in that timeline joins the held trigger's `groupedEventIds` (a trigger-bearing one resets the timer, bounded at `4 × trigger_hold_ms` from the hold's `holdStartedAt`, `TRIGGER_HOLD_MAX_MULTIPLIER = 4`; a non-triggering one rides the timer). The flush delivers the trigger once, rooted on the hold's first message, with `holdEndedAt`. Another sender's trigger opens its own hold, never replaces a held one (before, the hold was keyed by channel and kept only the newest trigger, so earlier held messages were never stored).
3. Reply-to-bot: after trigger detection, if no trigger was found but the message is a reply, `host.resolveReplyTrigger` is called with the referenced message id; if it confirms the reply target is a bot message, the trigger is injected before `host.onEvent`.

**Reply context extraction** (`extractMessageData`): gated on `message.reference?.messageId` alone (`message.mentions.repliedUser` can be null on partial payloads and must not suppress context). The referenced message body is read from `message.channel.messages.cache.get(messageId)` — the channel message cache (discord.js v14 does not expose `.referencedMessage` as a field). On cache miss, a stub is built from `message.mentions.repliedUser` if available (provides author info but empty body and zero timestamp).

**Edit vs late-embed discrimination** (spec §8.3): `MESSAGE_UPDATE` fires for both user edits and Discord's async embed resolution. The discriminator is `message.editedTimestamp !== null`:
- `editedTimestamp !== null` → user edit: normalize and route as `InboundChatEvent` with `edit: { targetExternalId: messageId }`. Trigger is always cleared on edits.
- `editedTimestamp === null` → late-embed: call `callbacks.mergeLateEmbeds` with the new embed previews. The event is NOT routed to `host.onEvent` — doing so would re-trigger the agent (double-processing hazard).

**Deletes**: `messageDelete` constructs a synthetic content-less `CanonicalChatEvent` with a `nanoid`-suffixed id (timestamped at receipt: the gateway event carries no deletion time) and routes it via the same `edit: { targetExternalId, deleted: true }` marker that Matrix redactions use. The stored message is marked deleted and keeps its content (§6 "Message edits"; before, a deletion wiped the stored body). Discord does not say who deleted a message, so the marker has no deleter and late input takes the deletion as the sender's. A message still in a trigger hold (`trigger_hold_ms > 0`; stored already, since the hold emits every message at once) leaves every open hold of its timeline that holds it (`dropFromTriggerHold`): its id leaves the held group; when it was the held trigger's root message, the first remaining part becomes the root; a hold left with no part is dropped, so a deleted held trigger starts no session even with late input off. The deletion itself marks the stored message like any other. A bulk deletion (`messageDeleteBulk`, a purge) is the same deletion once per message (`handleMessageDeleteBulk`: each id through `handleMessageDelete`, skipping what the account does not handle, one failure not stopping the rest), with no deleter either.

**Send** (`send(target, message)`):
- `@username` mention resolution (`resolveMentionTokens`): before chunking, the outbound body is scanned for `@username` tokens (word-boundary; `@everyone`/`@here` always skipped). Each unique token is resolved against the guild member cache first, then via `guild.members.search({ query, limit: 10 })` REST on cache miss. DMs resolve only the DM recipient. Resolved tokens are replaced with `<@id>` Discord mention syntax in the body, and the user ids are added to `allowed_mentions.users`. Unresolved tokens pass through unchanged as plain text.
- Custom emoji rendering (`EmojiCatalog.renderShortcodes`): `:name:` shortcodes that resolve in the channel's sendable set are rewritten to `<:name:id>` / `<a:name:id>` markup (Discord does not resolve shortcodes for bots). `editMessage` applies the same rendering.
- Body is chunked at 2000 characters using `chunkMarkdownText` (fence-aware) on the resolved body.
- `reply: { messageReference: target.replyToId, failIfNotExists: false }` on the first chunk.
- `allowed_mentions: { parse: [], users: [...resolvedIds], repliedUser: Boolean(replyRef) }` — `parse: []` prevents automatic @everyone/role pings; `users` carries only ids from `@username` resolution above; `repliedUser` controls whether the replied-to user receives a ping.
- Attachments (local-path files) are attached to the last chunk only (or the single chunk if there is only one).
- Returns a `DeliveryReceipt` with `externalId` pointing to the first sent message and `externalIds` listing all chunk message ids.

**Typing** (`setTyping`): starts a per-timeline refresh **chain** that calls `channel.sendTyping()` and re-schedules itself every `TYPING_REFRESH_MS = 8000 ms` (Discord clears the indicator after ~10 s). The chain is registered in `typingChains` from the moment `setTyping(true)` accepts it — including while the first REST send is still in flight — and the chain object's identity doubles as its cancellation token: `setTyping(false)` / `stop()` delete the entry, and the refresh loop re-checks map identity after every await before sending or rescheduling, so a stop landing mid-send can never be outrun by that send scheduling one more refresh (which would orphan the loop and leave the bot "typing" forever). Repeated `setTyping(true)` while a chain is live is a **no-op**: the runner's 1 s keepalive is tuned for matrix-sdk (which dedups internally), but Discord has none, so without the dedup every poll would be a real REST send; one chain per timeline is all the indicator needs, and if a send fails the chain deregisters itself and the next keepalive tick revives it.

**Guild allowlist**: per-account `guilds` config field (string array) restricts which guild ids the account listens to. DMs are allowed separately via `dm_enabled` (default `true`). The `isAllowed` filter applies on every inbound event before any processing.

### `DiscordProviderCallbacks`

Four callbacks are injected at `DiscordProvider` construction time (not via `IChatProvider.start`) because the storage layer is initialized before the providers map is built in `app.ts`:

- `mergeLateEmbeds(provider, externalId, timelineKey, previews)` — upserts late-embed link preview rows for an already-stored event. Called by `handleMessageUpdate` when `editedTimestamp === null`.
- `upsertUserIdentity(input)` — called from `handleMessageCreate` (for every inbound message author) and from the `guildMemberUpdate` listener (when `member_intent = true`). The call is fire-and-forget (`void … .catch(() => {})`); failures are non-fatal.
- `setChannelMetadata(timelineKey, meta)` — called from `handleMessageCreate` to upsert `display_name`, `server_id`, and `server_name` into `room_metadata`. For guild channels, `display_name = "#channel-name (Guild Name)"`, `server_id = guild.id`, `server_name = guild.name`. For DMs, `server_id` and `server_name` are omitted. `resolved_at` is bumped only when `display_name`, `server_id`, or `server_name` actually change (SQL CASE change-guard), so the hot per-message path avoids spurious writes when nothing has changed. Also fire-and-forget.
- `onSelfResolved?(accountId, selfId)` — optional; called from the `ready` handler after login completes and `readyClient.user.id` is known. `app.ts` uses this to mutate the pre-declared `botSelfIdsForLimits` Set and `gapBackfetchSelfIds` Map (declared before the providers IIFE so mutations are visible to downstream consumers).

### Emoji catalog (`src/discord/emoji-catalog.ts`)

`EmojiCatalog` is a per-account in-memory store for Discord custom emoji. It maintains three maps:

- **`guildEmoji`**: `Map<guildId, Map<emojiId, CatalogEmojiInfo>>` — guild-scoped emoji. Populated at READY from every allowed guild's emoji list, updated on `guildEmojisUpdate` and `guildCreate`, cleared on `guildDelete`.
- **`appEmoji`**: `Map<emojiId, CatalogEmojiInfo>` — application emoji (sendable in any guild). Populated at READY via `GET /applications/{id}/emojis` iff `application_id` is configured.
