Gap markers (`<omitted posts="N" files="M"/>`) are emitted between non-adjacent shown posts, before the first shown post when it is not at index 0 (leading gap), and after the last shown post up to `postCount-1` (trailing gap). File counts in gaps use `filesBefore` on the post node when available, otherwise approximate from the captured post list. `image_block="true"` appears only on files the context builder actually sent as image blocks in the current build (`AttachmentMeta.isImageBlock`, set by the yotsuba lane in the upgrading trigger's own session), so the same processed file renders with its path and caption but no `image_block` in later contexts; `auto="off"` marks stored (unprocessed) files. A video file's caption is the original's (video lane), the storyboard's only as a fallback. The `replies` attribute is omitted when `replies = 0`; reply counts and `replyNos` are computed from the full thread at capture. In an upgraded post-link rendering the linked post also carries the `[N replies: >>a >>b shown; M more not shown]` line. Cross-thread references stay inline in the text, annotated `(other thread)`. The headline post's text is capped at `upgrade.headlineChars` characters in trigger rendering, with a `[… N more characters]` suffix when cut. Board `<board code="/g/">` uses just the board code; `<thread board="/g/ - Technology">` uses the full label. `discord_embed` rows are suppressed when the same event has a yotsuba row for the same canonical URL (`filterYotsubaSupersededPreviews`). Gone rows render as a self-closing `<link_preview kind="4chan" status="gone" .../>`.

- **Persistence.** No new tables. One `link_previews` row per ref: `source_kind = "yotsuba"`, `site_name = "4chan"`, canonical URL, `payload_json = YotsubaPreviewPayload` (v1). Associated files go in `media_assets` with `role = "preview_media"` or `"reply_preview_media"`, `link_preview_id` set. Storage helpers: `getYotsubaPreviewByUrl(url, timelineKey?)` (reply reuse — scoped to the event's timeline when `timelineKey` is supplied), `getYotsubaPreviewsForTriggerGroup` (upgrade/builder), `writeYotsubaUpgrade` (atomic write).

**Code name.** "Yotsuba" is the internal and code name; prose-facing surfaces say "4chan". No identifier in the codebase uses "fourchan" or "4chan" — all symbols, filenames, config keys, and log labels use "yotsuba".

**Feature gate.** `[features].yotsuba = true` (default off) gates both the link-preview enrichment stage and the tool. The gate wires through `FEATURE_TOOLS` in `src/app.ts` (`yotsuba → ["yotsuba"]`). `createYotsubaSubsystem()` (also in `app.ts`) returns `undefined` when the feature is off; the enrichment pool and the tool registry skip initialization on `undefined`.

**`src/net/paced-limiter.ts` — PacedLimiter.** A generic paced request limiter extracted from `DanbooruRateLimiter`. Adds two priority classes (`interactive` / `background`) backed by separate FIFO queues drained in order: interactive first, background second, unclassed (Danbooru compat) last. The core algorithm is unchanged: start instants are reserved **synchronously** at acquire time (concurrent acquirers claim distinct slots, never start at once), and slot release uses **direct handoff** (the freed slot is transferred to the head waiter without decrementing the in-flight count, so no fresh caller can double-grant it). `DanbooruRateLimiter` now `extends PacedLimiter` for full backward compatibility; its unclassed `run()` calls travel the unclassed queue path.

**`src/yotsuba/url.ts` — URL recognition.** `YOTSUBA_BASE_HOSTS` (`boards.4chan.org`, `boards.4channel.org`, `4chan.org`, `www.4chan.org`). `isYotsubaHost(hostname, extras)` base-domain matching with subdomain tolerance and lookalike rejection. `parseYotsubaUrl(input, extras, siteBase)` returns `ParsedYotsubaRef | null` — a distributive union `Omit<YotsubaThreadRef, "bodyIndex"> | Omit<YotsubaBoardRef, "bodyIndex">` that preserves the `kind` discriminant for narrowing; a `#p` anchor equal to the thread number is normalized away. `extractYotsubaRefs(bodyText)` scans a message body for URLs, deduping by `(board, threadNo, postNo)`. `stripYotsubaUrls(bodyText)` removes all recognized 4chan URLs (for Synapse preview suppression). `parseToolInput(input)` accepts bare numbers, `>>N`, `>>>/b/N`, and `/b/` board codes for tool call tolerance.

**`src/yotsuba/types.ts` — API and persisted types.** Tolerant API types (`ApiBoard`, `ApiPost`, `ApiThread`, `ApiCatalogPage`, `ApiBoardPage`). Persisted payload types (`YotsubaPostNode`, `YotsubaPostFile`, `YotsubaPreviewPayload`, `YotsubaPreviewThread`). `YotsubaPostNode` carries `filesBefore?: number` — count of files in all posts before this one in the thread (for exact gap file counts in rendering). Raw and resolved config shapes (`RawYotsubaConfig`, `ResolvedYotsubaConfig` with sub-structs for enrichment, preview, and tool). `resolveYotsubaConfig(raw?)` applies defaults (API base `https://a.4cdn.org`, media base `https://i.4cdn.org`, 10 s freshness, 1000 ms pacing, etc.).

**`src/yotsuba/markup.ts` — Comment HTML → plain text.** `convertComment(html)` converts the `com` field from the 4chan API to plain text plus `{ quotes, deadQuotes?, crossQuotes? }`. Tag-by-tag conversion: `<br>` → newline, `<wbr>` removed, same-thread quotelinks (`href="#p123"`) → `>>N` + collected in `quotes`, dead quotelinks → `>>N` + collected in `deadQuotes`, cross-thread quotelinks (`href="/b/thread/456"`) → `>>>/b/456` + collected in `crossQuotes`, greentext → text preserved with `>`, spoilers → `[spoiler]…[/spoiler]`, prettyprint code → fenced ` ``` `, mod text → `[mod: …]`, entities decoded, all other tags stripped. `annotateQuotes(text, shownNos, opNo, deadQuoteNos)` adds render-time annotations: `(OP)`, `(not shown)`, `(deleted)`, `(other thread)`.

**`src/yotsuba/graph.ts` — Thread graph.** `buildThreadGraph(nodes)` assigns sequential `index` values, validates same-thread quotes (only existing posts), builds `backlinks` (reverse map). Helpers: `quotedPosts`, `repliesTo`, `latestReplies` (skips OP), `repliedToPosts`, `mostRepliedPosts` (threshold-based, not a hard cap; excludes OP), `searchPosts` (AND over term array), `ancestorChain` (follows first quote per post, max depth 3), `gapBetween(fromIndex, toIndex)`, `gapToEnd(lastIndex)` — all take 0-based thread indices, not post numbers.

**`src/yotsuba/view.ts` — Post-view engine.** Pure and deterministic: given a `ThreadGraph`, a `Slot[]`, a `ViewBudget`, and a token-cost function, `runView()` returns a `ViewResult` with placed posts in thread order interleaved with `GapMarker` values and trailing-gap metadata. Step 1 deduplicates slots by post number (highest-precedence role wins). Step 2 sorts by priority, then thread index. Step 3 places posts: pinned slots always placed (never budget-limited); non-pinned posts subject to `maxPosts` and `maxTextTokens`; `excerptFallback: true` retries a `full` slot as `excerpt` when it doesn't fit; `contiguous: true` stops at the first non-fitting non-pinned post. Step 4 allocates the `maxFiles` attachment budget. Step 5 emits items in thread order. Step 6 computes the trailing gap. `ROLE_PRECEDENCE` order: `linked > op > replied_to > reply > most_replied > match > latest > context`.

**`src/yotsuba/format.ts` — Rendering vocabulary.** Shared XML helpers used by both the context renderer and the tool: `threadOpenTag`, `postElement`, `fileElement`, `omittedElement`, `backlinksLine`, `renderViewContent` (assembles a full view's inner XML from a `ViewResult`), `compactLine` (flat text for compact zone), `ftsDescription` (flat text for FTS indexing), `boardLabel`.

**`src/yotsuba/client.ts` — HTTP client.** `YotsubaClient` with two `PacedLimiter` instances (API lane: 1000 ms / 1 in-flight; media lane: 250 ms / 2 in-flight). In-memory cache: up to 64 entries / 32 MiB, LRU eviction by insertion order. Freshness windows: boards 24 h; thread/catalog/page 10 s. Conditional GET with `If-Modified-Since` / 304. Negative cache for 404 (10 min TTL). Single-flight via a `Map<path, Promise>` registry: concurrent requests for the same path coalesce. Public API: `boards(cls?)`, `catalog(board, cls?)`, `page(board, n, cls?)`, `thread(board, no, cls?)` (null on 404), `fetchFile(board, fileRef, cls?)`. Factory: `YotsubaClient.create(config, httpProxyUrl?, fetchClient?)`.

**`src/media/storyboard.ts` — Storyboard helper.** `buildStoryboard(inputPath, opts?)` produces a 2×2 JPEG tile sampling frames at 12%, 37%, 62%, 87% of a video's duration. Uses `loadFfmpeg()` and `ffprobe` from `src/media/video.ts`. Multi-input ffmpeg approach: four separate `-ss` inputs, complex filtergraph scales each cell to `cellPx × cellPx` (with black padding to preserve aspect), tiles 2×2. Returns null when ffmpeg is absent, ffprobe fails, or the command times out.

**`src/media/pdf.ts` — PDF text extraction.** `extractPdfText(data, opts?)` loads a PDF buffer via `unpdf` (pure-JS pdfjs-dist wrapper, no canvas/native required) and extracts plain text page-by-page. Options: `maxChars` (default 8000) — stops extraction when the character cap is reached; `pages` — a "start-end" or "n" range string. Returns `PdfExtractResult`: `{ text, totalPages, fromPage, toPage, truncated, noTextLayer }`. `noTextLayer` is set when the document has pages but no extractable text (scanned image PDFs). `parsePageRange(rangeStr, totalPages)` converts a range string to `{ from, to }` (1-based, clamped).

**Config schema.** `FeaturesSchema` gains `yotsuba: Type.Optional(Type.Boolean())`. A `YotsubaSchema` TypeBox block covers `[yotsuba]`, `[yotsuba.enrichment]`, `[yotsuba.preview]`, and `[yotsuba.tool]`. `AppConfigSchema` gains `yotsuba: Type.Optional(YotsubaSchema)`. `config/00-defaults.toml` documents all defaults (the resolved values for every omitted key). Cross-field validation in `app.ts`: `page_tokens <= page_tokens_max`, `page_tokens_max <= agent.tools.result_max_tokens` (when that cap is on), `catalog_default_limit <= catalog_max_limit`, HTTPS `api_base`/`media_base`/`site_base`, bare-hostname `extra_hosts`.

**Skill.** `templates/features/yotsuba/skills/yotsuba/SKILL.md` (tools: `["yotsuba"]`). Trigger-first description: fires on boards.4chan.org links, or requests mentioning boards or generals.

---

## 8. Agent Sessions

### Core concept

When a trigger fires, an ephemeral **agent session** is spawned. It receives the timeline as carefully assembled context, does work, produces output, and terminates. Its internal state (tool calls, thinking, intermediate context) is discarded. Only the messages it sent persist on the timeline.

There is no persistent agent. There is a timeline, and there are ephemeral sessions that read from it and write to it.

### Session lifecycle

1. **Create** — `SessionManager.createPlaceholder()` → status `"created"`, id `s-{nanoid(10)}`; also fire-and-forget inserts the durable `agent_sessions` row (status `created`). The insert persists the trigger metadata **including the trigger sender's identity** (`trigger_sender_id` + `trigger_sender_display_name`, resolved like `buildSessionTools` does: `trigger.triggeredBy` when present, else the event sender) so a manual resume can rebuild the same sender-bound tool set from the row alone (see "Session parking & manual resume").
2. **Run** — `SessionRunner.run()`:
   - Set typing indicator with a 1-second keepalive interval (refreshed until session completes). The interval must stay well inside matrix-sdk's `(TYPING_NOTICE_RESEND_TIMEOUT=3s, TYPING_NOTICE_TIMEOUT=4s)` window: the homeserver expires the indicator 4s after each notice, and matrix-sdk dedups repeat notices until 3s have elapsed, so a short poll lets its own resend land just past 3s — comfortably before the 4s expiry. A keepalive at/near 4s lands the refresh *after* the server already dropped the indicator (interval drift + latency), which makes typing flicker on/off and appear only sparingly.
   - Prompt the agent with the **frozen final user turn** — the rich trigger group built once at creation (see "Frozen context" below), passed back by the factory as `finalTurn`. It becomes the first turn of the transcript; the runner does not echo the raw trigger body as a separate message.
   - Wait for agent idle
   - Check terminal condition; if not met, force-continue (up to `forced_completion_retries`)
   - The runner never sends messages itself — all delivery goes through the `send_message` tool
3. **Complete/Discard** — status transitions to `"completed"` or `"discarded"`, session evicted from all maps, trigger coordinator notified (may dequeue next trigger)
4. **Record turn** — a completed chat-lane or proactive session that did tool work then runs one more harness-prompted turn on the same agent to write its session record (§8i), registered in flight before the timeline slot is released and running after it. The row is already `completed`; the turn only appends to its transcript.

`SessionManager` owns the durable row's **status lifecycle** for chat sessions: `createPlaceholder` inserts `created`; `markRunning`/`markCompleted`/`markDiscarded` fire-and-forget the status + timestamp updates through the single-writer queue (synchronous `void` methods; failures are error-logged and never block or crash a live session — in-memory state is the source of truth, and boot healing covers crashes). FIFO ordering of the write queue guarantees the insert settles before any status update. `markCompleted(id, { noReply })` records `no_reply`; `markDiscarded(id, { error })` records the error. `SessionManager` takes optional `{ storage, logger }` deps — when `storage` is absent (e.g. unit tests) all row writes are skipped. The status set is `created | running | completed | discarded | interrupted | suspended | resuming | failed-resumable`: `interrupted` is set by **startup healing** (`storage.resetStaleSessions()`, called in `app.ts` before `provider.start()`, flips any `running`/`created` row left mid-flight by a prior crash) **and by the operator Stop button** (`SessionManager.interrupt()`, see "Interrupting a session" below) — and an `interrupted` row with viable resume material stays manually resumable from the console (Decision D, see "Session parking & manual resume"); `suspended` is reserved for future pause/resume (see "Appendix: Deferred designs"); `failed-resumable` is the parked state (see "Session parking & manual resume" below — `markFailedResumable` parks + evicts) and `resuming` marks an in-flight resume — set by the console resume's adopted record, and by the **reply-resume** acceptance CAS (`acceptResumeGeneration` flips `completed → resuming` while bumping `resume_generation`; see "Resumable sessions"); startup healing flips a stale `resuming` to `failed-resumable`, never `interrupted`, so a crash mid-resume stays manually resumable.

The session's **content** (frozen snapshot + transcript) is captured separately by the shared `attachSessionCapture` (see "Session capture" below), which is status-agnostic. In `app.ts` the chat path attaches it right after `attachAgent`, calls `flushNow()` on the run promise's `.catch()` (error/abort path) so a pre-`turn_end` failure still captures the transcript, and `detach`es it in the `.finally()`. The summarization worker drives the agent directly (not via `SessionManager`), so it inserts its own `agent_sessions` row inline — with a unique `s-{nanoid(10)}` id per attempt, since retries of one job would otherwise collide on the primary key — sets status `running`/`completed`/`discarded` inline, and reuses `attachSessionCapture` for content. Because the summarization worker inserts directly at `running` (bypassing `created → markRunning`), its `insertAgentSession` passes `startedAt` so the row carries a non-null `started_at` from the outset; the chat path inserts at `created` with no `startedAt` and leaves it null until `markRunning`.

**Status enforcement & timestamps.** The `agent_sessions.status` column carries a `check(status in ('created', 'running', 'completed', 'discarded', 'interrupted', 'suspended', 'resuming', 'failed-resumable'))` constraint (in the genesis `SCHEMA` block), matching the sibling `timeline_events`/`timeline_compaction_state` convention so a typo or raw write cannot persist an out-of-band status (the reserved `suspended` value is included for the future pause/resume path). `started_at` and `completed_at` are **forward-only** (write-once in practice): the lifecycle sets each exactly once (`markRunning`, then `markCompleted`/`markDiscarded`) and never rewinds them — the timestamps record when the session first entered each phase. The status save/update methods (`updateAgentSessionStatus`, `saveAgentSessionSnapshot`, `saveAgentSessionTranscript`) all target `where id = ?`; when that matches zero rows they log a structured warning (method + session id) so a lost write (a missing or deleted row) is visible, but they deliberately do **not** throw — they run on the fire-and-forget single-writer flush path, where throwing could destabilize the queue.

### Parallel sessions

Multiple sessions can run concurrently within the same timeline. Concurrency is bounded per-timeline by config (`max_concurrent`, `max_concurrent_dm`). Each concurrent session:

- Gets the timeline as it stands at creation time
- Gets runtime instructions describing other active sessions
- Operates independently — no shared mutable state
- Sends messages that immediately appear on the timeline

**Claim-and-visible-before-wait (one readiness-wait seam).** A triggered session is *claimed* (synchronously at the accept seam — see "Duplicate-reply mitigation") and *visible-as-running* (in `SessionManager.activeForTimeline`, the source of `<active_sessions>` + the `<coordination>` gate + the proactive eligibility gate) **before** it blocks on anything. The enrichment + caption readiness wait (`awaitTriggerReadiness`) — once the trigger group's slow dependency — lives at a **single seam inside `launchSession`**: after `createPlaceholder → markRunning → attach-claim` (so the session is already visible and its claim attributed) and after the missing-target + budget-admission gates (so a refused session never waits), and before `AgentSessionFactory.create` (so the build still renders an enriched, captioned trigger group). Order: `createPlaceholder → markRunning → attach → target check → budget gate → awaitTriggerReadiness → build`. The reply-resume path mirrors it (`adopt → markRunning → attach → awaitTriggerReadiness → buildResumeTurn`), so a media-bearing reply's appended turn is captioned too. `handleInbound`, the queued-trigger drain, the activation launch, and `spawn_session`/co-reply re-dispatch all funnel through `launchSession`, so each awaits readiness exactly once, after it is visible. Because the wait is now *behind* visibility, a sibling session that builds while this one is mid-captioning sees it in `<active_sessions>` with the `<coordination>` line that explains its `<handled_by_session>` marker — rather than a bare, un-explained marker over an empty active list (the failure spec CLAIM-VISIBILITY-SERIALIZATION fixed). The activation prelude keeps its own `awaitTriggerReadiness` (entangled with the `inactive → pending` bulk-flip ordering); `launchSession`'s internal wait is then a fast no-op the second time through.

### Message steering (interjections)

**Reply-based**: When a user replies (Matrix reply) to a message from a running session, the message is injected into that session via `agent.steer()`. The session sees it as an `<interjection>` wrapped user message. `steerReplyToActiveSession` (`app.ts`) resolves the replied-to message as `target` (it must belong to an active session in the same timeline) and renders the interjection. Because the steer path **bypasses** the trigger path's enrichment-readiness wait + `hydrateEvents`, the raw inbound event's `replyTo` carries only `externalId` — rendering it directly would emit the `[original message unavailable]` placeholder inside `<reply_to>`. Instead, the steer **hydrates `target`** (the same `hydrateEvents` the trigger path uses, pulling captions / media paths from the enrichment side-tables) and fills the reply context (sender, body, timestamp, attachments, linked media, link previews) from it onto a render-only copy of the event, so the injected turn quotes the original message just like a normal trigger would. Independently, the enrichment-pool nudge for the persisted reply row is issued **before** the steer's early return (in `handleInbound`), so the steered event's `reply_contexts` row is still resolved for any later context rebuild / summarization.

**Delegation**: The `delegate_to_session` tool allows one session to route its trigger message into another running session. On successful delegation, the delegating session terminates. If the target session is no longer running, delegation fails and the current session handles it.

**Interjections can carry image pixels (spec FOLLOWUP-FOLDING §3).** `InterjectionMessage` has an optional `imageBlocks?: ImageBlock[]`; `convert.ts`'s `interjection` branch builds the user message via `contentWithImages`, so a steered interjection with image blocks reaches the model as real `{type:"image"}` content rather than degrading to a caption. Two paths produce blocks (both § "Follow-up folding"): a steered **media** follow-up, and an image-bearing **co-reply** — the latter conditioned off the synchronous accept path by a detached `steerCoReplyWithPixels` (the co-reply steer cannot block on async conditioning, so it commits synchronously and finishes off the hot path, re-dispatching as its own session if the owner settled first). This also fixes the pre-existing latent bug where a co-reply that itself carried an image dropped it to a caption. **Both steer paths also mark the conditioned attachment `image_block` on the rendered event** (`ContextBuilder.markEventImageBlocks`, the public wrapper over the trigger-group-scoped `markImageBlocks` that the live `build` / `buildResumeTurn` paths use) so the `<attachment>` renders `image_block="true"` — telling the model the loose vision block and the quoted attachment are one image, instead of a loose block beside a caption-only quote. The mark mutates the event in place, so the steer conditions, marks, and renders the **same** object: `steerFollowUp` reuses its one `hydrated` event, and `steerCoReplyWithPixels` builds its `buildReplyHydratedEvent` once (off the hydrated stored event, so the co-reply's own attachments carry `localPath`) and passes it into `buildCoReplyInterjection` rather than letting that helper rebuild a separate copy.

**Durable interjection record (timeline → session).** The *timeline-originated* steer paths — reply-steer, co-reply, and follow-up (`kind: "reply" | "co-reply" | "follow-up"`) — additionally record the inject as a durable `session_interjections` row (a genesis-`SCHEMA` table, `SESSION_INTERJECTIONS_SCHEMA` in `src/storage/database.ts`; an existing DB that predates it gains it from the idempotent `writer.exec(SCHEMA)` reconcile on open, §7 "Schema versioning & migrations", with no migration step). `SessionManager.steer(sessionId, message, source?)` takes an optional `source` describing the inbound message behind the interjection (its `event_id`/`external_id`, sender, `kind`, and raw `body`); when present **and the inject succeeds**, it writes the row fire-and-forget on the single-writer queue. This mirrors how `createPlaceholder` denormalizes the trigger, extended to the mid-run user messages a session also acts on: the `body` is FTS-indexed (`session_interjections_fts`) so the console sessions search reaches a session by an interjection's text exactly as by its trigger (§11 "Sessions filter"), and the captured `event_id` is the durable backlink the "timeline message → session" debug path follows. The non-timeline injects — the cost-budget warning (§8d) and the `delegate_to_session` tool — pass **no** `source` (they carry no inbound timeline event to link) and are deliberately not recorded.

### Duplicate-reply mitigation

Parallel sessions create two duplicate-reply failure modes: **Case A** — a session cross-replies to a message another running session owns (its trigger); **Case B** — two users react to the same beat ~simultaneously and spawn near-identical twins. Both are addressed by one concept: **a running (or queued) session *claims* the message(s) that triggered it.**

**Claim registry (`SessionClaims`, `src/agent/session-claims.ts`).** A per-timeline, in-memory map from a trigger's Matrix external id → owning session. The decisive property is that a claim is inserted **synchronously at trigger-accept time** in `handleInbound` — immediately after `triggerCoordinator.accept` returns `spawn`/`queued`, before any `await` — so a concurrent inbound handler observes it even during the async gap between accept and the session placeholder's creation in `launchSession` (reusing `SessionManager.activeForTimeline` could not close that gap; the placeholder does not exist yet). The **activation path** claims its first trigger too (`ActivationCoordinator`, injected `addClaim`/`releaseClaim`): right after the prelude's `accept`, before the held-trigger replay, so the first session's message renders a `<handled_by_session>` marker like every other (there is no concurrent-session hazard during activation — later triggers are held and replayed only after this point — so claiming at the end of the prelude rather than at recognition is sufficient). Each claim carries two ids: the trigger's own external id (marker/guard key) and the trigger's `replyTo` external id (the message the trigger itself replied to — the co-target coalescing key). The owning session id is **backfilled** in `launchSession` once the placeholder exists. A claim is **released** when its session settles, via a `SessionManager.onSettle` listener registered in `launchSession` — mirroring how `activeForTimeline` empties, so a finished session stops deterring others. It is **also released on any pre-attribution failure** (`releaseClaimFor`): a throw between accept and `attachSession` — or a launch rejection on the queued-drain / activation / `spawn_session` paths — would otherwise leak the claim un-attributed forever (harmless when un-attributed claims were skipped, but a permanent false-positive once they deter — see read-side consumers). Idempotent: a throw past `attachSession` already released via settle. Queued claims discarded by a drain are dropped in `stop()` (`sessionClaims.clear()`).

**Arrival-order serialization (spec CLAIM-VISIBILITY-SERIALIZATION §4.4).** For two trigger messages M₁ (earlier) then M₂ (later) on the same timeline, M₁'s claim must land — and M₁'s session must become visible in `activeForTimeline` — before M₂ reads either signal, so a later message never observes an earlier one as unclaimed or not-running. The *claim half* holds because no variable-latency / order-breaking `await` precedes the `accept → addClaim` critical section on the active path (`gateInbound` returns `"active"` without yielding; `router.route` resolves strictly FIFO on the single-writer queue; the steer / synthesize / coalesce helpers are synchronous) — a documented, must-preserve invariant at that critical section. The *visible half* holds because `launchSession` reaches `createPlaceholder`/`markRunning` before its (now-internal) readiness wait. As a cheap regression tripwire, `SessionClaims.claim` logs `claim_out_of_order` when a strictly-older `triggerTimestamp` is inserted after a newer one on the same timeline — **advisory only** (never reorders or drops: `origin_server_ts` can tie or skew under the trigger hold; same-externalId re-inserts are excluded and the comparison is strict, so ties never warn). The one *designed* out-of-order inserter — `redispatchCoReply` (deferred co-reply / `spawn_session` replay re-claims its original, older trigger after newer ones have landed) — passes a `redispatch` flag through `addClaim` → `claim` to **suppress** the warn, so it is structurally excluded rather than left for operators to filter; the active and activation paths never pass it and remain genuine ordering points.

The registry backs three read-side consumers and one write-side fix:

1. **Co-target coalescing (write-side, Case B; §5).** In `handleInbound`, between the existing reply-steer and the spawn decision: a new reply whose target equals a running session's *trigger's own reply-target* (`coTargetClaim` hit) and falls within `agent.sessions.coalesce_window_ms` is **steered into that session** as a self-explaining `<interjection reason="co-reply">` instead of spawning a twin (`coalesceCoTargetReply`). The window (default 60 s) bounds it so only near-simultaneous reactions merge; shared-reply-target (not bare proximity) keeps the independent questions of Case A from wrongly merging. This generalizes reply-steer: that path is the special case where the target *is* the running session's own authored message. `coalesce_window_ms` is **optional**; unset → coalescing is **off** (returns at the `disabled` exit). `00-defaults.toml` ships it commented out (off by default), so a deployment that wants coalescing sets it in any config layer; the deep config merge (Deployment note, §"Configuration loading") then carries it through. **Observability:** every declined/non-applicable exit of `coalesceCoTargetReply` other than "not a reply" logs `co_target_not_coalesced` with a `reason` (`disabled` / `no_sibling` / `outside_window` / `no_hydration_target` / `owner_settling`), so a "spawned a twin instead of coalescing" decision is diagnosable from logs — the silent returns previously left it invisible.

   **Deferred coalescing (spec DEFERRED-COALESCING).** A co-target match is only *steerable* once its owning session is live, but the owner may still be in its accept→launch window, queued, or building its context (the `attachSession → attachAgent` gap). Matching only steerable owners left the headline Case B race open: a reply (or any enrichment-bearing message) keeps its owner un-attributed during `awaitTriggerReadiness` (up to 30 s), so a second co-reply arriving in that window found nothing and spawned a twin anyway. So `coTargetClaim` returns the first match **regardless of attribution**, and `coalesceCoTargetReply` decides: steer now (owner live); **defer** (owner un-attributed, or attributed but still in its build window — `coTargetOwnerSteerableSoon`), parking the reply in `pendingCoReplies` keyed by the owner trigger's external id and suppressing its spawn; or fall through to a normal spawn (owner settling/gone — a session built after it settles sees its already-sent replies, the content-level deterrent). A parked reply is drained the moment its owner goes live (`launchSession`, after `attachAgent`, steers it in). If the owner is **abandoned before going live** (the missing-target / factory-failed early returns, which route through evict→`fireSettle`; or a pre-`attachSession` throw caught in `handleInbound`/`spawnCoReplySession`), the parked replies are **re-dispatched as normal triggers** (`redispatchCoReply`) so they are never dropped. Parked replies are cleared on shutdown drain.

   **Coalesce→claim is await-free.** The owner reservation that closes Case B is the *claim itself*: the span from the `coalesceCoTargetReply` decision (which reads `coTargetClaim` keyed on the trigger's `replyTo` external id) through `triggerCoordinator.accept` to `addClaim` runs with **no event-loop yield**. `resolveTriggerGroup` (the one `await` formerly sitting between the coalesce check and the claim) is therefore performed **after** accept+claim, not before — it only mutates `inbound.trigger.groupedEventIds` / persists the group, which neither `accept` (it tests `inbound.trigger` truthiness, already established) nor `addClaim`/`coalesceCoTargetReply` consume; the grouped ids are read only later by `awaitTriggerReadiness` and the launch, all of which follow the claim. Were that yield left in place, two **distinct** replies to the *same* target could both pass coalesce — neither having claimed yet — and both spawn (the send-time `isClaimedByOther` guard keys on each trigger's *own* external id, so it cannot catch co-target siblings). The unfreeze replay burst of the startup gap backfetch (§7c), which re-enters `handleInbound` for a room's whole buffered live tail, made that window easy to hit; keeping the coalesce→claim span synchronous makes the first sibling's claim visible to the second.

2. **`spawn_session` tool (`src/tools/spawn-session.ts`) — the inverse of `delegate_to_session`.** A coalesced co-reply is retained (`coReplyInbounds`, keyed by external id, scoped to the session it was folded into). If the session judges it warrants independent handling, `spawn_session` re-dispatches that inbound through the normal spawn path (accept + claim + launch). Unlike `delegate_to_session`, the calling session does **not** terminate — it spun *off* a sibling. A concurrency miss queues like any trigger; a full queue returns an error so the session handles it inline.

3. **`<handled_by_session>` render marker (read-side, Case A; §9 context assembly).** Reflects claims at *build* time. **Un-attributed (queued / pre-launch) claims are surfaced too** (review #4, matching spec §3.1's queued-deterrence intent): such a claim has no session id yet, so the marker renders `pending="true"` instead of `id="s-…"` — the message is still flagged "another session will answer this," it just isn't nameable yet. This matters most in DMs, where a single-slot timeline (`max_concurrent_dm = 1`) makes queueing the norm; without it a queued trigger's message could be freely re-answered. Safe because a leaked un-attributed claim can no longer persist (release-on-pre-attribution-failure, above), so a pending marker never becomes a permanent false-positive.

4. **Live `send_message` reply guard (read-side, Case A backstop; §6).** `send_message` (built with an `isClaimedByOther` closure over the registry + this session's id) refuses to reply (`is_reply` + `reply_to_id`) to a message claimed by another session — a **live** lookup at send time, so it catches the residual the frozen marker structurally cannot: a sibling that started *after* this session's context was built. Un-attributed claims deter here too (review #4): the redirect names the owning session when known, else describes it generically ("a session that's starting up"). The error is a non-terminating redirect (names the alternatives: send without `is_reply`, or it's already covered), not a wall, and fires on exactly one mechanical signal (`reply_to_id`) so false positives are near-zero. Inline addressing without a reply marker stays the marker + coordination line's job.

The marker and guard are **complementary, not redundant** — the marker covers "claimed before my build, addressed any which way"; the guard covers "claimed after my build, at the reply chokepoint."

**Content: the duplicate-send check.** Neither stops two parallel sessions from *saying* the same thing (one sent a reply the other had not seen when it drafted its own). The output gate's `duplicate` check does (§8j "Duplicate sends", off by default): at every send it compares the draft with the messages the same agent's other sessions posted to the target channel since this session last saw it, and a repeat, a re-answer or a contradiction is sent back to the agent to rewrite.

### Interrupting a session

An operator can stop a running session from the console (the Stop button, §11 / §13). `SessionManager.interrupt(sessionId)` is the single entry point:

1. **Gate on run-in-progress (not `agent.signal`)** — returns `false` unless the session is `running` *and* has an explicit **run-in-progress** flag set. The `SessionRunner` sets this flag for the *whole* duration of `run()` (via `SessionManager.runLifecycle(id).markRunInProgress()` on entry, cleared in its `finally`). This is deliberately NOT gated on `agent.signal !== undefined`: `agent.signal` is defined only during an active `prompt()` and is transiently `undefined` in the **inter-turn gap** between forced-completion turns (after `waitForIdle()` returns, before the next `forceCompletion()` issues a fresh prompt). The session is genuinely mid-`run()` in that window, so a Stop landing there must be honored — gating on `agent.signal` would spuriously return "not running" (the inter-turn-gap 409 bug). (`isAgentLive`, used by the SSE liveness check, still gates on `agent.signal` — it answers a different question: "is there an active run to stream events from right now?")
2. **Mark `interrupted` first** — sets the in-memory status, the run-lifecycle `interrupted` flag (the runner's loop-break signal, next point), and fire-and-forget persists the status *before* aborting, so the run's natural settlement defers to it.
3. **Clear pending queues, then `agent.abort()`** — `interrupt()` calls `agent.clearAllQueues()` (guarded by `hasQueuedMessages()`) so no queued steering/follow-up message survives to re-prompt the agent, then `agent.abort()` (only when a signal is currently present) to abort the in-flight LLM call / tool execution via pi-agent-core's run `AbortController`. An aborted run **resolves** (it does not reject): pi-agent-core appends a synthetic assistant message with `stopReason: "aborted"` and emits `agent_end`.
4. **State-based loop break (authoritative)** — the `SessionRunner` force-completion loop breaks on the session's **interrupt state** (`runLifecycle.isInterrupted()`), not on message content. This is the authoritative termination signal: even if an in-flight turn finished streaming a hair before Stop landed and resolved *normally* (`stopReason:"stop"`, not `"aborted"`), the loop still terminates instead of issuing another `forceCompletion()` turn. The `wasAborted` tail-scan (it scans the recent assistant-message tail, not only the final message, for any `stopReason:"aborted"`) remains as a robust fast path / fallback for paths with no lifecycle wired (e.g. the summarization worker). The SSE stream closes on the `agent_end` so the console flips to the persisted terminal record.
5. **No eviction here** — `interrupt()` deliberately does *not* evict: `abort()` unwinds asynchronously and the SSE stream still needs the live agent ref to forward `agent_end`. Eviction happens once, from whichever terminal handler the settling run reaches — `markCompleted`/`markDiscarded`, which both **no-op the status write but still evict** when they find the session already `interrupted`. This is the status-precedence rule: `interrupted` wins over the run's own completion/discard outcome.

### Explicit send contract

The runner has no implicit send path. All message delivery goes through the `send_message` tool. The agent's text output is treated as internal scratchpad — it is never forwarded to users.

A turn is **terminally valid** when the last assistant message satisfies one of:

1. **`NO_REPLY`** — the concatenated text content (after trim) is exactly `NO_REPLY`. The agent chose silence.
2. **`send_message` tool call** — the last assistant message contains a `send_message` tool call. This happens when the tool returns `terminate: true` (driven by the required `final` parameter), which stops the agent loop immediately after tool execution.

Anything else — bare text, empty messages, tool calls that aren't `send_message` — is not terminally valid and triggers force-continuation.

Every ending is also reported to the session's output gate (`SessionRunnerOptions.endings`, §8j): a `NO_REPLY` text ending before the runner breaks, forced-completion exhaustion before the runner gives up, so a judged refusal at the ending can redo the turn. Interrupted and aborted runs are not reported.

### The `final` parameter on `send_message`

`send_message` requires a `final` boolean — there is **no default**. The agent must decide on every send whether the message ends its turn, exactly as it must for `is_reply`. When `final: true`, the tool result includes `terminate: true`, which stops the agent loop immediately — no wasted second turn; the common case (single reply) is a single LLM turn. Note: the framework requires ALL tool calls in a batch to return `terminate: true` for the loop to stop. If `send_message` is called alongside other tools in the same turn, `terminate` only fires if every other tool also terminates.

`final` was made required rather than defaulting to `true` because a silent default is a footgun in both directions: a default of `true` silently ends multi-step work when the agent forgets `final: false` (e.g. it sends a "let me go look…" progress message before a browser/tool sequence and the turn dies — a *silent, lossy* premature end with no recovery), while a default of `false` biases the bot chattier and lets forgotten ends surface a spurious extra message. Requiring the field keeps the terse one-send-ends-the-turn bias (continuing is an explicit `final: false` opt-in) while converting a forgotten value into a loud, safe TypeBox validation error — nothing is sent, the agent re-calls with `final` set, and no duplicate message can reach the user.

For multi-step flows, the agent uses `final: false` on early messages. The loop continues, the agent does more work, and the last `send_message` (with `final: true`) terminates the loop.

Error returns from `send_message` never set `terminate` — the agent gets another turn to fix the error or choose a different action.

### Forced completion

If a turn is not terminally valid, the runner injects a corrective user message. The prompt is context-aware:

- **No prior sends**: tells the agent to call `send_message` or `no_reply`.
- **Prior sends detected** (scanned from message history): tells the agent it already sent a message and should either send a follow-up or call `no_reply` to end cleanly. This prevents the agent from calling `send_message` with `final: false` in a loop.

If the last message role is not assistant, the runner calls `agent.continue()` instead.

Retry budget: `forced_completion_retries` from config. If exhausted without a terminal condition, the session completes with `noReply: true`. No fallback implicit send — silence is safer than sending unvetted text.

The corrective prompts are exported constants (`FORCED_COMPLETION_PROMPTS`, current and historical wordings) and each nudge is a user turn tagged `harness: { kind: "forced_completion", attempt, variant }` (`variant` `not_sent`, or `sent_not_final` when the transcript already holds a `send_message` call), so every attempt can be derived from the transcript (§8j "Send-contract records"). Each failed attempt logs `contract_attempt {sessionId, attempt, variant, type, types, model}`. At exhaustion the ending is judged first (a judged refusal with a matching rule redoes the turn on another model); otherwise, with `[agent.sessions].forced_completion_redo = true`, the runner discards back to the fork point and redoes once per failure point on the same model with a fresh budget (§8j "Redo and branches"); a second exhaustion at the same point logs `contract_exhausted` and settles as before. `SessionRunResult.retries` counts every nudge of the run. A redo request filed during the run (a refusal at a send) is taken after the run settles, before any of these checks, and resets the nudge counter.

**LLM failures can never enter this loop** (spec LLM-FAILURE-HANDLING §8.1): after every settle the runner checks `AgentState.errorMessage` first (`throwIfLlmFailure`) and throws a typed `SessionRunnerError` (`phase:"llm"`, carrying the failure class) for **any** `[llm-request]`-tagged failure — *before* `isTerminallyValid` or the forced-completion loop is consulted. Forced completion fires only for *clean* turns with invalid output — its original output-contract purpose. Previously a fatal-classified API failure (e.g. a bad API key) entered the loop, burned `forced_completion_retries` doomed paid re-prompts, and settled as a silent `completed/no_reply` row with no error recorded anywhere.

### NO_REPLY

Silence is a tool call: `no_reply` (see the `no_reply` tool below) ends the turn and the session completes normally with `noReply: true`. The exact literal `NO_REPLY` as the assistant's text output is still accepted for compatibility with older prompts and models; no JSON envelope, no variants. The shipped prompts, templates, and corrective messages teach the tool call only.

### Proactive sessions (§9g)

A background scheduler can spawn self-initiated sessions that are not triggered by any inbound message (ARCHITECTURE.md §9g). They reuse this entire lifecycle verbatim through `launchSession(inbound, false, { proactive: true })`; the only differences are: the placeholder uses the configured `proactive.session_type` (default `"proactive"`, which omits a `tools` allowlist so it inherits the full tool set), the factory builds context in **proactive mode** (no trigger group, a synthetic kickoff as the final user turn — §9g), and the runner is constructed with `suppressTyping: true` so the typing keepalive in step 2 of the lifecycle is skipped (the message appears spontaneously; a `NO_REPLY` leaves no typing artifact). Budget accounting is derived by counting these `agent_sessions` rows, so a `NO_REPLY` proactive session still counts. The `proactive`, `summarize`, `condense`, and `diary` session types all reuse `NO_REPLY`/the frozen-context build seam in the same way; only the chat and proactive paths run through `SessionRunner`. A proactive session that did tool work writes a session record like a chat session, but is given none at launch: a check-in has no request to match records against (§8i).

### Agent construction (`AgentSessionFactory`)

Factory creation is **async** — it loads workspace content from disk before constructing the agent. Each session creates a fresh `Agent` with:

- `systemPrompt` → assembled from workspace files + skills index (via `renderSystemPrompt`)
- `tools` → filtered by session type config if a `tools` allowlist is specified
- `thinkingLevel` → the model config's `thinking_level` (default `"off"`); pi-agent-core threads it per request as pi-ai's `options.reasoning` through the whole streamFn chain, so a non-off level actually enables extended thinking (adaptive effort hint on Opus/Sonnet 4.6+, token budget on older models). On the anthropic-messages path the wire shape follows the same adaptivity decision as the affordability basis (§8g): `adaptive_thinking` when set, else the id heuristic. Adaptive models get `thinking: { type: "adaptive" }` plus the effort the level maps to (`createModelFromConfig` sets pi-ai's `compat.forceAdaptiveThinking`, which pi-ai does not infer for a config-built descriptor); the rest get a token budget. Models that accept only adaptive thinking reject the budget form, so they must be declared with `adaptive_thinking = true`. Some also reject an explicit `thinking: { type: "disabled" }`: give those a `thinking_level`, or map off away with `thinking_level_map = { off = null }`, which omits the field and leaves the model on its own default. The model descriptor's `reasoning` flag is capability-only and never enables thinking by itself. On the openai-completions **Together** dialect the level is normally only a binary on/off (`reasoning:{enabled}`); to forward an actual effort the model sets `compat.supports_reasoning_effort = true` (pi-ai auto-disables `reasoning_effort` for `provider="together"`) plus a `thinkingLevelMap` translating the pi-ai level to the upstream's wire value — the live GLM-5.2 model maps `xhigh → "max"`, so it runs at max reasoning effort. A second dialect override, `compat.supports_developer_role`, forces the system-prompt role: pi-ai sends the OpenAI `developer` role whenever `reasoning` is on and it auto-detects that role as supported, but some OAI-compatible upstreams behind a gateway (a proxied DeepSeek, whose API only accepts `system/user/assistant/tool`) reject `developer` with a deserialization 400 — set `supports_developer_role = false` to force the plain `system` role (unset = pi-ai auto-detection). A third dialect override, `compat.requires_reasoning_content_on_assistant_messages`, disables pi-ai's DeepSeek safety net: pi-ai auto-enables (for `provider="deepseek"`) a rule that stamps `reasoning_content: ""` onto any assistant message that carried no thinking block, but DeepSeek V4 Pro **thinking mode** rejects a present-but-empty `reasoning_content` with a 400 (`"The \`reasoning_content\` in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API"`) on those reasoning-less turns — which include historical/plain context assistant messages (the bot's own live replies go out as `send_message` tool-calls and DO carry real reasoning via the independent thinking-signature path, so they are unaffected). Per DeepSeek's docs the field is optional and ignored on non-tool-call turns, so omitting it is correct; set `requires_reasoning_content_on_assistant_messages = false` to suppress the empty-string stamp (unset = pi-ai auto-detection). A fourth, `compat.supports_tool_search` (openai-responses only, **default true**), keeps dynamically loaded tools out of the cache-leading `tools` array — see §10 "Dynamic tool loading", Transport. A fifth, `compat.openrouter_routing` (openai-completions only, default unset), is an OpenRouter provider-routing table (`order`, `only`, `ignore`, `allow_fallbacks`, `zdr`, `sort`, `quantizations`, ...) sent verbatim as the request's top-level `provider` object (agent sessions and Chat Completions caption calls alike), to pin a model to specific upstream providers or restrict it to zero-data-retention endpoints; a gateway in front of OpenRouter must forward the field. Unset sends no `provider` object. Required reasoning on tool-call turns still round-trips
- `transformContext` → **append-only over a frozen prefix** (see "Frozen context" below) — it merges cached prefix + live runtime messages and never rebuilds per turn
- `convertToLlm` → all custom message types → standard `Message[]`
- `onPayload` → `makeBreakpointInjector` — injects explicit prompt-cache breakpoints (Bedrock Responses markers, Anthropic `cache_control`); gates per serving member via `model.compat.cacheBreakpoints` so direct-OpenAI fallback members in the same chain are never affected (see "Cache control" below)
- `steeringMode` → `"one-at-a-time"`
- `sessionId` → **timeline key** (not session ID), for LLM-side cache affinity across sessions on the same timeline
- `streamFn` → the chosen stream function (`streamSimple`, or `wrapCompleteAsStream` for non-streaming models), first pinned to `maxRetries: 0` (`withSdkRetriesDisabled` — see Layer-0 below), then **wrapped by scheduler admission (§8a), then by Layer-0 request retry** — `withRequestRetry(withSchedulerAdmission(withSdkRetriesDisabled(base)))`, so each retry attempt re-acquires a fresh scheduler slot. Between Layer 0 and the composite sits the refusal controller's sticky dispatch (`sessionStreamFn`): with a refusal pin or a same-model retry target set (§8j "Refusal rules"), every request goes to that model's composite instead of the session head's
- Refusal and redo handles (§8j): `CreatedAgent.refusal` (the session's `SessionRefusalHandle`: site, agent, tasks, serving and pinned model, rule matching and walks, `refusal_events` writes; Layer 0's `onRefusal` hook asks it on every refused attempt), `setRefusalSite` (the record turn's `record_turn` site), `redoControl` (the `SessionRedoControl` the gate files redo requests on; `Agent.shouldStopAfterTurn` stops the loop after the current tool batch while one is pending), `forkContext(deps)` (the fork core's context, adding the session id, agent, live-event bus and the re-derivation that unloads discarded dynamic tools and rewinds the running context counter), `gate` (the session's `OutputGate`, built from `AgentFactoryOptions.outputChecks`; none for internal job builds; its tap rides Layer 0's attempt tap through `withGateTap`, and the gated tools are wrapped inside the record-turn gate and outside the prefill stripping). `CreateAgentOptions.refusalPin` starts a session pinned (a mechanical job's rerun); `CreateAgentOptions.redoControl` passes a pre-made control. `onRequestCommitted` stamps each committed assistant message with the serving member's logical id (`served: { logicalId }`), and every agent-loop ledger row carries `systemPromptHash` (§8k)

### Layer-0 request retry (transparent inference recovery)

Mechanical LLM failures — a connection reset, a timeout, a 5xx, an upstream 429 — are frequent and normal. Left unhandled, a single blip synthesizes a `stopReason:"error"` message that discards a live session outright (no retry) and, for a synthetic session, burns a whole job-level *semantic*-retry attempt re-running the entire job from scratch.

`withRequestRetry` (`src/agent/request-retry.ts`) wraps the session's `streamFn` so a mechanical blip **re-issues the exact same request** before the failure is allowed to surface — transparently to the session and to pi-agent-core:

- **Commit point = the terminal event (spec LLM-FAILURE-HANDLING §4.1).** The wrapper buffers **all** events of an attempt and forwards them to the consumer only when the attempt terminates in a clean `done`. A terminal `error` at *any* point — before or after tokens were produced — discards the buffered partial and re-enters the retry loop as if the request had failed from the start, so mid-stream deaths retry exactly like start failures and a success after N failures is byte-equivalent to a first-attempt success (P1). pi-agent-core never sees a failed attempt unless this layer gives up; the synthetic `stopReason:"error"` turn and the Layer-2 teardown-and-rebuild stop being the mid-stream recovery path. An "empty stream" (ended with no terminal event) is synthesized into an environmental error and retried the same way. Buffering is bounded by `max_tokens` — no meaningful memory concern.
- **Live token streaming via the observability tap (spec §4.2).** Since the authoritative stream is buffered, the wrapper exposes `onAttemptEvent(attempt, event)` / `onAttemptDiscarded(attempt, reason)` on its context — invoked synchronously with every raw event as it arrives, best-effort (exceptions swallowed; the tap can never affect the run). The factory wires the tap to a per-session `SessionLiveEventBus` (`src/observability/live-events.ts`); the console session SSE merges those as **tentative** events (`tentative_event` / `attempt_discarded` — kinds distinct from the authoritative agent events) so the console renders tokens live and clears them with an "attempt n failed, retrying" notice when a partial is discarded. Tap payloads pass the same externalize/redact pipeline as all SSE writes; nothing from the tap is persisted.
- **Classification** (`classifyLlmError(errorMessage, stopReason, rawStopReason?)`, spec LLM-FAILURE-HANDLING §3): four-way, replacing the old retryable/fatal binary. **`refusal`** — the model or its provider's safety layer declined the request (`isRefusalSignal`, checked right after `aborted`); a matching refusal rule decides what happens next (a redo on its entry, possibly the same model), otherwise it is never retried on the member that refused and falls over to another chain member or fails terminally (§8a "Refusals", §8j). **`aborted`** — an intentional abort (`stopReason:"aborted"`: tool-call/turn cap, shutdown; plus the synthesized "scheduler stopped" admission rejection) is never retried. **`content`** — caused by *this request's* content, deterministic on replay: requires positive evidence (a 400/413/422 status, or an explicit context-length keyword like `prompt is too long`/`context_length_exceeded`); never retried at this layer, escalated to the semantic layer. **`environmental`** — everything else: timeouts, resets, empty streams, 408/409/425/429/5xx (incl. Anthropic 529), *and* the endpoint-level 401/403/404/405 + auth keywords (an auth/grant failure is fixed out-of-band and recovery is detected by retrying, not by refusing to) — retried. Every environmental failure (including the first attempt) logs `llm_request_attempt_failed` with `{class, status, attempt}`.
- **Per-class wall-clock budgets (spec LLM-FAILURE-HANDLING §6, maintainer decision).** There is no attempt count — a fixed count is meaningless under scheduler gating (4 attempts can elapse in seconds or hours depending on group/model state). The budget attaches to the session's **workload category**, derived from its session type's *own* priority class at factory time (a priority-inheritance escalation changes queue rank only, never the budget — an escalated background job is still background work): **interactive-class** (`interactive`, `proactive`) requests are wall-clock-bounded by `recovery.llm_request_max_wait_ms` (default 120 000 ms — the typing indicator runs during the wait; ~2 minutes is the outer edge of a reply still being conversationally useful), measured from the first attempt; on exhaustion they surface a tagged environmental error → the runner throws → the session parks `failed-resumable`. An attempt that was **in flight with zero tokens** when the budget expired is a **stall** and counts as an environmental failure of its model (Layer 0 aborts it with `LLM_STALL_ABORT_REASON`; the admission wrapper reads `isStallAbort(signal)` and feeds the §8a streak) — a silent hang is an outage, so a slow-failing model trips like a fast-failing one. The caller's own abort (drain / Stop) and a budget expiry during an admission-queue wait stay neutral. **Background-class** (`background`, `background_low`) requests are **unbounded** — they keep re-entering admission until success, drain/abort, or reclassification (P3: downtime is routine; summaries and diaries must eventually exist).
  - **The budget bounds only WAITING and RECOVERY, never a working generation.** There was never any intention to time out a request that is actively responding — an LLM may take arbitrarily long to produce a long answer. Concretely the budget governs three things and nothing else: the **admission-queue wait** (a budget expiry mid-acquire aborts the acquire — the one wait the spec sanctions cutting short — and is re-labelled environmental wait-exhaustion since the caller didn't abort, the clock did), the **inter-attempt backoff sleep** (also abortable by the budget), and a **stuck/silent attempt that has produced zero tokens by the deadline** (treated like any other environmental failure → parks). It does **not** abort an attempt that has produced output.
  - **Immune after the first token (incl. reasoning).** The first model-produced event of *any* kind — output text, **reasoning/thinking** (`thinking_delta`/`thinking_start`), or a tool-call delta; `start` is the stream opener, not content — flips the attempt to budget-immune for the remainder of its life. Mechanically (`src/agent/request-retry.ts`) each attempt is given its own `AbortController`; the caller's abort (drain/Stop) is always forwarded into it, but the budget's abort is forwarded **only while zero tokens have arrived**, and the first content event detaches the budget listener. A healthy interactive generation of any length therefore completes even if it streams long past `llm_request_max_wait_ms`; the budget can still abort it only *before* it begins producing tokens.
  - **Per-model override.** A model that is slow to *first* token can be granted a larger pre-first-token budget via `models.<name>.llm_request_max_wait_ms` (StrictObject field; unset = fall back to `recovery.llm_request_max_wait_ms`). The factory resolves `modelConfig.llm_request_max_wait_ms ?? recovery.llm_request_max_wait_ms` and threads it as the interactive-class `maxWaitMs`; it has no effect on background-class work (always unbounded). Shipped explicitly on `[models.default]` in `00-defaults.toml` per the explicit-config convention.
  - Between attempts, full-jitter local backoff between `recovery.llm_request_backoff_base_ms` and `…_max_ms` applies **only while the model is healthy and the group unthrottled** — once the admission queue is the wait point (model unhealthy / group backoff), the local sleep collapses to ~0 (`LlmScheduler.isQueueWaitPoint`; no double-waiting). The backoff sleep is bounded by the `(caller ∨ budget)` signal and an abort here is told apart by source: a **caller abort** (pool drain / operator Stop) mid-backoff surfaces a synthesized **`aborted`** event (`stopReason:"aborted"` + the `[llm-request:aborted]` class marker), so the run reads as an abort downstream and the worker pools' drain compensation fires (§9b) — surfacing the preceding attempt's stale *environmental* error here would silently send a drained job down the semantic-failure path and consume/refund its retry budget wrongly; a **budget expiry** mid-backoff (the caller did not abort — the clock did) loops once and exits via the wait-exhausted path, keeping its environmental wait-exhaustion semantics. The wrapper **always applies** — it owns the origin/class tagging below, which the runner's gate depends on.
- **Origin + class tagging (Decision C / spec §4.3).** Every terminal `error` event the wrapper surfaces — a provider/SDK failure, a scheduler-admission failure synthesized by `withSchedulerAdmission` (composed *inside* the wrapper, so those flow through it and need no tagging of their own), or its own throw-guard/empty-stream synths — gets `LLM_REQUEST_FAILURE_MARKER` (`[llm-request]`) **plus a machine-readable class marker** (`[llm-request:environmental|content|aborted|refusal]`, parsed back by `extractLlmRequestClass`) appended to its `errorMessage`. By the time a failure reaches the `SessionRunner`, pi-agent-core has flattened it into the `AgentState.errorMessage` *string* (its `handleRunFailure` flattens **any** executor throw — including programming errors in `transformContext`/tool plumbing — into the same field), so origin and class must be encoded in the string itself. Only tagged errors throw the runner's typed `phase:"llm"` rejection; untagged errors are our own code throwing and settle as plain failures. The markers are suffixes so the SDK's leading-status prefix still parses, and tagging is idempotent — the first surfacing point's classification wins.
- **Sole retry authority.** The provider SDKs pi-ai delegates to (Anthropic, OpenAI) silently default to **2 internal HTTP retries**; pi-ai forwards `maxRetries` to them only when defined. Left enabled, those retries' backoff sleeps would run *inside* the held scheduler slot (§8a), their absorbed 429s would never reach the group backoff, and their attempt count would multiply with Layer-1's. The factory therefore pins **`maxRetries: 0`** onto every base stream call (`withSdkRetriesDisabled`, `src/agent/factory.ts`) — providers without client-side retries ignore the option.
- **Throw guard.** A base stream fn that *throws* (synchronously or mid-iteration) instead of emitting a terminal `error` event — possible in scheduler-less compositions — is caught, synthesized into a terminal `error` event (an `AbortError` keeps `stopReason:"aborted"`), and fed through the same classification/retry logic; post-commit it is surfaced terminally without retry. Without the guard such a throw would escape as a process-fatal unhandled rejection and leave the consumer's stream unterminated.
- **429 backoff is unconditional and origin-blind:** a 429 is backed off + retried whether or not the gateway already handled it internally. Distinguishing a gateway-vs-true-upstream 429 is a deferred optimization, not a correctness requirement.

Net effect: a mechanical blip in a live session no longer discards it, and a blip in a summarization/diary run is absorbed here and **no longer consumes a job-level semantic-retry attempt** — that coarse retry is now reserved for genuine content failures.

### Session parking & manual resume (Layer-0 exhausted)

When Layer-0 gives up — an interactive request's wall-clock budget exhausted, or a content failure (mid-stream deaths retry inside Layer-0; background requests never exhaust) — the live session is **not** discarded (spec LLM-FAILURE-HANDLING §8). The old Layer-2 **auto-resume loop is deleted**: Layer-0 owns all in-run retrying, and once the interactive budget is exhausted the maintainer explicitly does *not* want delayed automatic replies (P3 — a bot replying long after it was asked is useless at best, and a herd of backed-up sessions resuming at once is a disaster; same reason nothing auto-resumes at restart). The pieces:

- **Surfacing.** pi-agent-core *resolves* a failed run (synthesizing a `stopReason:"error"` assistant turn and setting `AgentState.errorMessage`), so the `SessionRunner` checks after every idle (`throwIfLlmFailure`): **any** failure tagged with the Layer-1 origin marker (see "Origin + class tagging" above) — environmental, content and refusal alike — throws a typed `SessionRunnerError` with `phase:"llm"`, carrying the §3 class (preferring the embedded class marker; re-classifying the de-tagged message as a fallback). This fires *before* the forced-completion loop, so an API failure can never trigger doomed re-prompts or settle as a silent `NO_REPLY` completion. Untagged errors — programming throws caught by pi-agent-core (`transformContext`/tool plumbing) — and *genuine in-turn* aborts (operator Stop — `lifecycle.isInterrupted()`; tool/turn caps — the synthetic turn carries `stopReason:"aborted"`) keep their existing settle-in-place behaviour — re-issuing cannot help them. The **one** `aborted`-class case that does *not* settle in place is a **drain-caused scheduler-stop admission rejection**: it is class-tagged `aborted` but lands on a synthetic turn with `stopReason:"error"` (no operator interrupt), so it reaches `throwIfLlmFailure`'s final branch and **throws `phase:"llm"` like every other tagged failure** — the maintainer chose park-over-discard while draining (the pending user message must survive a shutdown), and re-entering forced completion against a stopped gate would add a P1-violating user turn per iteration before masking the drop as a `NO_REPLY` completion.
- **Park, never discard (P5).** `launchSession`'s catch routes every unrecovered `phase:"llm"` failure — environmental-exhausted, content *and* refusal (handled like content: no auto-retry, `isResumableRunError` is false, a resume attempt that hits it again reports the `content` outcome) — to `markFailedResumable` with the error recorded (`session_parked_failed_resumable` log, with the class). A 400/413/422 may be fatal to *this request*, but it is operator- or upstream-fixable; nothing about the session itself is unresumable. `markDiscarded` remains only for untagged errors (our own code) and unusable resume material. The same rule applies on the resume path: a `content` attempt outcome re-parks (auto-resume stops retrying it — deterministic on replay — and the manual resume reports it without discarding). Two refusal outcomes of the rules (§8j) settle differently: a rule exhausted with `on_exhausted = "withhold"` ends the run as a clean `NO_REPLY` (Layer 0's synthesized `refusal_withheld` turn, or the soft-refusal handler giving up), and a soft refusal exhausted with `park` throws the same refusal-class `phase:"llm"` error and parks here.
- **Persist-at-failure.** The run's `.catch` in `app.ts` calls `flushNow()` *before* any recovery decision, so the transcript durably captures everything up to and including the in-progress turn — exactly what resume seeds from. (The capture listener always flushes from the full `agent.state.messages`, never the run-scoped `agent_end` payload — so the one-element failure payload can't clobber the transcript either; see "Session capture" §8.)
- **Configurable failure notice (spec §8.3, default silent).** `recovery.failure_notice` (optional static phrase; empty/absent = silence) is sent best-effort to the session's outbound target when a **user-triggered** chat session stops trying on its own — it parked `failed-resumable`, or its build timed out waiting on summary coverage (`session_build_wait_timeout`). The actual error is never included. Suppressed for proactive sessions (nobody asked them anything; the scheduler fires again next cadence) and synthetic sessions (no room audience). A send failure is logged (`failure_notice_send_failed`) and never affects the park/discard.
- **Manual console resume — the sole resume path.** A parked session is terminal in memory with its durable row intact. The observability console's `POST /api/sessions/:id/resume` (its second mutating route, next to abort) drives the manual resume, whose whole policy lives in `createManualResumeSession` (`src/agent/recovery.ts`, a factory over injected deps so it is unit-testable; `app.ts` wires the runtime deps). It accepts **two source statuses** (Decision D): `failed-resumable` AND `interrupted` — an interrupted row (crash healing, operator Stop) carries the same snapshot/transcript, and viability is decided by `loadResumeMaterial`, not the status label; a row with nothing to redo (transcript ends at a clean boundary, or material unusable) is rejected 409 **with its status untouched** (an unresumable `interrupted` row is never converted to `failed-resumable`). `loadResumeMaterial` returns a **three-way verdict**, not a boolean: `{mode:"continue", snapshot, transcript}` is the normal replay material; `null` rejects (a transcript ending at a clean boundary — the run committed; corrupt persisted JSON; a transcript present *without* its snapshot, which violates the capture ordering and so is treated as corruption with possibly-committed turns; or an unexpected rehydration failure); and **`{mode:"fresh"}`** is the first-request-crash case — a hard process kill before the first `turn_end`/`flushNow`, so the transcript was **never flushed** (absent, or flushed-empty, or strips to empty under `stripFailedTail`). Fresh is **viable, not a rejection**: no turn ever committed (no side effect to duplicate, nothing to replay), but the durable row's persisted trigger fields (`trigger_body`/`trigger_sender_id`/…) still point at the original timeline event, so the session can re-run from scratch. This closes the one gap where a crash during a session's very first LLM request left an unresumable row — the failure that motivated the fix (an endpoint-config 404 retry-looping until restart, killed before any attempt succeeded). It is additionally gated to **user-facing session types**: rows whose `session_type` is a synthetic worker-pool type (`SYNTHETIC_SESSION_TYPES`: `summarize`/`condense` §9b, `diary` §9c — the literals hardcoded at the pools' insertion sites, so the denylist needs no config plumbing, unlike an allowlist over the configurable proactive type) are rejected 409 with status untouched. Those pools write `agent_sessions` rows directly with real timeline keys and captured transcripts; a crash mid-worker-run leaves such a row `running` → startup healing flips it `interrupted`, and without this gate a console resume would re-drive the worker transcript as a *chat* session — chat tools, `send_message` into the real room, bot identity. The session-type column is the discriminator (NULL sender columns are not — legacy proactive rows share them); the worker pools own their own job-level retries, and the console hides the Resume button for these types. Auto-resume-on-startup stays off. Guards, in order: a **synchronous double-POST guard** (an in-flight set + `SessionManager` record presence, checked/inserted before any await — the durable status read alone cannot prevent two near-simultaneous POSTs racing the async `markRunning` write) → status gate → synthetic-session-type gate → drain gate → viability gate → the **per-timeline trigger slot** (`TriggerCoordinator.tryAcquire`; 409 "timeline busy" when a live session holds it — a manual resume must never post concurrently with a live session on the same timeline; the slot is released in a `finally` that also drains the next queued trigger, mirroring `launchSession`'s `.finally`). The record + a synthetic inbound are then reconstructed from the durable row alone (`parseMatrixTimelineKey` rebuilds the outbound target — it accepts both `room` and `dm` timeline keys, the same shapes `roomIdFromTimelineKey` accepts, so DM sessions are resumable too; the inbound's sender is the **persisted trigger sender** — `trigger_sender_id`/`trigger_sender_display_name`, written by `createPlaceholder` — so sender-bound tools (`user_profile_read`/`user_profile_edit`, `recap`'s asker) bind to the same user the failed session had; `isSelf` is claimed only when that sender IS the bot, e.g. proactive sessions — never for user-triggered ones), `SessionManager.adopt` re-registers it — so a park survives process restarts — and the same `resumeSessionRun` runs once. Each resume attempt (`resumeSessionRun`) rebuilds the same tool set (`buildSessionTools`, shared with launch), loads the persisted material via `loadResumeMaterial` (`src/agent/recovery.ts`, async: externalized image refs are **rehydrated** through the media store — `getMediaAssetById(attachmentId)` → `local_path` bytes under the workspace root, traversal-guarded — so resumed requests carry real base64 again, with unresolvable refs degraded to a `[image omitted on resume]` text placeholder rather than a malformed `{type:"image"}` block that would 400 fatally; the snapshot is re-projected through `mapBuiltMessages` per the factory's resume vocabulary contract; the transcript's failed tail — trailing `error`/`aborted` assistant turns — stripped so it ends at the un-answered user/tool-result message), re-creates the agent with `factory.create({ resume })` (no context rebuild), and drives the runner in **continue-mode** (`kickoff: undefined` → `agent.continue()`), which **redoes the exact request that failed** — after an operator fixes an auth/config problem, the re-issued request is byte-identical and simply works. **Fresh-mode resume** (`material.mode === "fresh"`) diverges here: there is no transcript to replay, so `resumeSessionRun` instead calls `factory.create` **without** `resume` — a full context **rebuild** (passing `proactive` for proactive rows and `drainAbort.signal`), which yields a fresh `finalTurn` kickoff plus a new `snapshot`/`tokenEstimate`. It runs the runner in **launch-mode** (the rebuilt `kickoff` is prompted, not `undefined`) and passes the rebuilt `snapshot` to `attachSessionCapture` so the durable row's `context_snapshot_json` is **overwritten** to reflect the context this run actually used (the rebuild sees the timeline as of *now*, including anything that arrived after the crash — exactly as a launch would). A rebuild that throws is `fatal` (our own code), except a `BuildWaitTimeoutError` (an outage backing up summary coverage), which is `mechanical` → re-parks. A mechanical (environmental) or content failure — and an `unresumable` outcome — re-parks `failed-resumable`; a fatal (untagged) outcome discards on a live runtime but **re-parks when draining** (shutdown-caused, not content-caused). The `app.ts` wrapper tracks the in-flight resume promise in `activeRuns` so `stop()`'s `waitForRuns` awaits it before the scheduler stops and storage closes. There are no chat/operator commands; the console is the only manual surface (a Resume button on `failed-resumable` and `interrupted` sessions of user-facing types — hidden for synthetic summarize/condense/diary rows, which the agent would 409 anyway).

State machine: `running → (llm failure) → failed-resumable → (console resume) → resuming → running → …`, plus `interrupted → (console resume) → resuming → …` when the interrupted row still has something to redo — either `continue`-mode (replay the persisted transcript) or `fresh`-mode (rebuild from the durable trigger row when the transcript never flushed) (Decision D). `discarded` is reached only by untagged (our-own-code) failures and unusable resume material.

### Resumable sessions (reply-to-continue)

**Replying to a message the bot sent continues the session that produced it** — appending the user's reply as a new turn and continuing the same rollout — rather than spawning a fresh, amnesiac session (spec RESUMABLE-SESSIONS). This is the **awaited-input** resume the failure path's machinery was always able to support (Appendix B): a *completed* session is reconstructed from its persisted snapshot + transcript exactly as a parked one, but instead of `continue()`-ing the failed tail it gets a **new appended user turn** and `prompt()`s it. `@`-mentioning (or any non-reply trigger) still starts a fresh session. Off by default per context (`enabled.dm`/`enabled.group` both default false): session records (§8i) are the default way a later session carries earlier work, and with resume off a reply to a bot message starts a fresh session that is given that message's record. A wrong guess degrades to a fresh session, never to corruption or message loss.

**With records (§8i).** A deployment that turns resume on keeps the behaviour below unchanged, plus three rules: `tryReplyResume` takes its single-flight claim and then **waits for the target session's in-flight record turn** (`SessionRecordService.waitFor`, bounded by that turn's `wait_timeout_ms` deadline plus grace, without aborting production; an unfinished turn falls back to a fresh session) before the gate and the material load, so it continues the finished transcript and two agents never run one session; a reply that resumes injects nothing (the rollout, record turn included, is already there; `runResumeSession` passes no `injections`); and the resumed generation runs its own record turn on completion, which replaces the session's `session_records` row.

**The trigger pipeline stays resume-unaware.** Detection, hold/lookback grouping, claims, and coalescing are unchanged; the resume-vs-fresh decision is a single fork made downstream, at the top of `launchSession` (`tryReplyResume`). Two small touchpoints feed it:
- **Reply-as-trigger (`resolveReplyTrigger`, §5; spec SESSION-RECORDS §6.1).** A bare reply to one of the bot's own messages does not natively trigger (a Discord reply with the ping off, say). The **provider's trigger hold** classifies it as `trigger.type = "reply"` for a reply whose target resolves (via `agent_session_id`) to a message we sent — so it enters the pipeline through the *same* hold/debounce/grouping as a native trigger (exactly one held delivery; no late synthesis). The resolver always classifies qualifying replies as triggers regardless of whether reply-resume (`enabled`) is on for the context; the resume-vs-fresh decision is made later at `tryReplyResume`. The provider stays resume-unaware: `emitWithTriggerHold` calls the `resolveReplyTrigger` callback (wired at provider construction in `app.ts`), which owns the timeline lookup and only answers "reply to one of my messages?". (In DMs every message already triggers as `dm`, so the resolver — gated on `!inbound.trigger` — only ever fires in groups. Replying to a *non-bot* message still doesn't trigger; self-replies are excluded.) The resolver runs *before* `handleInbound`, so by the time `steerReplyToActiveSession` runs a reply to a *running* session still interjects, and the resume fork sees an already-classified trigger. (This replaced an earlier app-level `maybeSynthesizeReplyTrigger` that synthesized the trigger *after* the hold — which double-handled the event and skipped grouping.)
- **The fork (`tryReplyResume`).** Returns true when the reply continues a completed, eligible session (the resumed run then owns this trigger's timeline slot + claim lifecycle, released on settle, exactly like a fresh launch); returns false → `launchSession` proceeds to the normal FRESH path.
