A **synchronous single-flight guard** (`resumeClaims` + `SessionManager.get`) ensures one reply resumes a given state; a concurrent second reply degrades to FRESH (once the first `markRunning`s, later replies steer via the running-session path).

**Single-consumption via `resume_generation` (§6).** A session cannot be resumed from the same state twice — linear chains are allowed (reply to the latest output → resume → reply to *its* new output → resume again), branching is not. Mechanism: `agent_sessions.resume_generation` (NOT NULL DEFAULT 0) and `timeline_events.agent_session_generation` (nullable; NULL ≡ 0). Every outbound agent message is tagged at send time with the session's current generation (threaded through `send_message`); a reply-resume of a completed session is accepted only when the **target message's generation equals the session's current `resume_generation`** — a reply to a superseded output → FRESH. Acceptance is the atomic `storage.acceptResumeGeneration` CAS: `completed → resuming` AND `resume_generation += 1` in one statement, so the prior run's outputs (tagged with the pre-bump value) become stale forever and a racing reply that already consumed the state gets nothing. A resume that is accepted then fails parks `failed-resumable` (no longer `completed` → the fork yields FRESH; the orphaned bump is harmless).

**Eligibility gates** (`tryReplyResume`, cheap→expensive; any failure → FRESH): the target resolves to a bot message, resume is `enabled` for the context, the session is not live in-memory (running/resuming is the steer path's job) and not still revivable (a `lateInputEntries` entry, §8 "Late input": the completed session keeps its agent for `revive_max_ms`, and a resume from the DB beside a revival would run two agents on one session; `reply_resume_revivable`, checked again after the record wait, so with late input on a reply within that window starts a fresh session) → row is `completed` (failed-resumable/interrupted keep the console path; synthetic worker types excluded) → **generation** matches → **intent heuristics** (`same_user_only`: the replier is the original trigger sender; `window`: `now − completed_at ≤ window[ctx]`) → **capability** (the persisted `context_tokens` is below the model ceiling, else a resume would immediately re-park — no compaction is built, §12) → **work gate** + **material viability** (one load of `loadCompletedSessionMaterial`). The pre-CAS gate sequence (everything before `acceptResumeGeneration`) is the factored-out `evaluateResumeGate`, wrapped in a try/catch so an *unexpected throw* — a DB read, ceiling resolution, or material load — also degrades to FRESH (`resume_gate_threw`) rather than escaping `tryReplyResume` → `launchSession` (no try/catch at the call site) → the dispatch rethrow, which would drop the message with no reply; the never-drop invariant holds for exceptions too.

**The work gate (`src/agent/work-gate.ts`, §7a)** is the core protection against resuming pure conversation: resume only continues *stateful* work (≥1 **non-exempt tool call** in scope). A rollout of only chat-surface tools holds nothing a fresh session lacks — the chat history already carries it — and resuming it just buries another stale satellite. Thinking/content blocks never count. Always on; two knobs tune *how* work is measured, per context:
- **scope** — `since_last_turn` (work must appear in the latest resume-generation's rollout, delimited by the last real `triggerGroup`/`satellite` turn — interjections are *within* a segment, never boundaries; the group default, so a single lookup can't swallow the room's back-and-forth) vs `any_in_history` (work anywhere so far; the DM default, so research carries through toolless follow-ups).
- **extra_exempt_tools** — extra names (incl. `mcp__…`) to treat as non-work atop the built-in set.

The built-in exempt set is **declared on the tool** via a `resumeWorkExempt: true` flag (a module-augmented optional on `AgentTool`), not a hidden central list — `collectExemptToolNames` derives the gate's name set from the flags, and `test/work-gate.test.ts` pins it to the spec's enumeration. The set is built **context-free** (`BUILTIN_RESUME_EXEMPT_TOOL_NAMES`, `src/tools/resume-exempt.ts`): a fixed enumeration of the exempt-candidate factories, constructed once with a stub context, independent of `roomId`/target — *not* from a per-inbound `buildSessionTools` probe (whose room-scoped exempt tools would drop out for a falsy `roomId`). `tryReplyResume` then unions the per-context `extra_exempt_tools`. **15 built-in exempt tools**: the chat-surface tools (`send_message`, `react`, `edit_message`, `delete_message`, `create_poll`, `poll_vote`, `pins`, `set_profile`), the control tools (`spawn_session`, `delegate_to_session`), `media` (its source is in the chat and its caption is regenerable), and the four control-flow tools `no_reply`, `load_skill`, `tool_search`, and `session_record_tool` (pure harness/control flow, no stateful external work). The session-record read tools (`read_session_record`, `read_session_transcript`) count as work when the **model** calls them (§8i). Everything else — `browser`, `bash`, file edits, `image_generate`, `find_source`, the `web_*`/`x_*` and retrieval/read tools (their *results* live in the rollout, not the chat) — counts as work. Classification leans exempt for anything ambiguous: the safe failure direction is "didn't resume".

**Nothing injected counts as work.** Only the model's own tool calls are work. The reasons: an injection is not work the agent did (the decision model chose it, at a much lower bar than the agent itself would act on, so the agent might never have made that call); when the agent made no call of its own, a preloaded skill went unused and a record turn over an injected record would only re-summarize the earlier session's record; and counting injections lets too many sessions pass the gate. Showing where an answer came from is no reason to count them: injected memories (`<retrieved_memory>`) never counted either, a follow-up session retrieves the same records or memories itself, and the link between an injected record and the reply already exists in the decision rows and the transcript's synthetic call. A harness-made message (any message with a top-level `harness` marker: the records point's injected `read_session_record` pairs, routing's `load_skill` preloads, the synthetic `tool_search` select that loads a deferred injection target, the record turn's load, corrective prompts, a withheld-refusal ending) never counts, whatever its tool name. One shared helper, `src/agent/harness.ts` (`isHarnessMade`, `harnessKindOf`, `modelToolCalls`), is how every predicate that judges work or the model's tool use reads a transcript: the work gate here (reply-resume and record eligibility, §8i), the send-contract derivation and its history reconciliation (`deriveContractEvents`, §8j), the offline audit's contract runs and check items (§9i), the redo helpers and the runner's ending check. The marker is a plain JSON field: it survives transcript persistence and the resume path's reload (`test/work-gate.test.ts`), so the gate reads stored transcripts the same way. Paths that only count paid tool use for cost (`SessionUsageTracker`, the usage page's per-session tool costs) are unaffected: an injection records no tool usage. The `max_tool_calls` loop-breaker counts in the agent loop's `beforeToolCall`, which synthetic calls never pass through.

**The appended turn** (`ContextBuilder.buildResumeTurn` → factory `resumeContinuation` → runner kickoff, §9/§11) is a fresh `triggerGroup` message — the runner `prompt()`s it onto the end of the resumed rollout. The frozen prefix is the **original snapshot, reused verbatim** (never rebuilt — that would reintroduce the incoherence the freeze invariant prevents). The trigger group it renders is resolved (`resolveTriggerGroupIds`) as the trigger's id ∪ its in-memory `groupedEventIds` ∪ the **durable `trigger_group_id` column** (`storage.getTriggerGroupMemberIds`, the same key `getMediaAssetsForTriggerGroup` uses for the image path). The column union matters because the resume path hydrates the trigger by re-reading it from `event_json` (provider-hold group only), which drops any backward-lookback members the live build had grouped in — without the union those members' **text** would silently vanish from the resume render while their image survived via the column. It is a no-op for the live `build` path, where the in-memory event already carries the full group (and the column holds exactly the same ids). Layout mirrors the live final turn (`[gap, satellite, trigger]`):
- **Fresh satellite (§11).** The original satellite is now doubly degraded (stale data, buried mid-rollout), so a fresh one is rendered at the new position; the buried copy is left untouched (a frozen-context rewrite is out of scope — `runtime_state`'s current time orders the two latest-wins). Split by volatility: `runtime_state` always re-rendered (+ a one-line **browser note** when the browser tool is configured — the prior tab closed on settle but its login/cookies persist, §11b); `retrieved_memory` always omitted (volatile, marginal; a genuinely new sub-topic is a fresh-session case); tail instructions are the single toggle (`satellite.tail`, default on — a long resumed rollout is where adherence drifts worst). The work gate is what keeps fresh satellites from piling up across ordinary back-and-forth.
- **Gap backfill (§9, off by default).** Optionally surfaces room messages the session missed while away: a contiguous newest-first run in `(lowerBound, trigger]` — `lowerBound` = the persisted `agent_sessions.chat_upper_bound_ts`, the timestamp of the **trigger group's latest member the session already covers** (its original trigger on creation, advanced to each accepted resume's trigger via `storage.setSessionChatUpperBound` — read-old-then-write-new, the old value captured into the gap before the queued advance). This is *not* the bot's last send: bounding on the send would drop every message that arrived between the original trigger and the bot's (possibly much later) reply and would never render the bot's own sends, both of which §9.2 wants surfaced. NULL only on a legacy (pre-v27) row's first resume → a one-time bounded fallback to the replied-to message's timestamp. The window excludes trigger-group members, is claim-marked (`<handled_by_session>` so the resumed session doesn't duplicate-handle another session's trigger), and is truncated oldest-first to the budget with a marker reporting the **true** omitted count. The whole window is fetched (no pre-budget query cap), so `max_messages = -1` is genuinely unlimited and the marker never undercounts; only a far-above-normal safety ceiling bounds a pathological away-window, and hitting it turns the marker open-ended. Two independent budgets (`max_messages`, `max_tokens`; both must be non-zero to surface anything, the two never both `-1`); DMs stay off because a DM's gap is entirely other sessions' triggers.

**Config** (`[agent.sessions.resume]`, cross-field validation in `app.ts`): `same_user_only` (global); per-context `enabled`/`window`/`gap.{dm,group}.{max_messages,max_tokens}`/`work_gate.{dm,group}.{scope,extra_exempt_tools}`; `satellite.tail`. The interjection table (§ "Message steering") now has no dead-end: a reply to a `running`/`resuming` session interjects, to a `completed` + eligible session resumes, and to a stale/gated/non-resumable one starts fresh.

### Follow-up folding (quick same-sender follow-ups)

**A quick same-sender follow-up is folded into the session its immediately-prior triggering message produced** (spec FOLLOWUP-FOLDING; the settled branch per spec SESSION-RECORDS §7), instead of being lost, answered half-blind, or spawned as a parallel twin. Matrix can't carry text and an image in one event — they arrive as a pair (`@miku look at this` then the image, or the image then `what do you think?`), and the slow side (upload, federation, decryption, captioning) routinely lands the second event *after* the trigger hold (§6) has flushed and the session launched. The same shape covers a quick **re-`@`** correction (`@miku weather in Paris` then `@miku actually London`), which otherwise spawns a second parallel session answering the superseded ask. Folding is the **same-sender** axis (the sibling of co-target coalescing's *reply-target* axis); it never touches **replies**, which keep their reply-specific routing (reply-steer / co-target coalescing / reply-to-continue).

**Three forms, three levers** (`classifyFollowUpForm`, `src/agent/follow-up-watch.ts`), mutually exclusive by precedence: an explicit re-address (`mentionedSelf`) is **mention**; otherwise an image-bearing event is **media** (forced-split, highest confidence); otherwise bare text is **text**. Each lever is a **two-clock gate** (`followUpGateDecision`), both clocks required: the **user gap** (`|followup.origin_ts − trigger.origin_ts|` ≤ the form's `user_gap_ms`) guards false-merges as the user experienced the timing — sound *because* the scope is same-sender (one homeserver clock, no federation skew); the **wall-clock lifetime** (`now − armedAt` ≤ the form's `wall_clock_ms`) absorbs upload/decrypt/caption lag without resurrecting an ancient session. Windows tighten as the address gets more explicit — media `10 s`/`30 s`, text `7 s`/`15 s`, mention `5 s`/`12 s` (defaults) — because confidence-it's-a-continuation falls (a re-`@` can legitimately be a new ask).

**The watch registry (`FollowUpWatch`, `src/agent/follow-up-watch.ts`).** A per-`(timelineKey, senderId)` in-memory map of the most-recent session that sender triggered — analogous to `SessionClaims`, but **persists past settle** (the settled branch must find the just-completed session) and is GC'd purely by wall-clock lifetime (a per-entry timer at the widest lever's `wall_clock_ms`, with a lazy expiry check on read). It is **armed at the claim-attribution seam** — inside `launchSession` (fresh) and `runResumeSession` (resumed), right after `sessionClaims.attachSession`, *before* `awaitTriggerReadiness` — so it always names the session that actually handled the trigger (the §6 trigger hold owns the pre-launch regime: an event inside the 2 s hold is grouped into turn 1 because the watch isn't armed yet) and is observable while that session is still blocked on captions (CLAIM-VISIBILITY-SERIALIZATION made the session claimed + visible-as-running before it blocks). Proactive and synthetic worker sessions never arm a watch.

**The fold fork (`foldFollowUp`, `app.ts`)** runs in `handleInbound` immediately after reply-steer and **before** the `!inbound.trigger` return / `accept` — so it catches both a group's non-triggering bare follow-up and a trigger-bearing one (re-`@` / DM message) whose parallel spawn it suppresses. It is **fully synchronous** (it preserves the accept→claim serialization invariant), making only the steer/park/settled decision and firing the actual delivery as detached promises. It skips replies (the reply axis owns those). A trigger-bearing follow-up reaches `handleInbound` twice (raw + post-hold, §6); it is folded on its **post-hold** delivery (which carries `inbound.trigger`, so native-fate reversion has a real trigger to re-dispatch), the earlier raw delivery falling through to `!inbound.trigger → inert`. Delivery depends on the owner's state at fold time:

| Owner state | Delivery |
|---|---|
| running, agent **attached** | **steer** an `<interjection reason="follow-up-*">` (real image pixels for media — see below) |
| created / queued / `resuming` / pre-`attachAgent` | **park** (`pendingFollowUps`, keyed by session id); drained on go-live, like co-replies |
| settled (`completed`) | **revival** when the follow-up was sent before the owner's run ended, else native fate (§8 "Late input"; fold-after-settle is gone). Folding never resumes |

A present record in `resuming` (a reply-resume's `runResumeSession` adopt→markRunning gap, no agent attached yet) is the resume analogue of running-pre-attach, so `decideFollowUpRoute` routes it to **park** (it drains on go-live) rather than letting it fall through to the durable row's fate; the genuinely-terminal-ish present states (`suspended`/`interrupted`/`failed-resumable`) intentionally fall through to native fate.

- **Steer (`steerFollowUp`).** Builds the interjection and `agent.steer()`s it. For a **media** follow-up it first waits only on the event's enrichment **download** (NOT captioning — the slow pool, irrelevant to pixels; the event is still captioned normally for history), then conditions the image to real `ImageBlock`s via the new `ContextBuilder.conditionEventImages` (which reuses `selectImageBlocks` over the single hydrated event); on any miss it steers caption-only rather than block. The steered follow-up is retained for `spawn_session` (reusing `coReplyInbounds`), so the agent can break it out if it judges it doesn't belong (named in the interjection text). A steer that fails because the owner settled meanwhile (it completed during the media download wait) revives the owner when it is revivable (`tryReviveWithSteer`, §8 "Late input"), else takes its native fate (`owner-settled`).
- **Park / drain / abandon.** Mirrors deferred co-reply coalescing exactly: parked follow-ups are steered in at `attachAgent` (`drainPendingFollowUpsIntoSession`), or — if the owner is abandoned before going live — reverted to native fate by the owner's settle listener (`revertAbandonedFollowUps`).
- **Settled owner (revival).** A follow-up whose owner already completed never starts a fresh session with the owner's record and never resumes it: when the owner is still revivable and the follow-up was sent before its run ended (`lateInputEntries` + `sentBeforeRunEnd`), `reviveWithFollowUp` revives it with the fold's interjection (§8 "Late input"); otherwise the follow-up takes its native fate (`fold-owner-not-revivable`; a revival that throws logs `follow_up_revival_threw`).
  - **Settling-window discrimination (`resolveFollowUpRoute`).** `SessionManager.markCompleted` updates the in-memory record to `completed`, enqueues the `completed` persist on the single-writer queue, then **synchronously evicts** the record. In the window between that evict and the queued write draining, a fold observes the record *absent* while `getAgentSession` still reads the row's pre-completion status (`running`/`resuming`) — so the naïve route (record gone + row not `completed`) would yield `none` → native fate, demoting a just-settled session in the feature's hottest window. `resolveFollowUpRoute` wraps the pure `decideFollowUpRoute` and routes that record-absent + raw-status-`running`/`resuming` case to the settled route (still named `resume` in the route type), which then needs the owner's late-input entry, not the row. A genuinely-terminal non-completed row (`discarded`/`interrupted`/`failed-resumable`) or a missing row stays `none`. (`decideFollowUpRoute` is left untouched — its `recordPresent:false, rowCompleted:false → none` contract is the *post-drain* truth.)

**Native fate** (`revertFollowUpToNativeFate`, the precedence-3 fallback for a parked follow-up whose owner is abandoned before going live (`owner-abandoned`), a settled owner that cannot be revived (`fold-owner-not-revivable`), a steer whose owner settled meanwhile and cannot be revived (`owner-settled`), or an unread steer at settle that cannot revive its session (`steer-unread`)): a **trigger-bearing** follow-up is re-dispatched as its own trigger (reusing `redispatchCoReply`'s spawn tail) so it never goes unanswered; a **bare group** follow-up reverts to inert (it is already a normal persisted timeline event — no loss). The fold has already consumed the event (`markSteered`, suppressing its trigger-hold twin), so reverting on a failure is what keeps a re-`@`/DM follow-up from vanishing; `tryReplyResume` mirrors this for reply-resume (the reply, always trigger-bearing here, is re-dispatched on a `runResumeSession` setup throw — and since the row is no longer `completed`, the re-dispatch forks FRESH rather than looping). Single-consumption is enforced by `steeredEventIds` (suppressing the trigger-hold twin) plus the raw-skip. Folding is an *extra delivery*, never a substitute for ingestion: the follow-up is enriched, captioned, summarized, and indexed as any normal event regardless.

**Config** (`[agent.sessions.followup.{media,text,mention}]`, cross-field validation in `app.ts` — each lever's `wall_clock_ms ≥ user_gap_ms`): per-lever `enabled`/`user_gap_ms`/`wall_clock_ms`. The whole block is optional (omitting it leaves folding off); `00-defaults.toml` ships all three levers on.

### Late input (trigger edits, late additions, redo, the hold, revival)

A request can be corrected after its session started. Source: `src/agent/late-input.ts` (`LateInputSession`: hold, effects, replay store, pending steps), `src/agent/request-progress.ts`, the runner's `lateInput.next` step (`src/agent/runner.ts`), the factory's `lateInput` / `timelineCutoff` options, and the "Late input" section of `src/app.ts`. Config `[agent.sessions.late_input]` (global; shipped `enabled = true`): `hold_ms` 8000, `extend_ms` 4000, `max_hold_ms` 20000, `max_redos` 3, `first_event_wait_ms` 10000, `replay_max_age_ms` 300000, `revive_max_ms` 300000, `skew_tolerance_ms` 0. Design record: spec LATE-INPUT.

- **Controller.** Every human-triggered chat session (not proactive, not bot-triggered, with an external trigger id) gets a `LateInputSession`, registered in `lateInputEntries` from launch until `revive_max_ms` after its run ended (a session discarded before it ran is unregistered, and a correction still in flight for it takes its native fate). Phases: `building` (also while a redo rebuilds), `running`, `ended` (and `running` again on a revival). The run ends when the runner passes its last late-input check (the runner's `lateInput.ended` hook, called first thing when the run settles); a step still pending then is never taken, and its correction revives the settled session instead. Until the run has settled the session still receives steers, so the revival test treats anything sent up to then as sent before the run end; the settle moment is the run end it compares against afterwards.
- **Routes** (`handleInbound` order: `routeReplyToRequest` before reply-steer, `routeLateAddition` before the quick fold, `maybeImplicitReply` at the untriggered return):
  - *Trigger edits* (`applyEdit` calls `onRequestEdited`): an edit of a trigger-group message by its own human sender. A formatting-only edit (same normalized text, attachments and mention) is a no-op. Removing the bot mention from a group mention trigger, or deleting the trigger, cancels; a deleted grouped part leaves the group. A deleted trigger message whose group still has a part standing (not deleted by its sender: a message deleted and sent again, corrected, inside one trigger hold) is no cancel: it leaves the group like a part, and the first surviving part (group order) becomes the trigger message (**re-rooting**, `rerootRequest`, log `late_input_rerooted {from, to}`): the session's trigger inbound is changed in place (it is the object the session record, its late-input entry and every build or redo read), and the session row's trigger columns (`Storage.updateAgentSessionTrigger`: id, external id, body; the reply-resume upper bound never moves back), the claim and the persisted trigger group follow, so `getSessionIdForRequestEvent` resolves the request through its new root. A cancel needs every part withdrawn. Discord deletions and Matrix message redactions reach this path as an edit with `edit.deleted = true`, once the stored message is first marked deleted (a repeated deletion does nothing; §6 "Message edits"); the correction compares the stored message with an in-memory deleted view. A deletion whose `edit.deletedBy` names someone other than the message's sender (a moderator's redaction) only marks the stored message (`late_input_ignored {reason: "deleted_by_other"}`); the request keeps it, and its trigger group still renders its content. An edit that adds a bot mention to a recent message (within the late-addition candidate window, not already a request) triggers it.
  - *Deletions before launch.* A deletion can land before the session has a controller (the provider's trigger hold, the trigger queue, the activation hold, a re-dispatch, a reply-resume's gate). `registerLateInputEntry` replays it in the same synchronous span as the registration (`replayPreLaunchDeletions`): every stored member of the trigger group that carries a marker goes through `onRequestEdited` as a synthetic deletion with the marker's deleter, so a sender's deleted trigger files a cancel, a deleted part leaves the group (before the build read the timeline, so no redo is counted), and a moderator's deletion changes nothing. `launchSession` takes a cancel filed this way right after the registration and discards the session before anything is built (`late_input_cancelled {phase: "launch"}`). Two earlier checks (`inputWithdrawn`: late input on, a human sender, the stored message deleted by its sender) keep a withdrawn message from doing anything at all: `handleInbound` drops an inbound whose stored message is already marked, right after routing, so a trigger delivered after its hold creates no session row (`late_input_ignored {reason: "deleted_before_launch"}`; when parts of its trigger group still stand, it is re-rooted on the first of them there instead, before the accept and the claim, `late_input_rerooted {phase: "hold"}`, and a queued one is re-rooted by the registration's replay), and `tryReplyResume` never resumes for one (checked on entry and again right before the resume takes the slot; a resumed run has no late-input controller, so a deletion after that point is not seen).
  - *Deleted steered input* (`onSteeredInputDeleted`, called by `applyEdit` beside `onRequestEdited`). A message steered into a session with a controller outside its trigger group (a reply-steer, a co-reply, a follow-up, a late addition or reply to the request delivered as an interjection, or a revival carrying one) is recorded on its entry (`steered`, by the ids of its trigger-hold group, with whether it is part of the request: a follow-up, an addition or a reply to the request is; a reply-steer or co-reply is not). Its deletion is treated like a deleted grouped part while the run is live: a moderator's deletion only marks the message (`late_input_ignored {reason: "deleted_by_other"}`); after the run ended nothing happens (`after_run_end`). Its sender's deletion withdraws it: one still parked for a building session is dropped, one still in the agent's steering queue is taken back (`withdrawQueuedSteers`; `late_input_withdrawn {parked | unread}`), and neither is redelivered at settle nor by a redo (`withdrawn`). One the session read already gets a short note ("{sender} deleted a message ({id}) they sent while you were answering. Leave it out.", kind `delete_part`, no content), or, when it was part of the request and the session can still redo, a redo from scratch without it (the rebuilt context never had it: it arrived after the first build's cutoff). A message deleted before it is steered is never steered with its content (`withdrawnBeforeSteer`): a parked co-reply or follow-up its sender deleted is neither steered nor re-dispatched (`late_input_ignored {reason: "deleted_before_steer"}`), and one a moderator deleted (or any, with late input off) is steered as the deletion placeholder, without its pixels. A session without a controller (proactive or bot-triggered) is never redone, but with late input on it still hears of a deletion: the messages steered into it (a reply-steer) are recorded the same way (`uncontrolledSteers`, by the ids of their trigger-hold group, dropped when the session settles), and its sender's deletion takes one back while it is still queued unread, else steers the same short note (`late_input_interjected {kind: "delete_part", controller: false}`); a moderator's deletion only marks the message, and nothing happens after the run ended. With late input off nothing is corrected.
  - *Late additions* (`routeLateAddition`): a message from the trigger's sender, sent after the request and before the session's first delivered message, within `candidate_window_ms`, not a reply. With `[decisions.late_addition]` on (§8h) each candidate (up to `max_judged`) is judged in parallel with the session's work, and its verdict decides it whenever it arrives (the decision call is bounded by its own timeout). The hold waits for the verdict and the join it leads to until the later of the trigger's arrival + `max_hold_ms` and the candidate's arrival, plus the point's timeout (the vision timeout for an image candidate with a vision chain); past that the held call goes ahead (`late_input_verdict_timeout`) and a later verdict that belongs is interjected. Without a verdict (the point failed) the quick fold windows decide. At most `max_folded` join: the bound is checked and reserved when an addition joins, so candidates judged in parallel cannot all join; one over it (or one that reached no session) takes its native fate, and neither a rejected candidate nor one whose join delivered nothing (its redo fell back to an interjection or revival that could not be delivered) uses the budget. A trigger-bearing addition brings its trigger hold's group with it. A message goes to the newest request its sender made before it (causality), and to none when the sender made a newer request in between that has no session yet (queued, still in its trigger hold): a message from that sender addressing the bot (or any of theirs in a DM, or one with a trigger claim) after the request, not consumed as a correction (one judged as a late addition and released to its native fate, e.g. rejected and redispatched as its own request, counts as a request). The quick fold defers to late input for sessions that have a controller.
  - *Replies to the request* (`routeReplyToRequest`): a reply from the trigger's sender to the trigger or a grouped part always belongs (no gate, no judgement; it counts toward `max_folded`). A reply that triggers (a DM, a mention) is decided on its trigger-bearing delivery after the trigger hold, never on the raw one, like a late addition. After the run ended it triggers like a reply to the bot's message; the session is resolved through the trigger (`getSessionIdForRequestEvent`, also used by `planRecordInjections` for its record).
  - *Implicit replies* (`[decisions.implicit_reply]`, §8h): a yes records the bot message as the candidate's reply context (`reply_contexts`) and handles it as a reply (reply-steer into a still-running session, else a reply trigger).
- **Delivery** (`deliverCorrection`): while nothing irreversible happened and `max_redos` is not used up, a correction **redoes the session from scratch** (a withdrawal cancels it: nothing is sent, the session is discarded). The redo or cancel is filed synchronously when the correction is decided, before anything is awaited, so a held call cannot proceed in between; it carries a fallback (the correction's interjection). When the runner applies it, the rollout is checked again: an irreversible effect that happened since (or an undoable one that cannot be compensated) turns it into that interjection (`late_input_redo_impossible`, `late_input_cancel_impossible`). A cancel compensates undoable effects (a reaction) before the session is discarded. Otherwise it is **interjected** (the text names the correction, e.g. "{sender} edited the message you are answering. Before: … After: …"). A settled session is **revived** when the message was sent (server time) before the run ended (plus `skew_tolerance_ms`) and the run ended within `revive_max_ms`. Anything else is ignored: an edit after the reply only updates the stored message.
- **Redo from scratch.** Abort rule: a request still queued for scheduler admission is aborted at once; one sent but without its first stream event is waited for (bounded by `first_event_wait_ms`), because an abort before the first event loses the provider's cache write and may still be billed (`scripts/probe-redo-cache.ts` measures it). Undoable effects are compensated first (`compensationFor`), newest first, each marked once compensated so a partial failure never undoes one twice; an effect the tool reported as a no-op (`details.changed = false`: `react` removing a reaction that was not there, `pins` pinning a message the pin list already holds, checked against the list first with a 3 s bound) is not compensated. A state the tool cannot know is compensable: an unpin is always a change (the pin list can be incomplete: a page of pins on Discord, unfetchable events left out on Matrix), and so is a pin whose list read failed or timed out. Known gap: `react` adding a reaction the agent had already placed is not detected (it would cost a reaction lookup per call), so compensating it removes the earlier reaction too; when one cannot be undone the correction is interjected instead. A repeatable call still executing is let finish before the abort (its result lands in the replay store); a redo-safe one is aborted. The whole rollout becomes a branch at index 0 (`edit_redo` / `addition_redo`, `cause_event_id` = the correcting message, decision rows re-anchored). The trigger is refreshed from the store, readiness is awaited for added media, and the context is rebuilt with `timelineCutoff` set to the first build's `BuiltContext.timelineCutoff` (the latest `receivedAt` it read, or when it read the timeline if it read no raw event) and `summaryCoverage` set to the first build's (its final summary selection and the compaction state it read; the rebuild neither selects coverage again, nor waits on summary jobs, nor saves compaction state): later messages from others stay out, a summary job that completed between the builds changes nothing, the trigger group comes in whenever it arrived, so the prefix up to the final turn is byte-identical (test/late-input-rebuild.test.ts). Routing and record planning run again and the refusal pin is cleared. The new agent gets a new capture, gate and redo handler; interjections already delivered are steered into it again, and so are steers the old agent queued but never read (some reach it while the rebuild runs, when it is still the session's agent). While the context is rebuilt the session is `building` again: a correction meanwhile joins the rebuild (built again, no request sent for the stale build) and an interjection is parked until the new agent runs. A restart filed while the redo compensated or forked the old rollout (still `running`) joins the same rebuild. The runner checks for a pending redo or cancel (`lateInput.pending`) before every request it issues after an await (the run's first request, the continue after a refusal or contract redo, the request after an applied step) and applies the step instead: a step filed while the agent was idle found nothing to abort, and a later correction aborts again. Its first visible call is held again. `agent_sessions.redo_count` counts redos. A correction during the build rebuilds in place before the first request, with no branch; one past `max_redos` is interjected. Concurrent corrections merge into one pending restart.
- **The irreversibility hold.** The hold wrapper sits outside the output gate, so the gate's evaluation (started at `toolcall_end`) runs during the wait. The first `irreversible` or `undoable` call of a running chat session waits until `trigger receivedAt + hold_ms` (each correction extends it by `extend_ms`, bounded at `max_hold_ms`) and for pending late-addition verdicts. A correction during the wait cancels the call: it never executes and its span is discarded. Later irreversible calls, the record turn and synthetic injections are never held. A visible call's effect is recorded before it executes, so a correction arriving while it runs (a send on its way out) interjects; only a failure the tool reports cleanly (`error: …`) downgrades it, and a throw, an abort included, still counts. A call a wrapper stopped before it ran (the output gate's block of a send, the record-turn gate) throws a `NotExecutedError` (`src/tools/side-effects.ts`; the agent sees the same error message): it leaves no effect, and the hold applies again to the next visible call. The wait is stamped on the tool result as `lateInputHold { heldMs, reason }` (log `irreversible_hold`).
- **Abort and interject.** The interjection is steered; a generation in flight is aborted under the same abort rule (`turn_aborted_for_interjection`), the runner moves the aborted partial turn into a `turn_aborted` branch and continues. An executing tool is left to finish.
- **Replay.** Redo-safe and repeatable results are stored per call key (name and canonical arguments, without the prefill's `analysis`) and served when no call with the same key exists on the live lineage. Both sides use the transcript's own arguments for the call (never the executed parameters, which validation coerced and stripped), so only discarded spans are replayed, at most once per lineage (`redo_replayed_call`). Never replayed: `load_skill`, `tool_search`, `no_reply`, `browser`, `session_record_tool`.
- **Revival.** A completed session keeps its agent, capture and gate for `revive_max_ms` (the expiry timer is cleared while a revived run runs and armed again when it ends). A revival stops the record turn (`SessionRecordService.abortForRevival`; a record turn not started yet is skipped), forks it away (`revival` branch), re-registers the session as running, takes the timeline slot when it is free, and runs the agent again with the interjection ("{sender} sent this before your reply reached them.") as the kickoff. The record turn runs again at the new end. This replaces fold-after-settle: a settled fold, a steer that found its owner settled, and an unread steer at settle (`steer_unread_redelivered`) revive the owner or take their native fate. A session no longer in memory (after a restart) is not revived, nor one a reply-resume has claimed (`resumeClaims`; a resume refuses a revivable session in the first place, §8 "Resumable sessions").
- **Trigger hold.** With late input on, every provider's `trigger_hold_ms` is clamped to at most 500 ms at startup (`trigger_hold_clamped`); the shipped Matrix default is 250 ms.
- **Logs:** `late_input_redo_requested`, `late_input_redo`, `late_input_withdrawn`, `late_input_redo_impossible`, `late_input_cancel_requested`, `late_input_cancelled`, `late_input_cancel_impossible`, `late_input_step_after_run_end`, `late_input_interjected`, `late_input_revived`, `late_input_ignored {reason}`, `late_input_rerooted`, `late_input_addition`, `late_input_verdict_timeout`, `late_input_compensated`, `irreversible_hold`, `turn_aborted_for_interjection`, `redo_replayed_call`, `implicit_reply_evaluated`. Storage (v30): `agent_sessions.redo_count`, `agent_session_branches.cause_event_id`, `usage_events.estimated`; `session_interjections.kind` gains `edit`, `revival`, `addition`.

### Model-scoped OpenAI prefill (§8)

`[models.<name>.prefill]` with `enabled = true` and `text = "We must "` forces every
tool call on that model to begin with an `analysis` argument matching the configured
prefix. This anchors persona adherence on models (GPT-6 Sol, Luna) that refuse to
answer as the persona under normal prompting.

**Contract**: validation requires non-empty `text`, `provider = "openai"`, and
`api = "openai-responses"`. `enabled = false` disables an inherited setting. The
option applies to agent sessions only; standalone caption calls are unaffected.

**Wire transform** (`src/agent/openai-prefill.ts`, `applyPrefillToParams`): on every
request to an enabled member, every function tool's parameters schema is transformed
to strict-compatible form (recursively: optionals to nullable, `additionalProperties:
false`, unsupported keywords removed) and `analysis: { type: "string", pattern:
"^<escaped text>[\\s\\S]*" }` is inserted as the first required property with
`strict: true`. Deferred definitions in `tool_search_output` items receive the same
transform. `tool_choice` is set to `"required"`.

**Per-serving-member gating**: the transform is applied via the `onPayload` hook
(composing with the Bedrock cache-breakpoints injector). Each serving fallback
member's wire Model descriptor carries `compat.prefillText` (the configured text,
or null if disabled), set by `createModelFromConfig`. The decision follows the member
actually serving the request, not the chain head.

**Analysis in canonical schema**: each tool's canonical schema gains an optional
`analysis` string property so pi's validator accepts it and stored transcripts retain
the argument as the model's own past function-call arguments. The `execute` wrapper
strips it before the real tool runs. On non-prefill fallback members the optional
property is harmless (non-strict, optional, never sent).

**Past analyses are never replayed**: the wire transform strips `analysis` from every
replayed `function_call` input item, so the model sees the forced prefix only on the
call it is producing, never repeated down its own history (a long working session
would otherwise put the same opening in context dozens of times). The stored
transcript keeps them all. The strip is deterministic and applied to every past call,
so consecutive requests replay byte-identical history and the Bedrock checkpoint at the
previous request's end still matches; a windowed variant (keep the last N) would
rewrite a history item every turn and forfeit that cache, which is why it does not exist.
The encrypted native reasoning items still carry the chain of thought between steps.

**`no_reply` tool** (`src/tools/no-reply.ts`): part of every chat session's catalog,
registered next to `send_message` and filtered by the same session-type allowlist; it is
not prefill-specific. Under a prefill-enabled member the wire transform gives it the
leading `analysis` argument like every other tool; otherwise it takes no arguments.
Its result carries `terminate: true`, so it ends the run the way a final
`send_message` does; under `tool_choice = "required"` nothing else could.
`isTerminallyValid` and `isExplicitNoReply` in `src/agent/runner.ts` recognize it as
terminal and as explicit no-reply, with the same dedup/claim/diary semantics as the
text-based `NO_REPLY` marker, which remains accepted for compatibility but is no
longer what the shipped prompts and templates teach. Under dynamic tool loading it is
always in the initial wire set (both the live registry and `splitDefsForDynamic`
promote it regardless of the configured `immediate` list): deferred behind
`tool_search` it could not serve its purpose.

**`drop_reasoning`** (default false): when true, native thinking blocks are stripped
from outgoing assistant history on the wire (via `onPayload`) without mutating frozen
snapshots.

**Why the argument form**: native function calling, pi's parsing, dynamic tool
loading, Bedrock cache breakpoints, fallback, and budgets all work unchanged. The
analysis argument is the most in-distribution form for replay. Compared to the
grammar/wrapper approach in MR !1: no re-billing on skill load, no JSON-in-text
encoding, no decoder layer needed.

### Model prompts (§8)

A model can carry its own **system-prompt preamble** and **tail** (spec MODEL-PROMPTS), so a session whose requests move between model families (routing §8h, per-user selection §8g, fallback §8a) gives each model the framing it was trained on without forcing it on the others.

**Config.** Named profiles, each with an optional `preamble` and `tail`; each position takes exactly one source: inline `text`, `file` (relative to the config directory, made absolute at load), or `workspace_file` (relative to the serving agent's workspace, which is also how agents get different text for the same profile):

```toml
[model_prompts.claude]
preamble = { file = "model-prompts/claude.md" }
tail     = { workspace_file = "MODEL_TAIL.md" }

[models.claude_opus]
model_prompt = "claude"                       # default for every session type

[agent.session_types.summarize.model_prompts]
claude_opus = "claude_worker"                 # this model in this session type
"*" = "none"                                  # every other model in this session type
```

**Resolution** (`resolveModelPromptProfile`, `src/agent/model-prompts.ts`), per session type `T` and serving member `M`: `session_types.T.model_prompts[M]` → `session_types.T.model_prompts["*"]` → `models.M.model_prompt` → none. The first rung present wins, including `"none"`; an override replaces the whole profile. Startup errors (`validateModelPrompts`, config loader): an undefined profile name, a key that is neither `"*"` nor a `[models.*]` id, a profile named `none`, a profile with neither position, a position with zero or several sources, a missing `file`, `model_prompt` on a `system-one` model. A missing `workspace_file` is not checked at startup.

**Loading.** `AgentSessionFactory.create` reads the profiles of every member reachable from the session's heads (the session-type model plus, under per-user selection, the routed cascade and preference list, plus every model of a refusal rule whose scope admits the session's site (and `record_turn` for chat sessions), agent and tasks, plus a resumed refusal pin's model (§8j), each expanded through its fallback chain) once, before building the composites, and holds the text for the session's lifetime: a running session never sees its bytes change; the next session (or a resume, which re-creates the session) reads the current files. An empty or whitespace-only source means **not set**: the position is omitted silently, and since that profile was the one resolved, no lower rung is consulted (an override pointing at an empty file acts like `"none"` for that position), so an operator can keep placeholder files and fill them in later without touching config. A `workspace_file` that does not exist is likewise silent (debug log): it is how one agent goes without a profile another agent's workspace provides. Any other unreadable source (a vanished config-dir `file`, an escaping path) omits the position with a `model_prompt_source_missing` warning. Each resolved member logs `model_prompt_resolved` (profile, rung, sources, hash).

**Preamble.** Applied per attempt by `withModelPrompt`, installed through `buildModelFallback`'s `wrapMember` hook as the **outermost** per-member wrapper (outside admission; never on the background prober's bare stream fn): `"<preamble>\n\n<system prompt>"`, nothing before it, no wrapper element. pi-ai maps `systemPrompt` to each API's native slot. `AgentState.systemPrompt`, the builder's system message and `systemPromptSegments` stay model-neutral.

**Tail.** Inserted after `TAIL.md` and the routed tail files, before `<session_instruction>`, as `<tail_instructions source="<workspace path>">` (for a `workspace_file`) or a bare `<tail_instructions>`. **Nothing is written into the stored text**: `renderSatelliteBlockWithTailSlot` returns the slot as metadata, the builder records it on the satellite-bearing turn as `modelTailAt: { offset, join }` (fresh build, generation build, and each reply-resume turn when `resume.satellite.tail` is on; independent of `tail_file = null`), and it persists with the snapshot/transcript like `tier`. `convertToLlm` copies it onto the wire `Message` under the `MODEL_TAIL_AT` symbol (symbol keys never reach a payload), and `withModelPrompt` splices the member's tail in at every recorded slot (the leading text part of an image-bearing turn). A member without a tail sends content byte-identical to the feature-off render; messages without a slot keep their object identity (other per-member wrappers key on it). Because insertion runs over the whole message list per attempt, a failover rewrites every earlier kickoff turn to the new member's tail, so each member sees a byte-stable history of its own.

**Accounting.** `memberOverheadTokens` subtracts each member's model-prompt tokens from its operative window for fits and enforcement (`memberWindows`, `maxOperativeContextWindow`); its Model descriptor keeps the real window. The §5.3 running counter stays model-neutral so the overhead is never counted twice. Provider caches are per upstream model, so per-member text adds no cache misses; editing a prompt file makes the next session's first request cold for that lineage.

**Observability.** Agent-loop `usage_events` rows carry `model_prompt` (profile) and `model_prompt_hash` (12-hex sha256 of the exact preamble + tail bytes sent) for the served member, beside `system_prompt_hash` (the frozen model-neutral system prompt's hash); a change in either is a `prompt_changed` marker on the model behaviour page (§8k). `GET /api/sessions/:id` returns `modelPrompts` (`Storage.getSessionModelPrompts`: one row per served member × profile × hash, with request counts) and the console session panel lists them. Context dumps record the head member's resolution (`modelPrompt`) and each turn's `modelTailAt`. The prompt text itself is not persisted; the hash plus the source files identify it.

**Out of scope.** Decision models (`system-one`) and the fetch-chain lanes that are not sessions (captioning, embeddings, x_search, image_gen).

### Frozen context (built once)

A session's context is built **once, at creation, and is append-only thereafter** — it is never rebuilt per turn. `factory.create()`:

1. Calls `ContextBuilder.build()` a single time and dumps the result.
2. Splits the output (`splitBuiltContext`) into:
   - **`frozenBase`** — the prefix (system prompt is held in `AgentState`, plus the summary/compact/rich tiers). Cached in the `transformContext` closure and never rebuilt.
   - **`finalTurn`** — the last message: the rich `triggerGroup` (chat) or the `satellite` (generation builds: summarization cutoff, condense, and diary-range). Returned to the caller — for a summarization session it is delivered as the sole kickoff (§9b).
3. The caller kicks the loop with `agent.prompt(finalTurn)` — or, on the chat lane, with `CreatedAgent.kickoff` = `[finalTurn, ...synthetic call pairs]` (routing skill preloads and session-record injections, executed inside `create()`; §8h "Routing", §8i "Injection") — so the final turn is the **first message of the live transcript** — delivered once, not duplicated. The synthetic pairs follow it, so the frozen prefix and its cache are untouched.

`transformContext` then just returns `[...frozenBase, ...liveMessages.filter(isLiveRuntimeMessage)]` on every call. Because the final turn now arrives as a genuine live message, the filter **keeps** `triggerGroup`/`satellite` and **drops** historical `chatEvent`s (those remain in the prefix).

Why: rebuilding the prefix between tool turns invalidated prefix caching on every tool round-trip, re-spliced ambient timeline traffic above the trigger mid-session, and echoed the session's own sent messages back as history. Building once makes the prefix byte-stable (cache-optimal), coherent (the session sees the world as it was when it started), and a clean foundation for durable persistence and resume. (The full Phase-0 drift rationale that motivated frozen sessions is captured in this section.) A `resume` option on `create()` reuses a stored snapshot as `frozenBase` instead of rebuilding (the continue-mode manual resume path — see "Session parking & manual resume"; fresh-mode resume rebuilds rather than passing `resume`); the resume path **defensively copies** both the stored snapshot (into `frozenBase`, then freezes it) and the stored transcript (into `agent.state.messages`) so the live, in-place-mutated runtime state never aliases — or corrupts — the caller's persisted `context_snapshot_json` / `transcript_json` arrays (§6).

Alongside `frozenBase`, the factory surfaces a richer **frozen snapshot** on `CreatedAgent` for persistence and verbatim rendering (§10a): `snapshot` is the frozen context **prefix** — `built.messages` minus the final live user turn, returned by `splitBuiltContext` from the **same** boundary cut as `frozenBase` (so the two never diverge) — kept as `ContextMessage[]` that **retains the leading `system` message and the summary/compact/rich tiers with their `tier`/`tokenEstimate` metadata**. This is deliberately richer than the runtime `frozenBase`, which drops the system message (held separately in `AgentState`) and discards tier metadata; the verbatim renderer needs the system block and per-tier structure to reproduce exactly what the session saw. The per-tier token totals (`tokenEstimate`, `compactTokens`, `richTokens`) ride along for the §11 top bar.

The **final live turn** (the popped `triggerGroup`/`satellite`) is *not* in the snapshot — it becomes the persisted transcript **head** instead. `mapBuiltMessages` carries the builder's per-message **`tier` and `tokenEstimate` onto that head message** (the `TriggerGroupMessage`/`SatelliteMessage` types hold both, optional), so the default-expanded final user turn in the verbatim renderer (§10a/§11) shows its real token count and contributes to tier subtotals — matching the byte-identical room-mode (preview) turn rather than reporting `0 tok` / tier `trigger`. These fields are presentation metadata only; `convertToLlm` ignores them.

**System-prompt segment breakdown (live preview only).** The single `system` message carries one whole-string `tokenEstimate`, but the prompt is assembled from named, separable blocks (`renderSystemPromptWithSegments`, `src/workspace/prompt.ts`): one per workspace file (`<agent_instructions>`/`<soul>`/`<tools_guide>`/…), one per inlined skill (`<skill_instructions>`), and the `<available_skills>` index. The same string that drives each block also drives its own `estimateTokens`, so the breakdown (`SystemPromptSegment[]` — `{tag, label, source, tokenEstimate}`) can never drift from the rendered text. It rides on `BuiltContext.systemPromptSegments` (computed on every build) but is surfaced **only** by the live room-context preview endpoint, attached to the `system` message wire (`segments`); the persisted frozen snapshot stays a flat string blob and never carries it — the breakdown is a live affordance, not session state, so no schema/migration is involved. In the verbatim renderer (`MessageBlock`), expanding the system block reveals a per-segment table (largest first) with a `segments Σ` subtotal that sits a few tokens under the block's whole-string estimate: the `\n\n` joiners between blocks and BPE boundary effects are deliberately left unattributed, with the authoritative figure staying on the message header.

**Tool-definition block (the dominant estimate-vs-actual gap).** Every request also carries, *out of band* from the message list, the full set of tool definitions — each tool's name, description, and JSON-schema parameters, serialized by pi-ai into the request's `tools[]` field. For a real chat session that block is ~10–14k tokens (measured ~13.5k for the full 39-tool set under the GLM tokenizer; cross-checked against real provider `input_tokens` to within ~0.4% by `test/measure-context-overhead.ts`) and it is the single largest contributor to the gap between the message-sum estimate and what the provider actually charges — historically uncounted, because the estimate summed only `messages`. `renderToolBlock` (`src/context/tool-block.ts`) renders it into the **same shape the system prompt uses**: a whole-block `tokenEstimate` (`estimateTokens` of the serialized `tools[]`, primary tokenizer) plus a per-tool `ToolSegment[]` breakdown, and the pretty-printed wire JSON for the inspector body. When `BuildContextOptions.tools` is supplied (the live `create()` path passes the session's real post-allowlist `filteredTools`), the builder folds the whole-block estimate **into `BuiltContext.tokenEstimate`** — so the frozen per-session estimate and the room-preview Σ both account for it — and surfaces the breakdown on `BuiltContext.toolBlock`. The block is **never a message**: it is not in `messages[]`, never sent to the model as content, and never persisted into a snapshot (so it can't be replayed on resume) — it is a display + accounting artifact only. The on-disk context dump carries `toolBlock` (whole + per-tool) for parity debugging. Both inspector endpoints prepend it as a synthetic `tools` item **above** the system message: the room-context preview from `built.toolBlock` (live), and the session-detail view by recomputing it (`AgentSessionFactory.toolBlockFor` → the `buildToolDefs` hook `app.ts` wires, building the set on demand from `buildSessionTools` with a timeline-key-synthesized inbound and applying `filterMcpToolsByAllowlist` (per-agent MCP scoping) followed by the session type's `filterTools` allowlist — the same two-stage sequence, in the same order, that `create()` froze the estimate from — memoized per agent+session-type pair; its estimate is already inside the row's frozen `tokenEstimate`). The block renders **hierarchically**: each tool's name, token cost, and its own definition text ride on a dedicated `tools[]` wire array (`{name, tokenEstimate, text}`), and the `tools` item (a `MessageBlock`, collapsible + default-closed in both verbatim views — room preview and session input — like the system prefix) — when expanded — shows one collapsed row per tool (name + tokens, heaviest first; `ToolRow`), each of which expands to that tool's schema. `content` is empty; there is no flat dump.

### Session capture

`attachSessionCapture()` (`src/agent/session-capture.ts`) is the shared helper that persists a session's durable record (see "Session capture", §8). On attach it enqueues the frozen `snapshot` **once** via `saveAgentSessionSnapshot`; thereafter it subscribes to the agent and on every `turn_end` / `agent_end` flushes the raw transcript via `saveAgentSessionTranscript`. The **first** transcript flush is chained behind the snapshot enqueue, so the snapshot row is always enqueued before any transcript write (without blocking the agent loop — the listener awaits an already-settled promise). The transcript source is **always the live `agent.state.messages`** — never the `agent_end` event's `{ messages }` payload. That payload is *run-scoped*: pi-agent-core's loop emits only the messages produced by that one `prompt()`/`continue()` call (`newMessages`), and `handleRunFailure` emits `[failureMessage]` alone — flushing from it would overwrite the transcript with the latest run only, silently dropping every earlier turn of a multi-prompt session (e.g. the trigger turn and first assistant response once a forced-completion follow-up fires). `state.messages` is canonical in every path: the loop pushes each message — including the synthesized failure message — into state via `message_end` before `agent_end` reaches listeners. Before serializing (`serializeForPersistence`, which the fork core also uses for discarded branches, §8j), both snapshot and transcript are sanitized: image base64 is externalized to lightweight refs (`{eventId?, attachmentId?, mimeType, sizeBytes}`) and `redactSecrets` strips credentials. The externalizer is **exhaustive** across every base64-bearing shape — `ContextMessage` `dataBase64` blocks (snapshot, retaining `eventId`/`attachmentId` for media-endpoint rehydration), Anthropic `{type:"image", source:{type:"base64", data}}` blocks plus a structural `source.type==="base64"` backstop, pi-ai inline `{type:"image", data:<base64>, mimeType}` content blocks (no `source` wrapper; the branch guards on the *absence* of `source` so it never collides with the Anthropic branch — used in `UserMessage`/`ToolResultMessage` content arrays), OpenAI-style `{type:"image_url", image_url:{url}}` and bare `{url}` blocks whose `url` is a `data:…;base64,` URI (sibling fields preserved), and a string-level backstop that replaces any `data:[mime];base64,<…>` substring inside ANY string with a compact size-bearing marker — so raw image bytes can never survive into persisted JSON (blobs are recoverable later via the media endpoint, and `loadResumeMaterial` rehydrates `attachmentId`-bearing refs back into bytes for the manual resume — see "Session parking & manual resume"). Decoded sizes are computed arithmetically from the base64 length (no full decode). The helper returns a `{ detach, flushNow }` handle and is **status-agnostic** — it only writes content, never touching session status — so it is shared verbatim by the chat and summarization paths. On the **error/abort path** both callers (`app.ts`'s run `.catch`, `worker-pool.ts`'s `catch (err)`) call `flushNow()` — a best-effort one-shot transcript flush — before `detach()`, so a run that rejects before any `turn_end` still durably captures the kickoff turn (and any partial assistant message). `flushNow()` never throws (failures are logged) and is additionally wrapped by each caller so it can never mask the original run error.

---

## 8a. LLM Request Scheduling

The deployment's LLM budget is scarce and **shared**: one gateway account (≈4 rpm) spans every agent session type (`default`/live, `proactive`, `summarize`, `condense`, `diary`) **plus** the `image_generate` tool (the gateway multiplexes the Anthropic and Gemini hosts onto the *same* rate-limited account), while captioning rides a separate, generous OpenRouter budget. The gateway queue is FIFO and provider-blind, so without local coordination a background summarization request can occupy the budget slot a live reply needs — **local starvation**, not 429 storms, is the failure mode. `LlmScheduler` (`src/agent/scheduler.ts`) is the process-wide answer: a priority admission gate in front of every LLM request.

### Groups: one admission queue per shared budget

A **rate-limit group** names one shared upstream budget. Groups are declared in `[rate_limits.llm.*]`; there is always a `default` group (declaring it merely tunes it) and **everything lands in `default` unless its model block opts into another group** via `rate_limit_group` (on `models.*`, `captioning.model` / per-modality model overrides, or `retrieval.embedding.remote`). The group is **never derived from the endpoint host** — a gateway can multiplex several provider hosts onto one rate-limited account, so host-derivation would falsely split a shared budget. Cross-field validation at app wiring fails fast on a `rate_limit_group` that names an undeclared group (a typo); an *unset* group is fine and means `default`.

`max_in_flight` per group is the **single lever**: the number of outstanding (sent-but-unfinished) requests the group will hold. Because the upstream drains FIFO at a fixed rate, local priority is only meaningful if the upstream queue stays shallow — bounded admission is what makes prioritization effective. Small (default 2) for the scarce `default` bucket; high for a generous one. There is deliberately **no local `max_rpm`**: a fixed local rate cap only ever slows an idle budget; the upstream-hard-limit case is handled reactively by backoff.

### Priority classes & ordering

Each group's queue is ordered by **class** — `interactive` (live chat; also the image-gen tool) > `proactive` > `background` (summarization) > `background_low` (diary) — FIFO within a class. **Group attaches to the model; priority attaches to the session type**: the live `default` session and the `summarize` session can resolve to the same model (same group, same budget) yet differ in urgency. The class comes from `agent.session_types.<key>.priority`, defaulting per session type (`default` → interactive, `proactive` → proactive, `summarize`/`condense` → background, `diary` → background_low, unknown → interactive; `defaultPriorityForSessionType`). Non-agent callers: captioning and remote embedding admit at a single implicit `background` (they sit on separate budgets and never contend with `default`); the **image-gen tool admits at a fixed `default`@`interactive`** — it shares the scarce budget, and pi-agent-core's tool ABI (`execute(toolCallId, params)`) exposes no caller context to inherit a class from, while every session type that carries the tool is user-facing anyway.

### Admission wrapping & composition with Layer-1 retry

The agent path composes `streamFn = withRequestRetry(withSchedulerAdmission(baseStreamFn, {group, priority, key}), …)`. The ordering is load-bearing: admission sits **inside** the retry, so each Layer-0 attempt re-acquires a fresh slot at the same `(group, priority)` — re-entering the queue under the same **model key** too, which is what makes N waiting sessions produce one probe during an outage instead of N retry loops — and **no slot is held across backoff sleeps** (holding one would defeat the shallow-queue invariant). The wrapper acquires before invoking the base fn, releases when the stream settles, and reports the terminal outcome on both axes via `noteOutcome` (see "Per-model health" below). If the inner stream *ends without ever forwarding a terminal `done`/`error` event* (an "empty stream"), the wrapper itself feeds an `environmental` outcome and pushes a synthesized terminal error — without this the consumer (pi-ai's `EventStream` only terminates on a terminal push or `end()`) would block forever and, when the empty stream was the half-open probe, the probe would never settle (the probe-settle safety net in §8a is the belt-and-suspenders backstop). An admission failure synthesizes a terminal error the Layer-0 classifier treats as **`aborted`** — an aborted wait (run abort/drain) carries `stopReason:"aborted"`, a stopped scheduler the `"scheduler stopped"` keyword — so shutdown stragglers settle in one attempt instead of spinning backed-off re-acquires against a gate that can only reject; because admission sits inside `withRequestRetry`, these synthesized errors flow through it and receive the Layer-0 origin tag (§8 "Origin + class tagging") like every other request-layer error. A *thrown* abort from the base fn itself (an `AbortError`, or the caller's signal already aborted) is likewise synthesized `aborted` and reported with a neutral outcome — never counted on the model streak (mirroring the retry wrapper; defensive, since pi-ai providers emit `aborted` internally today). The three non-agent inference clients — captioning, remote embedding, and the `image_generate` tool — each acquire around their network call only and feed `noteOutcome` on **both** the response path (status → group throttle + model streak) **and** a *thrown* request (connection refused/reset, DNS, timeout abort → an `environmental` model-streak hit, so a hard-down endpoint trips half-open probing even though it never returns a response). The one exclusion across all three is the **shutdown stop-signal abort**: a fetch (or admission wait) aborted by the client's stop signal is a neutral teardown event and is *never* counted on the model streak. Captioning (`InferenceClient`) is the sole concurrency control for caption inference via group admission (`max_in_flight`; the old per-modality `concurrency` alias is removed); its `stop()` aborts an internal `AbortController` whose signal is passed to both `acquire` and the in-flight caption fetch, so at shutdown a caption call queued behind a half-open probe is rejected immediately — `app.ts` stops the caption clients **before** `captionPool.stop()` awaits in-flight workers, so the pool never stalls for probe-window multiples during a caption-model outage. Remote embedding acquires per batch **before arming its HTTP timeout** (a queue wait or group backoff must not burn the request's wall-clock budget; a rejected acquire arms nothing); `embedQuery` also accepts an optional signal so an interactive build's inline auto-retrieval embed wait is bounded (§9d). The `image_generate` tool acquires at fixed `default`@`interactive` and composes a per-call wall-clock timeout (`recovery.llm_request_max_wait_ms`) with the agent's abort signal into `acquire`, so an image-model outage gives up within the interactive budget instead of parking the chat turn until the next probe window. Local ONNX embedding never touches the scheduler (no network). The scheduler is a singleton wired in `app.ts` (factory, caption clients, image-gen tool, retrieval subsystem) and stopped after in-flight runs drain.

### Escalation: priority inheritance only

`escalate(key, class)` raises the entry registered under a stable key: a **queued** entry is re-ranked in place; an **in-flight** entry is a no-op; a **not-yet-registered** key is **sticky** — recorded and adopted when the key registers (closing the claim/admission race), and dropped via `clearEscalation` once its subject is terminal. Escalation only ever raises, never demotes. There is no other escalation path (no backlog/age-driven pre-escalation).

**Priority inheritance** is the one escalation driver: when a context build must wait on a specific summary job (§9b wait-or-omit), needing it *now* promotes it to **the waiting session's own class** — the factory threads the building session's resolved priority into `ContextBuilder.build({ priority })`, so a live build escalates its blocking summary to `interactive` while a proactive build escalates at `proactive` (never outranking live replies); an unset priority (e.g. the console room preview) defaults to `interactive`. A needed summary can be in either of two states, so inheritance is a *pair* of escalations keyed by the stable job id: (1) **not yet claimed** — `summarization_jobs.priority` is raised (`Storage.escalateSummarizationJob`, raise-only, non-terminal rows only) so `claimNextSummarizationJob` (which orders by class rank desc, `created_at` asc) picks it next, and every future attempt's request admits at the inherited class; (2) **claimed, request queued at `background`** — `scheduler.escalate("sumjob:"+id, class)` re-ranks the queued entry (or pins it stickily if the request hasn't registered yet). The builder calls one injected `escalateSummary(jobId, class)` callback (it imports neither the scheduler nor the pool), built by `createEscalateSummary` (`src/summarization/escalation.ts`), which performs all three writes in order — job row → scheduler → `pool.notifyNewWork()` — with an **escalate-vs-terminal race guard**: after the job-row write resolves, it re-reads the job (synchronous read) and skips the scheduler pin + pool wake when the job is already terminal or gone. Without the guard, a job completing between the row write and the continuation would have its sticky entry re-inserted *after* the pool's `clearEscalation` ran — and since job ids are never reused, that entry would leak for the process lifetime. No deadlock or inversion is possible: the waiting build runs inside `factory.create()` → `build()`, which returns **before** the agent issues any LLM request, so a waiter holds no slot in the group it is waiting on.

### Unconditional 429/503 backoff — `Retry-After` honoured

Every group always honours a throttle: a request that terminates with a 429/503 pauses the group's **admissions** (in-flight requests are unaffected); any non-throttle outcome resets the streak. This is a **code invariant, independent of all config** — an unconfigured/`default` group still backs off, and configuring a group never disables it. Throttles reach the scheduler through two tiers:

- **Precise (status + `Retry-After`).** The admission wrapper injects a pi-ai `onResponse({status, headers})` hook into the stream options (chained in front of any caller-provided hook), so a throttle response observed at the HTTP layer reports its exact status and the server's `Retry-After`/`retry-after-ms` (parsed by `parseRetryAfterMs`: ms header > delta-seconds > HTTP-date). Fetch-based pi-ai providers surface error statuses to the hook; callers that hold the response directly (`image_generate`, remote embedding) call `noteStatus` themselves, the embedding caller passing the parsed `Retry-After` along. When a `Retry-After` is present, the **server-specified wait replaces the exponential window, clamped to the group's `backoff_max_ms`** — the same ceiling the exponential path obeys, so a hostile/absurd header can never black-hole the group beyond config (default 60s).
- **Fallback (string sniffing).** The Anthropic provider is SDK-based and throws on non-2xx *before* pi-ai's hook fires, so its throttles arrive only as a terminal `error` event whose flattened, status-prefixed message is parsed by `noteResult` via the same `extractStatus` the Layer-1 classifier uses — no headers survive that path, so no `Retry-After` (exponential backoff + jitter between `backoff_base_ms`/`backoff_max_ms` applies). A throttle already counted via the hook is not double-counted when its terminal error event arrives.

(The first landing of the scheduler simplified spec §5.3 to plain exponential backoff inferred from error strings; that simplification is gone — `Retry-After` **is** honoured as described above, this section being authoritative over the spec's implementation notes.) Group backoff composes with (does not replace) the Layer-1 retry's own backoff: the failed attempt's retry sleeps without holding a slot, then re-enters admission, which waits out whatever group backoff is active.

### Per-model health — half-open probing & mass re-awakening

Health is scoped to the **configured model**, not the rate-limit group (spec LLM-FAILURE-HANDLING §5) — two orthogonal axes: the *group* is the budget ("the common upstream only allows ~4 r/m"), the *model* is the **failure domain** ("this specific model is down right now"). Empirically a model can be broken independently of the shared gateway being fine, and a gateway 429 says nothing about any model's health; scoping health to the group would false-couple them (with every model in `default`, one broken model would gate every healthy one behind its probe).

- **Health key** — derived, not configured: `modelHealthKey(model)` = `(endpoint/baseUrl, model id)`, as carried by the `Model` object every stream call already receives. Agent sessions, captioning inference clients, image-gen, and remote embedding all land in the correct failure domain with zero config plumbing, and config entries pointing at the same upstream model share one health state. The scheduler holds a `Map<modelKey, ModelHealth>` alongside (and independent of) its groups.
- **States.** `healthy` (no effect on admission) → `unhealthy`, entered when the model's **consecutive environmental-failure streak** reaches `recovery.llm_unhealthy_threshold` (default 3). While unhealthy: **half-open admission** — at most one in-flight request for the model at a time, the **probe** — for a model with a registered **background prober** (below) a synthetic out-of-band request, otherwise the highest-priority waiter for that model (a background waiter probes when no interactive one is queued) — admitted on a **per-episode capped exponential backoff** (spec MODEL-FALLBACK §4.1, *replacing* the old fixed `llm_probe_interval_ms`): the first probe fires `recovery.llm_probe_backoff_base_ms` (default 10 000 ms) after the model turns unhealthy — aggressive, to catch a quick recovery and return to the primary fast while work rides any fallback — then each *failed* probe doubles the delay (capped at `recovery.llm_probe_backoff_max_ms`, default 300 000 ms; a model can pin a tighter ceiling via `models.*.llm_probe_backoff_max_ms`, threaded through admission), and recovery resets it to base. An *inconclusive* settle (a plain 429 that absorbed the probe slot, or the stale-on-release safety net) reschedules at the **current** delay without growing it — a 429 is shared-budget pressure, not failed-probe evidence. Probe fails → stay unhealthy, next (grown) window. Probe succeeds → healthy, streak reset, delay reset to base, and **all of the model's waiters become admissible and drain in priority order** (the mass resume, paced by group `max_in_flight`). The capped backoff is a strict improvement for the no-fallback case too (faster initial detection; the cap bounds the long-outage tail). **Probe-settle safety net:** a slot admitted *as* the probe always settles that probe when its slot is released (`settleStaleProbe`, called from the release closure) even if `noteOutcome` was never called for it — a missing/forgotten call site, or an empty-ending stream that bypassed counting, can therefore never leave `probeInFlight` stuck and gate the model until restart. It is idempotent with the normal `noteOutcome` settle (when the streak path already cleared `probeInFlight`, it is a no-op — no double-settle).
- **Background probes.** `registerProber(key, prober)` attaches an out-of-band prober to a failure domain (the agent path's fallback builder registers one per chain member — `backgroundProbe: true` — idempotent, last-writer-wins). While such a model is unhealthy the scheduler arms a timer at each `nextProbeAt` and fires the prober itself — a minimal synthetic request (`"ping"`, no tools, 64-token cap, the member's own configured `thinking_level` when it is on, through the member's bare stream fn outside group admission; the thinking level keeps the probe's reasoning shape equal to real traffic, since a reasoning model that rejects thinking off would otherwise fail every probe and never recover) bounded by a 60 s probe timeout. It holds the same single `probeInFlight` slot as a live half-open probe, so the two never overlap (a timer that finds a live probe in flight yields; that probe's settle re-arms it). Any clean `done` (a `length` stop included) recovers the model (the same mass resume); **every** other failure is a failed probe (backoff ×2) whatever its class — a trivial request that errors means the model is not serving, and routing a 4xx through the neutral path would re-probe in a tight loop — except a plain 429 (inconclusive, current delay). Probes are logged (`llm_model_probe { background: true }`, `llm_model_probe_failed`) and never enter the usage ledger (an unhealthy model's probes fail unbilled; the one successful probe costs a few tokens). `hasProber(key)` lets the resolver skip the live canary for such models. Consumers that do not register probers (the fetch-shaped clients) keep live-probe recovery.
- **Read-only resolver hooks.** `modelHealth(key)` (`state ?? "healthy"`) and `isProbeDue(key)` (`unhealthy && !probeInFlight && now ≥ nextProbeAt`) expose health to the model-fallback resolver (below) **without any new mutable scheduler state** — the resolver only reads the same `probeInFlight`/`nextProbeAt` gate the pump uses, so resolver and pump agree.
- **Outcome accounting** (`noteOutcome(group, modelKey, classification, status?, retryAfterMs?)` — the generalization of `noteResult`/`noteStatus`, which remain as group-axis-only wrappers): a clean success resets the streak (and recovers an unhealthy model); an `environmental` failure (including a budget-cut stall, §8) feeds the streak — **except a plain 429**, which feeds only the group's throttle backoff (budget pressure is not evidence the model is unwell; 503/529 feed *both* axes); `content`/`aborted`/`refusal` outcomes are neutral — neither count nor reset (one session's oversized context must not pause the model, and a refusal is an answer, not an outage; an in-flight probe settled by a neutral outcome is inconclusive and re-probes promptly). None of them throttles the group (only a 429/503 status does).
- **Pump selection.** The pump no longer gates the whole group on one signal: it selects, in priority-then-FIFO order, the first queued entry that is **admissible** — group slot free, group not in throttle backoff, and the entry's model healthy (or unhealthy with an open probe window and no probe in flight).
