The default `[agent.session_types.summarize]` and `[agent.session_types.condense]` `session_instruction` text includes a bullet directing the model to refer to participants by display name rather than by account ID or handle. This makes every summary useful to any reader — including agents running under a different account that cannot resolve the sending account's ID — without requiring any per-deployment configuration.

### Budget-driven eager condensation

When `context.tiers.summary_target_tokens > 0` (disabled by default), the `SummarizationIndexer` adds a **summary-layer token budget** pass after the normal generation-threshold logic. After each reconcile, it estimates the rendered cost of the current summary layer (`renderSummaryLayer` over `selectSummaryCoverage`'s output) and uses a per-timeline **episode latch** to drive absorption-based eager condensation until the layer shrinks to the target.

**Episode latch.** The latch is an in-memory per-timeline boolean (reset on process restart). It enters (`phase: start`) when `layerTokens > effectiveMax` and exits (`phase: end`) when `layerTokens ≤ summaryTarget`. `effectiveMax = summary_max_tokens` if non-zero, else `summary_target_tokens` (no hysteresis band). Both transitions emit a `summary_budget_episode` structured log event. While the latch is set the indexer enqueues at most **one** condensation job per reconcile pass; the pool's completion callback fires a new reconcile, so each landed summary drives the next step.

**Live-edge guard.** A run whose last member has `latestTimestamp ≥ newestLatestTs` (the maximum `latestTimestamp` across all selected summaries) is never eagerly processed — it is the live edge and is still accumulating content.

**Job selection — lowest level first, selection-based candidate discovery.** The indexer scans levels from 1 upward and selects the first eligible run it finds. Within a level, runs are tried oldest-first. At most one job is enqueued per pass. **Candidate discovery is selection-based:** `tryEagerJobAtLevel` receives the `selectSummaryCoverage` output already computed for the layer-cost estimate (`sel.summaries`) and filters it by level — `selectionSummaries.filter(s => s.level === level)`. Pre-lineage-era phantom summaries (no `summary_parents` rows) that fall within a higher-level selection entry's timestamp span are pruned by `selectSummaryCoverage` and never appear as candidates, eliminating the production stall where such phantoms monopolised every discovery pass. **Run-splitting** uses the same selection: a gap between two consecutive same-level candidates is treated as an interruption when any selected summary at a strictly higher level has its `latestTimestamp` after the first candidate and its `earliestTimestamp` before the second (replacing the prior `hasSummaryBetween` DB query). **Absorption candidate parents** (`level+1`) are likewise taken from the selection — only resident (non-condensed) summaries at that level appear, enforcing the same invariant as the old `getCondensedSummaryIds` exclusion via the selection instead.

**Shape choice — absorb or bootstrap.** For each candidate run the indexer looks for an adjacent parent P (at level+1) — first left-adjacent (P ends at or before the run's start), then right-adjacent (P starts at or after the run's end):

- **Absorb**: P has spare capacity (`childCount < eager_absorb_max_children`; default `2 × condense_fanout`). A new level+1 job is enqueued covering P's original children ∪ the oldest run members that fit within capacity (oldest-first truncation). The job carries `absorbedParentId = P.id`. When the result summary P′ is persisted via `insertSummaryWithLineage`, P and the absorbed run members (those in `parentIds(P′)` but not in `parentIds(P)`) are atomically set to `superseded`. P′ replaces P at the same level with wider coverage — **same-level supersession**.
- **Bootstrap**: no adjacent parent exists, or all candidates are at capacity. A new level+1 job is enqueued over the oldest `condense_fanout` members of the run. This is an ordinary condensation job with no `absorbedParentId`.

**Top-level guard.** Bootstrap never mints a new abstraction level at the timeline's current `maxLevel` — `tryEagerJobAtLevel` returns without enqueueing when `level === maxLevel` and no absorb candidate exists.

**Guaranteed-saving guards.** Before enqueueing, both shapes verify that the LLM call is worth making:
- Absorb: `rendered(P) + Σrendered(runToAbsorb) − condenseTarget ≥ condenseTarget` (equivalently: combined rendered ≥ `2 × condenseTarget`).
- Bootstrap: `Σrendered(chunk) ≥ 2 × condenseTarget`.

**Soft-threshold / no-loop guarantee.** The episode latch cannot busy-loop: each pass either enqueues a job and returns (the pool drives the next pass on completion) or finds no eligible run and stops. A timeline stuck above budget with only live-edge or saving-guard-failed runs quiesces cleanly with no job.

**P4 idempotency.** Before enqueueing, `tryEagerJobAtLevel` checks `getActiveSummarizationJobs(timelineKey, level+1)` — a run that overlaps an active job is skipped, so a repeated reconcile before the job completes never double-enqueues.

**Mirrored timelines.** `isMirroredTimeline` is checked before `runEagerCondensation` is called; mirrored timelines are unconditionally skipped.

**Schema additions.** `summarization_jobs.absorbed_parent_id TEXT` nullable column (v11→v12, migration `addAbsorbedParentIdColumn`): a job that absorbs an existing parent P carries `absorbed_parent_id = P.id`; `insertSummaryWithLineage` marks the named parent and the absorbed run members as `superseded` inside the same write-queue transaction. `summarization_jobs.input_child_ids TEXT` nullable column (v13→v14, migration `addInputChildIdsColumn`): see below.

**Explicit child id list and span-integrity guard.** The absorb and bootstrap enqueue paths each compute a declared child id list at enqueue time (`declaredChildIds = allChildren.map(c => c.id)` for absorb; `chunkChildIds = chunk.map(s => s.id)` for bootstrap) and store it as `input_child_ids` (JSON-encoded ordered array). Before enqueueing, a `spanIntegrityOk` helper calls `getSummariesBetween(timelineKey, firstId, lastId, level)` and verifies the result contains exactly the declared set (same length, same ids in timestamp order); if not, the candidate is skipped (continuing to the next run in the same pass) and a `summary_budget_span_integrity_skip` log event is emitted. This is now defense-in-depth: selection-based candidate discovery (see "Job selection") prevents pre-lineage phantom summaries from becoming run candidates in the first place, so the guard's primary historical motivation no longer applies. The guard remains relevant for residual cases — for example, a phantom L1 inside an absorb parent's historical coverage that is masked from the selection (and thus not a run candidate) but still present in the DB at level 1 within the absorb span; in those cases `getSummariesBetween` returns it as an interloper and the guard correctly fires.

**Worker pool input resolution.** At build time, `resolveInput` for level≥2 prefers `job.inputChildIds` — when set, it calls `resolveInputFromChildIds`, which loads each child by id via `storage.getSummaryById`. If any declared child is missing or not in a terminal-success state (`complete` or `truncated`), the function returns `undefined` and the job fails terminally (no truncation fallback at this stage). This replaces the prior `getSummariesBetween` span query at build time, so interlopers cannot inflate the condense request even if the enqueue guard is bypassed. `assertDeclaredInputsRendered` (post-create, pre-prompt check) uses `job.inputChildIds` as the declared set for level≥2, verifying each declared child's content appears in the rendered condense input.

**Legacy-row handling and job deletion.** Rows that have `absorbed_parent_id` set and `input_child_ids` null (poisoned pre-fix eager jobs, deleted at the DB level by the v13→v14/v14→v15 migrations) are also handled defensively in the worker pool: when `resolveInput` returns no material for a level-2+ job — a legacy eager row, or a declared child that vanished or was superseded after enqueue — the worker DELETES the job row (`deleteSummarizationJob`) and logs `summarization_job_deleted`, rather than marking it `failed`. Jobs never linger in a terminal failed state: a failed level-2+ row would block the evaluator's chunk-skip guard for that range and surface as a permanently-actionable failure in the pipeline monitor, while deletion leaves the children re-eligible and lets the next reconcile enqueue a fresh, well-formed replacement. Legacy lazy rows (`input_child_ids` null and `absorbed_parent_id` null — ordinary condense jobs enqueued before v13→v14) fall through to the span-based `getSummariesBetween` path as a safe backward-compatible fallback, since they were never affected by the phantom-interloper bug.

**Observability.** Three structured log events are emitted:
- `summary_budget_episode` with `phase` (`start` | `end`), `layerTokens`, `targetTokens`, `maxTokens`.
- `summary_budget_condense_enqueued` with `shape` (`absorb` | `bootstrap`), `summaryLevel` (named to avoid colliding with the logger's own `level` field), `runLength`, `childCount`, `parentId` (absorb only), `layerTokens`, `jobId`.
- `summary_budget_span_integrity_skip` with `timelineKey`, `level`, `shape`, `startId`, `endId`, `declaredCount`, `materializedCount` (or `materializedCount: -1` and `reason: "boundary_unresolvable"` when the boundary summary is missing or has a bad status).

---

## 9c. Diary Memory

The agent keeps a **durable, first-person diary** of its own participation, written automatically and stored as the existing `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` files, then surfaced back into chat sessions so it actually reads what it wrote. This is the third memory artifact, distinct from the other two by *scope*, not tone: a **summary** (§9b) is a neutral, per-channel record of everything in a range; a **user profile** holds durable per-person facts; the **diary** covers only the moments the agent took part in, in its own voice, **across all channels in one shared store**. The cross-room sharing is a feature — it gives the agent unified memory of people and running bits that siloed per-channel summaries cannot.

### Trigger & unit

The unit is the **level-1 summary range** (one room, ~`generation_threshold_tokens` of messages). One range → one diary session → one appended entry. The trigger is a persisted level-1 summary: the diary runs *after* the summary lands and reads the raw lineage events at leisure, so it never races compaction (summarization never deletes events). Because summaries are per-channel, a diary session's input is always one room; because memory is global, every channel writes to the same day files. A given day file is therefore a heterogeneous append-log of blocks from many rooms — each block is self-describing via its header (room + date + time-range).

### Queue (the `diary_status` column)

There is **no new job table** — `diary_status` on the `summaries` row *is* the queue, identical to the `enrichment_status` / `caption_status` / `summarization_jobs.status` idiom:

- `summaries.diary_status` (`pending` | `processing` | `done` | `skipped` | `failed`, NULL for level 2+) and `summaries.diary_attempts` (persisted, incremented at claim time) are part of the genesis `summaries` schema. `insertSummaryWithLineage` sets `diary_status='pending'` on **every level-1 insert, unconditionally** — *not* gated on `diary.enabled`. When the feature is off the pool simply doesn't drain, so rows accumulate as `pending` and flush when it is turned on (no backfill machinery).
- `claimNextDiaryJob` claims the oldest pending level-1 row via CAS (`pending → processing`, incrementing+persisting `diary_attempts` in the same transaction). A startup `resetStaleDiary` sweep moves crash-stranded `processing → pending` with attempts preserved (a crash un-sticks the row without refunding its retry budget). Only `pending` is ever claimed → the DB is the sole idempotency authority; correctness never depends on file contents (crash-window worst case is a duplicate appended entry, never a loss).

### Pipeline (`src/diary/`)

`DiaryWorkerPool` is structurally identical to the summarization pool (poll, claim, `worker_count` concurrency, stale-reset on startup, await workers on shutdown). Per claimed job:

1. **Load** the range's events via the `summary_events` lineage (`getSummaryLineage`) — consulted only for the skip-gate; the session's *context* comes from the diary-range build below, not from lineage rendering.
2. **Skip-gate**: if the range has zero assistant (bot) messages, set `skipped` and stop — no session. This is the entire filter (the range is already small, so no participation-cluster filtering; scope is enforced by prompt). `skipped` is reserved exclusively for this case, distinct from an agent-judged empty `done`.
3. **Build the dictated header** (below) *before* spawning the session — the worker always needs a room label.
4. **Spawn one diary session** via the agent factory in the **diary-range build mode** (`CreateAgentOptions.diaryRange = { earliestTimestamp, latestTimestamp, summaryId }`; mechanics under "Diary-range build mode" below). The build produces the summarize-style prefix — system prompt, prior chunks' summaries leading up to the range, the range's raw events as real chat turns — ending in a popped `satellite` final turn. The worker delivers that satellite followed by one kickoff user turn carrying the read-only **recent-memory window** (`<your_recent_memory>`) plus the substituted instruction, mirroring the summarize worker's `[finalTurn, instruction]` delivery. The recent-memory window deliberately stays in this final-turn packaging — NOT as the interactive-style recent-diary layer after the system prompt (read side below) — so generation builds keep a memory-free prefix. The build also yields a real snapshot, giving diary sessions `context_snapshot_json` observability parity with summarize sessions.
5. On a valid finalize the worker **appends** the draft to the target day file (the range's last day, `latest_timestamp` in the canonical zone) and sets `done`. An empty (never-created) draft is the legitimate "nothing worth recording" skip → also `done`, nothing appended. On terminal failure, `failed` (no truncation fallback — a missing diary entry is acceptable, unlike a summary). The pool carries the same **post-claim terminality guard** as the summarization pool (§9b): any rejection escaping the job body's unguarded awaits (`insertAgentSession`, `appendEntry`, status writes, …) is routed to the retry/fail terminalization (via a `getDiaryStatus` re-read that acts only on a row still `processing`), so a storage failure can never strand a row at `diary_status='processing'` until the next restart.

Different rows (incl. different rooms) process concurrently.

Refusals mirror §9b: an exhausted hard-refusal rule for site `diary` fails the entry at once; with a soft rule a written entry is judged as an `artifact` and a run with no entry (or an invalid one) as a `rollout`, a judged refusal reruns it pinned to the rule's next entry (`diary_refusal_redo`), exhaustion marks it `failed` (`diary_refusal_exhausted`).

### Diary-range build mode (context parity with summarize)

Diary and summarize sessions see **identical context except for the final turn and the cut point** (the design intent the shipped lineage-rendered kickoff originally diverged from — see spec/DIARY-CONTEXT-PARITY.md for the history). `BuildContextOptions.diaryRange` / `CreateAgentOptions.diaryRange` is one of three mutually-exclusive (validated) "generation" build modes — alongside `summarizationCutoff` (level-1 summarize) and `condenseInputs` (level-2+ condense) — that share every gate: no trigger group, no recent-diary layer, no auto-retrieval, no reactions, per-event oversized truncation applied, label cache bypassed, compaction-state never persisted, no image blocks, runtime state suppressed, **wait-or-omit skipped** (the range is the work product; prior chunks' summaries are normally complete because jobs process oldest-first — a gap simply renders raw, never wait, never fake), `activeSessions` forced empty, and a `satellite` final turn. They differ **only in what they render as material**:

- **Cutoff** (level-1 summarize) cuts everything at the range **end** and re-bounds the summary layer before the first event being summarized; the rendered raw events are the material.
- **`condenseInputs`** (level-2+ condense, spec SUMMARIZATION-JOB-INPUT-INTEGRITY §3.1) renders an **explicit ordered child-summary list** as the summary layer and reads no timeline state at all — input-addressed, no coverage selection, no raw events.
- **Diary-range** bounds the summary layer at the range **start** (`selectSummaryCoverage(storage, timelineKey, earliestTimestamp, excludeRange)` — the same inclusive `beforeTimestamp` semantics) and cuts raw events at the range end. The diary runs *after* its range's summary exists, so an end-bounded selection would fold the work range into its own summary layer; the start bound plus an explicit exclusion of any summary **extending into** the range (and of `summaryId` by id) keeps prior chunks' summaries in the layer and the range raw. The exclusion is strict at the start boundary: a prior chunk's summary whose `latest_timestamp` equals the range start (millisecond collision from Matrix batch sends) is kept, exactly as the cutoff path's inclusive bound keeps it; a single-event range whose own summary sits exactly on the bound is still excluded. Uncovered pre-range events ride along as raw turns (benign continuity, same as the summarize build).

One asymmetry: the satellite for a diary-range build **omits the session type's `session_instruction`** — the diary instruction is a per-job *template* (`{{room}}`/`{{date}}`/`{{header}}`) that only the worker can substitute, and it is delivered substituted in the kickoff turn immediately after the satellite; rendering it in the satellite too would put the raw template into context.

### Diary editor tool

`diary_tool` (`src/tools/diary-tool.ts`) is a `summary_tool` variant over an in-memory `SummaryDraft` that **starts empty** (`create`/`view`/`str_replace`/`insert`/`finalize`). The agent writes only its new entry; the worker appends it. Old entries are never in the draft, so the diary session physically **cannot** alter or delete them. Two per-edit checks (revert-on-fail, refusing to terminate even on `finalize`; a failed check throws, an `isError` tool result exactly like `summary_tool`'s, and the worker still judges by draft state): (1) draft tokens ≤ `diary.per_session_budget_tokens`; (2) the draft, whitespace-normalized, **begins with the exact dictated header**. The header is dictated and enforced strictly — house style is not relied upon. As with `summary_tool` (§9b), the session ends via either `finalize: true` on the editing call or the standalone `finalize` command; the one special case is `finalize` on an empty draft, the legitimate "nothing worth recording" skip (the standalone command terminates the empty draft directly, replacing the older `view`-with-`finalize:true` idiom).

### Dictated header & split regex

Every entry begins with a uniform header the worker dictates and the tool enforces:

```
## <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM> → <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM> · <TZ> · <ROOM>
## 2026-06-03 22:30 → 2026-06-04 01:15 · America/Los_Angeles · #general (Earendil)
```

Timestamps are `earliest`/`latest_timestamp` rendered via `compactAgentTimestamp` (so header and body agree by construction); ` → ` is a literal U+2192 arrow (not a hyphen/en-dash, so the split regex can't false-match prose); ` · ` are U+00B7 separators; `<TZ>` is the **IANA zone name** from `agent.timezone` (the codebase has no abbreviation renderer; the IANA name is unambiguous and DST-stable); `<ROOM>` is the channel label, free-form to end-of-line. The read side splits/trims on `/^##\s+\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}\s+\d{2}:\d{2}\s+→\s+\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}\s+\d{2}:\d{2}\s+·\s+\S.*$/m`, which anchors entirely on the machine part. Legacy header-less files (imported OpenClaw memory) yield zero matches → whole-file is the only droppable unit. The single-`#` daily top header can never collide with `^##`.

### `channelLabel` provider seam

The `<ROOM>` token comes from `MatrixNativeClient.channelLabel(timelineKey)` — a thin wrapper over the existing `channelInfo` that builds `displayName ?? canonicalAlias ?? roomId`, suffixed ` (parentSpaceName)` when present (it is NOT on the `ChatProvider` interface). The native `MatrixChannelInfo` gains `parent_space_name`, populated in `channel_info_internal` by iterating `Room::parent_spaces()`: only **spec-legitimate** parents (`ParentSpace::Reciprocal`, `::WithPowerlevel`) are kept (`::Illegitimate`/`::Unverifiable` dropped), with a deterministic single pick (prefer `Reciprocal`, tie-break by lowest room id) and display-name-else-canonical-alias. The worker resolves the label with a small bounded in-call retry and falls back to the room id parsed from the timeline key, so the header (mandatory) never blocks a diary job.

**Placeholder dropping.** matrix-sdk's `display_name()` synthesizes a placeholder (`RoomDisplayName::Empty` / `EmptyWas`, rendered as the literal `"Empty Room"` / `"Empty Room (was …)"`) for a room/space with no name, no canonical alias, and no resolvable heroes. A shared native helper `display_name_or_none` matches on the **variant** (not the rendered string, which is localization-fragile) and maps both placeholders to `None`. It is applied in two places in `channel_info_internal`: the main-room `display_name` field (so `MatrixChannelInfo.displayName` is `None` rather than `"Empty Room"`, letting `channelLabel` fall through `displayName ?? canonicalAlias ?? roomId`) and inside `resolve_parent_space_name` (a placeholder parent falls through to its canonical alias, and if that is also absent no space suffix is emitted). All `channelInfo.displayName` consumers already treat the field as optional.

### Memory-file single-writer (`src/storage/memory-writer.ts`)

The diary worker appends to `memory/*.md` while chat sessions may concurrently `write_memory`-edit the same file, so **every memory-file mutation routes through one `MemoryFileWriter` FIFO**, mirroring the SQLite single-writer idiom (`tail` promise chain; a rejected op never poisons the chain). It exposes `ensureDailyFile(date)` (the sole routine creator of day files, writing the `# <date> Daily Memory` top header), `appendEntry(date, block)` (guarantees a `\n\n` boundary so the multiline split regex stays valid), and `editorCommand(args)` (wraps the text-editor abstraction). One instance is constructed in `app.ts` and injected into both the `write_memory` tool and the diary pool. `write_memory` is re-routed through it (chat edits serialize with diary appends). `appendFile`-level crash tear is the accepted crash-window cost.

### The recent-memory window (`recentMemoryWindow`, shared)

Both continuity inputs — the diary session's read-only context and the chat-side surfacing — resolve "recent diary" through one helper: list every `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` whose filename date is ≤ the anchor day, sort descending, take the first `diary.recency_file_count` (default 2), concatenate newest-last, then trim to `diary.recency_max_tokens` (default 6000) by splitting on the header regex and dropping earliest-in-text blocks (header-less legacy content is hard-truncated). It walks the **N most recent *existing* files**, not calendar `[anchor−1, anchor]` — day files are sparse, so a calendar window would silently surface nothing for a slow room; unbounded staleness is accepted (a dead room surfaces its last real entries). The anchor differs per caller: the diary session uses the range's last day; the surfacing layer uses the latest in-context message day. Both callers pass a per-day-file filter (`filterFile`) that removes the blocks hidden by the agent's memory filters ("Memory filters" below) before the files are joined and trimmed, so block boundaries match the index.

### Read side — recent-diary surfacing (core)

Normal **chat** sessions load recent diary so the agent reads back what it wrote — without this the diary is write-only. A dedicated context layer (`src/context/diary-layer.ts`) sits **after the system prompt and before the summaries layer** (top-to-bottom: system → diary → summaries), anchored at the latest in-context message day (NOT wall-clock, so backfill/replay stay correct). It is a flat cross-room recency dump (exactly what worked in OpenClaw; each block's `· <ROOM>` header gives attribution), bounded by the same window + trim as above. It is **omitted from generation builds** (summarizer cutoff, condense, and diary-range) — temporally wrong and a feedback risk; the diary session's own continuity window rides in its final-turn kickoff instead (write side above). It changes a few times/day (on diary writes), invalidating the cached suffix below it — an accepted cost. Recency surfacing (this layer) is the *what-I-wrote-lately* read-path; **relevance**-based retrieval over the same corpus (hybrid lexical+semantic search, the `recall_memory` tool, and cache-safe auto-retrieval) is implemented separately in **§9d**.

### Memory filters (`src/retrieval/filters/`)

The operator defines criteria for memories that should not be pushed into the agent's context: a reversible alternative to editing or deleting diary entries that keeps working as new entries are written (e.g. entries describing behaviour the operator no longer wants, which would otherwise reinforce it in a loop). It is **not access control**: direct file reads (editor, bash) stay unfiltered by design.

**Kinds** (`[retrieval.filters.<key>]`, resolved and validated at startup by `resolveMemoryFilters` / `validateMemoryFilters`):
- **judged** (`description`, optional `examples = { hide, keep }`, `threshold` default 0.8): a `noul` on the `memory` decision point's chain (or `[retrieval.filters].model`);
- **keyword** (`keywords`): case-insensitive whole words or phrases (the check catalogue's word-list compiler);
- **pattern** (`patterns`): regular expressions over the block text (a leading `(?i)` makes one case-insensitive), compiled at startup; an invalid one is a config error.
- A judged filter with keywords/patterns uses them as a **pre-gate**: only matching blocks are judged.
- **Time scope** (`after` inclusive, `before` exclusive; a date is the start of that day in the agent timezone, a datetime without a zone is read in it, `Z`/offsets are honoured): compared with the block's entry time (its header's end time, else the dated file's noon); a block outside the range never touches the filter, and a block with no entry time is out of range for any bounded filter.
- `enabled` per filter; `[agents.<name>.retrieval.filters]` deep-merges over the global table, recursively (`mergeFilterTables`: an agent's `examples.keep` alone keeps the global `examples.hide`; an agent can disable a global filter or add its own; `pending`/`model` override). An agent `enabled = false` for a key the global table does not define is ignored, and startup warns `memory_filter_disable_unknown`.
- `model` (global or per agent) names the **decision** model (`api = "system-one"`) that judges the filters; startup rejects a chat model or an unknown key with a clear error (`validateDecisionsConfig`).

**Evaluation** (`MemoryFilterService`): time scope first, then the mechanical match; judged filters only where a block is about to be shown, **lazily, with no corpus pass and no backfill**, cached in `memory_filter_verdicts (agent, content_hash, filter_key, filter_hash, probability, hidden, model, served_version, evaluated_at)`. `filter_hash` covers the description, examples, threshold, pre-gate and time range, so an edited filter's verdicts are stale and re-judged the next time the block surfaces; a disabled filter is simply not consulted. Where verdicts come from: auto-retrieval asks the pending filter questions inside its per-passage relevance requests (§9d) and stores them; the recency layer, the diary writer's continuity window and the memory search tools judge a block without a fresh verdict in one request of its own (`memoryFilterPoint`, all such blocks in parallel, bounded by the point's timeout). An unavailable verdict (timeout, chain outage) follows `[retrieval.filters].pending` (`"show"` default, or `"hide"`) for judged filters only; mechanical filters always apply and cached verdicts keep applying during an outage. **Judged filters need the memory point**: without it they do not apply, and startup logs `memory_filters_without_decisions` per agent; keyword and pattern filters apply regardless.

**Enforcement** on every surface that pushes diary text to the agent:

| Surface | Effect |
|---|---|
| Auto-retrieval (§9d) | hidden blocks are never candidates (cached and mechanical), and a passage judged hidden in its relevance request is dropped |
| Recency diary layer | hidden blocks removed from the layer (judged once when they enter it, then cached); the layer changes only when a verdict does |
| Diary writer's continuity window | hidden blocks removed, so a new entry never continues an unwanted one |
| `recall_memory` | hidden results dropped (the search over-fetches a little to keep the count) |
| `search_memory` | ripgrep lines inside a hidden block dropped: each file with hits is split into its blocks, and only the blocks the output shows (a matched or context line inside them) are checked, in output order, 8 per call, until `max_results` lines are kept or 48 blocks were checked; the output stops before the first unchecked block (`truncated`) |
| Direct file reads | not filtered |

File surfaces split a file into blocks exactly like the indexer (`splitFileBlocks`), so a header block's hash is its index chunk's and the cache is shared (an oversized block the indexer sub-splits is judged as one unit there).

**Calibration.** `scripts/calibrate-checks.ts --point filter --filter <key>` (§9i) calibrates a judged filter's `threshold`, also for a filter defined only in a side file.

**Audit.** `memory_filter_hits` records each block a filter hid (kind, the matched keyword/pattern or the probability, citation, surface, first/last time, count; throttled to one write per block and filter per hour), backing the console's filters page; `memory_filter_hidden { surface, hidden, byFilter }` is logged per enforcement (counts only). Write-time filtering is not done: display-time filtering is reversible and auditable.

### Runaway termination (shared with summarization)

Worker-driven sessions have **no wall-clock timeout** (LLM latency is unbounded; aborting on elapsed time would fail healthy-but-slow runs). The degenerate case to catch is a *loop*, so worker session types set high tool-call + turn caps purely as loop-breakers. Session-type `max_tool_calls`/`max_turns` (new on `SessionTypeConfig`) override the global `agent.sessions.max_tool_calls`; the factory enforces the tool-call cap via `beforeToolCall` (hard-abort) and the turn cap by counting `turn_end` events and aborting. This same fix is applied to the `summarize`/`condense` session types (defaults: 30 tool calls / 15 turns); chat sessions leave both unset (unbounded).

Hitting either cap settles into the normal catch → failure → retry path, but only because the worker **explicitly checks for it**: pi-agent-core's `runWithLifecycle` *catches* the cap-driven `agent.abort()` (and any stream error) and **resolves** the run promise — it synthesizes a final assistant message with `stopReason: "aborted"`/`"error"` and records its text in `AgentState.errorMessage` (`handleRunFailure`) rather than re-throwing. So `agent.prompt()`/`waitForIdle()` return without throwing; left undetected, a runaway (cap-aborted) or errored run would commit its partial draft as a success. Both worker pools call the shared `assertRunSettledCleanly(agent)` (`src/agent/factory.ts`) immediately after `waitForIdle()`, inside their existing `try` block — it throws when `agent.state.errorMessage` is set (the documented "most recent failed or aborted assistant turn" seam), routing the run into the failure → retry path. A clean completion — including the legitimate empty-draft "nothing to record" finalize — leaves `errorMessage` unset and does not throw.

### Config & validation

`[diary]` (`enabled`, `worker_count`, `max_retries`, `per_session_budget_tokens`, `recency_max_tokens`, `recency_file_count`) and `[agent.session_types.diary]` (model, a `tools` allowlist, the prompt, and the loop-breaker caps) mirror the summarization shape. The pool starts after summarization and stops before it during shutdown. When `diary.enabled`, startup validation fails fast unless the `diary` session type resolves, its `model` key exists in `config.models`, and — if it declares a `tools` allowlist — that allowlist includes `diary_tool` (the editor), symmetric with the summarization check.

**Read/enrich tools in generation sessions.** Beyond their one writer tool (`diary_tool` / `summary_tool`), the generation session types allowlist read/enrich escape hatches for content the rendered window cannot carry — a tweet behind a `[truncated]` hint or an enrichment mosaic, an aged-out or never-captioned asset, a referenced non-X URL. `diary` and `summarize` allow `x_fetch`, `media`, `read_image`, and `mcp_exa_web_fetch_exa`; `condense` (over summary text, no raw media) allows only `x_fetch` and `mcp_exa_web_fetch_exa`. Web fetch is the **Exa MCP** tool, not the native `web_fetch` — the latter is intentionally in `disabled_tools`, and the global disable is applied before the session-type allowlist (`filterTools`), so it never resolves; the **keyless Exa MCP server ships in `00-defaults.toml`** (so `mcp_exa_web_fetch_exa` is live out-of-box), and an MCP-tool name in an allowlist is simply a no-op for any deploy that removes the Exa server. These hatches inherit the session's background priority and are expected to fire rarely; the per-session `max_tool_calls`/`max_turns` caps bound their cost.

---

## 9d. Memory Retrieval (hybrid search & auto-retrieval)

The §9c recency layer surfaces *what the agent wrote lately*; this subsystem (`src/retrieval/`) surfaces *what it wrote that's **relevant** to the current conversation*. It is a hybrid lexical+semantic index over the **same `memory/*.md` corpus**, exposed two ways: on demand via the `recall_memory` tool (§10), and automatically via a small, cache-safe block injected into every trigger (read side below). It is additive — the recency layer (§9c) and the ripgrep `search_memory` tool both stay.

### Corpus & chunk unit

The corpus is `memory/*.md` only (not summaries or raw timeline events — both add index noise for marginal recall; the index is corpus-agnostic by construction via a `source` column, so adding a corpus later is additive), **minus a non-content denylist** (`README.md`, matched case-insensitively): that file is the agent's own scratchpad *about* the memory directory (how to log, what to keep), so its query-like prose ("notable room events", "user-profile updates") otherwise topped almost every auto-retrieval result — meta, not a diary entry, and never a retrieval candidate. Chunking (`src/retrieval/chunk.ts`) reuses the §9c diary-header boundary: a **header-delimited file yields one chunk per diary block**, whose `## … · <TZ> · <ROOM>` header gives free, accurate metadata — `room`, and an `entry_ts` parsed from the header's end timestamp **in the header's own embedded zone** (via `parseZonedWallClock`, so it stays correct across `agent.timezone` changes). Header-less legacy files (imported OpenClaw memory) and any oversized block fall back to ~`fallback_chunk_tokens` token windows with `fallback_chunk_overlap` overlap; their `entry_ts` is the filename date at local noon (else file mtime), `room` null. Pure-title/whitespace leading segments (a file's `# <date> Daily Memory` line) are dropped. Per-block granularity is what lets a citation be `path:startLine-endLine` and snippets stay short (a pointer, not the payload). Token measurement here uses the **injected, embedder-matched** tokenizer (`[tokenizer].retrieval`, default `gpt-tokenizer`), not the module-level chat tokenizer (§9 "Tokenization"): `chunkMemoryFile`/`MemoryIndexer` take a `Tokenizer` so chunk sizes and `token_count`s track the embedding model — switching `[tokenizer].primary` to `glm` therefore leaves chunk boundaries, content hashes, and embeddings untouched.

### Two layers, graceful degradation

Retrieval has two independently-useful layers, combined when both are present (`src/retrieval/search.ts`):

1. **Lexical (FTS5/BM25)** — built into bundled SQLite, no extension, written *synchronously* during reconciliation. **Always on**; a strict upgrade over ripgrep (ranked, not just matched).
2. **Semantic (vector)** — needs an embedding model + `sqlite-vec`; populated asynchronously by the embedding worker. If embeddings are unavailable (native dep missing, no chunk embedded yet, or query-embed fails at recall time), retrieval **degrades to lexical-only** for that query — never an error, never a cross-space mismatch.

So the feature works on day one with zero external dependencies; semantics are an opt-in quality upgrade.

### Schema (§7)

The `RETRIEVAL_SCHEMA` constant (interpolated into the genesis `SCHEMA`) defines, all plain SQLite + built-in FTS5:

- **`memory_chunks`** — one row per chunk. `rowid integer primary key **autoincrement**` (never reused, so a deleted chunk's rowid can't bind a stale vector to a new chunk); `agent text` (NULL = legacy / not yet stamped; set to the owning agent's name in agents mode — see §4c "Memory scoping"); `id` = `hash(path+text)` (content identity — an insert above existing blocks leaves their ids intact, refreshing only the mutable `ordinal`/line columns); uniqueness constraint is `UNIQUE(agent, id)` — not `id` alone — so two agents indexing identical seeded files get two rows, one per owner; `content_hash` = `hash(text)` (the embedding-cache key); `room`, `entry_ts`, `start_line`/`end_line` (citation); `model_id` + `embed_status` (`pending`/`processing`/`done`/`failed`/`skip`) + `embed_attempts` — the embedding queue.
- **`memory_chunks_fts`** — external-content FTS5 (`unicode61`, English) kept in sync by insert/delete/update triggers. The update trigger (`memory_chunks_au`) is gated on `WHEN new.text IS NOT old.text OR new.room IS NOT old.room` so the frequent embed-queue-only updates (`embed_status`/`model_id`/`embed_attempts`, and the whole-corpus `embed_status` rewrite in `resetAllEmbeddings`) don't needlessly delete+reinsert the FTS row (issue #11; the guard is part of the genesis trigger definition).
- **`embedding_cache(text_hash, model_id, embedding)`** — identical text under the same model never re-embeds.
- **`index_meta`** — `active_model_id`, `active_dim`, and the corpus-freshness signature. In legacy mode the signature lives at `corpus_signature` (bare key). In agents mode each indexer's signature is namespaced `corpus_signature:<agentName>`, so each agent has an independent freshness signal without global invalidation.

The judged-retrieval tables (`MEMORY_RETRIEVAL_SCHEMA`, schema v34) key on a block's `content_hash`, never a rowid, so a block that moves in its file keeps its tags, verdicts and token vectors: `memory_block_provenance` / `memory_block_participants` (participant tags), `memory_filter_verdicts` / `memory_filter_hits` (§9c "Memory filters"), `memory_late_vectors` (late interaction), `memory_index_failures` (bounded retries of the primary embedder's and the late indexer's encodes), `memory_retrievals` (one row per build). `agent` is `''` in legacy mode.

The `sqlite-vec` `memory_vec` virtual table is **not** in `SCHEMA`: it depends on the extension being loaded on the connection and on the active model's dimension, so it is created at subsystem init.

### Indexing pipeline — reconciliation, not a row trigger (`MemoryIndexer`)

Memory is *files*, not DB rows, so there is no insert site to stamp `pending`. Instead **content-hash reconciliation** (`src/retrieval/indexer.ts`), a per-file set-diff against `memory_chunks` (one transaction, so a search never sees a torn diff): new/changed-hash chunks are inserted `embed_status='pending'` (lexical is live immediately); vanished chunks are deleted (and their vectors pruned); chunks present in both with shifted line/ordinal metadata are updated in place (text identical → embedding preserved). In agents mode the reconciler scopes its set-diff to the owning agent (`WHERE agent IS ?`); when it encounters a NULL-agent row with a matching `id` (a legacy row from before agents mode was deployed) it **stamps it in-place** — setting `agent` to the current agent's name — without touching `embed_status`, `model_id`, or the vector index (rowids are stable, so the embedding is preserved at zero cost; the term for this is "stamp-in-place"). Three triggers converge on this same idempotent diff (the DB is the idempotency authority; a missed trigger costs latency, not correctness):

- **`MemoryFileWriter` hook** — `onAfterWrite` fires after every memory *mutation* (diary append, `write_memory` str_replace/insert — never a read-only `view`), enqueuing a reconcile of the touched file. The precise, low-latency path: a diary entry is searchable seconds after it lands.
- **Startup full sweep** — `reconcileAll()` over `memory/` (`listMemoryFiles` applies the non-content denylist, so a `README.md` indexed by an older build is treated as off-corpus and its chunks pruned), pruning index entries for files deleted off disk (catches out-of-band edits, e.g. the bash tool, and first-run legacy import). In agents mode the subsystem (`createRetrievalSubsystem`) runs these walks **sequentially** — one agent at a time — so each agent's stamp-in-place step on its NULL-agent legacy rows completes before the next agent walks. After all per-agent walks finish, the subsystem does a single **null-orphan sweep** using the union of every agent's on-disk paths: NULL-agent rows whose path no longer exists under any workspace root are deleted then. This ordering guarantees stamp-in-place runs before any sweep could misidentify a still-live legacy row as orphaned, preserving both rowid stability and embed_status across the upgrade. In legacy mode there is exactly one indexer (agentName = null); its per-agent prune already handles all NULL rows for its own paths, and no additional null-orphan sweep is needed.
- **Lazy on-search** — before each query, a corpus-signature check (dir listing + mtimes/sizes hashed into `index_meta.corpus_signature`); reconcile only if changed. Near-free when clean; the safety net if a hook was missed. The reconcile is incremental: the indexer keeps each file's `(mtime, size)` stamp from its last reconcile in this process (the hook's included), so after a diary append it re-chunks nothing, and after an out-of-band edit only the changed file. Concurrent searches share one check (auto-retrieval runs one per build and its searches skip theirs), and while the startup sweep runs, searches use the index as it stands instead of queueing behind it. At query time the per-agent reconcile does **not** sweep NULL rows (it has no knowledge of other agents' workspaces); NULL-orphan cleanup is a startup-only step.

### Embedding worker (`EmbedWorkerPool`)

The standard poll-status-column idiom (`src/retrieval/embed-worker.ts`): `resetStaleEmbedding` at startup (`processing → pending`), claim a batch of `pending` chunks (CAS → `processing`, attempts++), serve each unique `content_hash` from `embedding_cache` or embed the misses in one batched call, store the vectors + `model_id`, mark `done`. Like the other worker pools it honors `index.worker_count` concurrency: `start()` spawns N concurrent `run()` loops, `stop()` awaits all of them. The CAS claim is per-row (`where embed_status='pending'` filtered on `changes > 0`, inside the single-writer queue), so concurrent loops serialize their claims and never double-process a chunk. A `notifyNewWork()` sets a **sticky pending-wake flag** (and wakes any idle loops), so a notify that lands while a batch is processing isn't lost — the loop re-polls immediately rather than waiting out the 5s idle interval. **Partial-batch failure:** if the provider throws, only chunks whose embedding was actually missing (the cache *misses*) are routed to retry/`failed`; chunks served from `embedding_cache` in the same batch never touched the provider, so they still persist as `done` and don't burn unearned attempts. Failures retry to `max_retries` then `failed`; the lexical index is untouched, so search degrades to BM25. **Shutdown** threads an `AbortSignal` (aborted in `stop()`) into `embedDocuments`, cancelling an in-flight remote request so teardown doesn't block up to the remote per-request timeout (the per-request timeout still applies independently for a normal call); any chunk left mid-flight stays in `processing` and is reset to `pending` by `resetStaleEmbedding` on the next start. Independent of the diary/reconcile pools: a fresh block flows diary-worker → `appendEntry` → writer hook → reconcile (`pending`) → embed-worker.

### Embedding-provider seam & the single-active-model invariant

A query vector and the document vectors it is compared against **must come from the same model** (cosine across spaces is meaningless), so there is **one active model at a time**, recorded in `index_meta` as `(active_model_id, active_dim)`. Resolution (`src/retrieval/config.ts`): an explicit `provider` wins; an unset `provider` defaults to **remote** when a resolvable `[retrieval.embedding.remote]` block is present, else the bundled **local** model (the zero-config default + safety net). So `provider="local"` alongside a populated `[remote]` block runs **local** (the explicit knob is honored, not overridden) — `createRetrievalSubsystem` emits a startup `logger.warn` (`retrieval_remote_block_ignored`) for that likely-misconfiguration without being fatal, an asymmetry with `provider="remote"`-and-no-block (a fail-fast).

- **Local** (`LocalEmbeddingProvider`, `fastembed` / onnxruntime-node) — default `bge-small-en-v1.5` (384-dim, English). The native module + weights load **lazily on first use** (cached under `<data_dir>/models/fastembed`), so first-run download happens in the background worker, never on a trigger or at startup. **Model table** (`src/retrieval/embedding/local-models.ts`): each supported model name maps to its weight source and its trained prefixes. The BGE v1.5 English models (`bge-small-en-v1.5`, `bge-base-en-v1.5`) download BAAI's own fp32 ONNX export from a **pinned Hugging Face commit** (`ensureHfModel`: files land in `<cache>/<owner>_<repo>@<rev12>/`, each written to `.part` and renamed when complete, the graph checked against its pinned sha256; present files are skipped, so an interrupted download resumes) and load as a fastembed custom model with CLS pooling. fastembed's own source for these models is an fp16 GPU-optimized export with the same vectors that runs several times slower on CPU, which matters because query embeds run on the main thread. Every other model loads through fastembed's built-in table, which downloads from Hugging Face; an unknown name is passed to fastembed as a model id. The Hub base URL honors `HF_ENDPOINT`. **Prefixes**: documents and queries go through fastembed's `embed()` with the model's own prefixes (BGE: the retrieval instruction `Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ` on queries and nothing on passages; e5: `query: `/`passage: `; MiniLM and unknown models: none), overridable with `[retrieval.embedding.local].query_prefix` / `passage_prefix` (`""` = none). fastembed's `passageEmbed`/`queryEmbed` are not used because they prepend the e5 prefixes for every model. Still one model, comparable spaces. **Model id**: `local:<name>#<hash12>`, the hash covering the weight source (repo + pinned revision + file + pooling, or the fastembed id + a source epoch) and both prefixes, so any change that alters the vectors changes the id and the active-model switch below re-embeds the corpus. fastembed pads every input to the model's full 512-token max length; onnxruntime-node runs inference synchronously on the main thread, so the provider **disables that padding** after init (padded positions are masked, so vectors are unchanged) — a short query costs a short forward pass instead of a full-length one. Because fastembed sizes each batch tensor from its first row, unpadded documents are embedded one per forward pass.
- **Remote** (`RemoteEmbeddingProvider`) — OpenRouter/OpenAI-compatible `POST {endpoint}/embeddings`; batched `input`, optional HTTP proxy. Remote models are symmetric (query == document). The response is validated before use: a complete no-gap/no-dupe index permutation, one `dim`-correct vector per input, each element's `embedding` an array (a malformed element throws a descriptive error rather than a raw `TypeError`), and an advertised `content-length` above a 16 MiB cap is rejected before the body is read. Any mismatch throws so the batch routes through the normal retry path instead of misaligning vectors with content-hashes.

All vectors are L2-normalized. Vectors live in a `sqlite-vec` `vec0` table `memory_vec(chunk_id, embedding float[dim] distance_metric=cosine, source partition key)` (`src/retrieval/vector-store.ts`); `chunk_id` is bound as a **BigInt** (better-sqlite3 binds plain numbers in a form vec0 rejects) and `k` is interpolated as a validated integer (same quirk). **Switching the active model** (a different `model_id`, or a `dim` change that drops+recreates `memory_vec`) re-queues every chunk for embedding (`resetAllEmbeddings`: `done`/`failed`/`skip` → `pending`, `model_id` cleared) — the **lexical index stays valid throughout**, so search never goes dark. A query-time remote failure does **not** fall back to local (that would cross spaces); it falls back to lexical-only for that one query.

### Hybrid ranking (`MemorySearch`)

In agents mode `MemorySearch` holds one `MemoryIndexer` per configured agent and refreshes all of them in `ensureFreshForQuery` before each search. Every caller threads an `agentName` through `SearchOptions`; the `"__legacy__"` sentinel and `null` both mean "no filter" (legacy mode: all chunks visible). When `agentName` names a real agent, both the FTS half (`searchMemoryLexical` adds `AND c.agent = @agent`) and the vector half (`getChunksByRowids` adds `AND agent = ?`) filter to that agent's rows exclusively — un-stamped NULL-agent rows are invisible in agents mode (safe-by-default for the legacy→agents migration). The same `agentName` is threaded through `AutoRetrievalInput` (auto-retrieval), `RecallMemoryToolContext` (`recall_memory` tool), and `ContextBuilder.resolveAgentName` (a closure injected in `app.ts` that maps a timeline key's account prefix to its agent name).

The shared query path behind both the tool and auto-retrieval: lazy reconcile → embed the query (skip on failure → lexical-only) → in parallel, top `K·candidate_multiplier` from `memory_vec` KNN and from FTS5 BM25 → merge by chunk rowid into a pre-decay **`relevance = vector_weight·vecScore + text_weight·bm25Score`** (weights normalized; `vecScore = clamp(1−distance)`; lexical-only → all text weight) → derive the ordering **`score = relevance · 2^(−ageDays/half_life_days)`** via **temporal decay** from the real `entry_ts` (**default ON** — for a dated diary, recency is intrinsically relevant; differs from OpenClaw's default-off) → optional MMR diversity re-rank (default off; uses stored vectors, no-ops if unavailable) → **drop candidates whose *pre-decay* `relevance` is `< min_score`** → top-K by `score`, each with a `{path, lines, room, date, score, snippet}` citation. The `min_score` floor is applied to **pre-decay relevance**, with decay used **only for ordering** — so `min_score` keeps its absolute-relevance meaning and a high-relevance *old* match survives the floor (it merely ranks below a fresher equal-relevance one) rather than decaying below the cut and vanishing. The outcome reports `mode` (`hybrid`/`lexical`), `degraded`, `ignoredDateBounds` (date filters that were given but failed to parse and so were ignored), and `contradictoryDateBounds` (both `after` and `before` parsed but the window is empty because `after >= before`, so nothing can match — distinct from "no such memory"). The `recall_memory` tool surfaces all three in its header so the agent knows when the range wasn't applied or was empty.

The KNN/FTS halves filter differently. FTS5 BM25 applies `room`/`after`/`before` **in SQL**; the `memory_vec` KNN ranks purely by vector distance and **cannot carry the predicate**, so vector hits are filtered **post-hoc** (via `getChunksByRowids`). Two consequences are handled: (1) when a room/date filter is active the KNN is **over-fetched** (a larger `k`, `candidate_multiplier·K × FILTERED_KNN_OVERFETCH`, capped at `MAX_KNN_CANDIDATES`) so enough in-range neighbours survive the post-filter rather than the nearest-but-out-of-range neighbours crowding them out; and (2) the reported `mode` is computed from the **post-filter** survivors — `hybrid` only when at least one vector neighbour actually passed the room/date filter, so a query whose semantic half was entirely filtered out honestly reports `lexical`. The lexical half is wrapped in a try/catch mirroring the semantic half: an FTS failure degrades to empty lexical results (logged) rather than throwing out of `search()` into context assembly.

**BM25 → absolute score.** `bm25Score` uses a **saturating absolute transform** `rel/(rel + k)` (k = `BM25_SATURATION` ≈ 1.5) over the flipped BM25 relevance `rel = max(0, −bm25())` — *not* a within-candidate min-max normalize. This gives `min_score` **absolute** meaning: it is a quality floor in [0,1], so a weak lone match scores low and can be dropped, rather than the old behaviour where the best candidate was always 1.0 (a relative rank cut). FTS query tokens are stopword-filtered and scoped to the `text` column (`{text} : (…)`), so common function words and a token equal to a `room` label can't surface off-topic chunks. The `before` date filter is fully day-inclusive (the bound is the exclusive start of the next day, `entry_ts < nextDayStart`).

### `recall_memory` tool (read side)

- **`recall_memory`** (§10) — natural-language `query` plus optional `max_results`/`min_score`/`room`/`after`/`before` (YYYY-MM-DD) and **`user`** (a sender id as shown in context, or a current or earlier display name, resolved by one indexed lookup on `memory_sender_names`, at most 20 tagged senders): only blocks of conversations that person took part in (participant tags below) or that name them; an unknown person returns an actionable miss naming the fix. Answers *"what do I remember about X"* (ranked, fuzzy); complements ripgrep `search_memory`'s *"find exact string X"*. Results carry the compact citation and a **match-centred, cleaned excerpt** of `[retrieval.query].excerpt_max_chars` (default 600) characters ("Excerpts" below), so the agent can tell what was discussed and open the full block with its existing editor/bash. A scoped search scores exactly the scope's chunks (FTS restricted by rowid, cosine against their stored vectors). Memory filters apply (§9c). Registered for chat sessions only; **excluded from generation sessions** (their `tools` allowlist).

### Judged retrieval (auto-retrieval, `src/retrieval/auto/`)

A cited `<retrieved_memory>` block injected **inside the final user turn, before the trigger messages** (the trigger stays last; the final turn is volatile every trigger, so this costs the prompt cache nothing), built by `MemoryRetrievalPipeline.plan`:

```
query set ─► wide recall (hybrid lanes + user lanes + person-cued, fused, ~60 blocks)
          ─► drop recency-layer and filter-hidden blocks (§9c)
          ─► late interaction (exhaustive recent window + re-score) ─► top_n        [optional]
          ─► cross-encoder ─► top_n                                               [optional]
          ─► the `memory` decision point as the final filter, one passage per request (§8h)
          ─► excerpts ─► <retrieved_memory>: 0..N items within a token budget
```

**Placement.** Every session build gets a judged plan: `planMemoryRetrieval` in `app.ts` starts it at launch, right after the admission gates and in parallel with the readiness wait, routing, records planning and the context build, for any trigger (human or bot) and any session type; a proactive session's conversation stands in for the request, and a crash-recovery fresh rebuild plans like a launch. The plan is a `MemoryPlanTicket` (`{ plan, waitMs, bestEffort, confirm, abandon }`, `src/retrieval/auto/ticket.ts`) threaded through `CreateAgentOptions.memoryRetrieval` to the build, which awaits it only when it assembles the final user turn, for at most the memory point's timeout (default the global `[decisions].timeout_ms`) plus a 1.5 s grace (`waitBudgetMs`, spec §8). When that wait expires the build calls `bestEffort`: the plan is told to finish now (`PlanInput.finishNow`), its open judge and filter requests and the re-rank stages abort (freeing their slots), and it resolves within 1 s with what is ready, the judged keepers so far plus the fallback rule over the unanswered passages, with unscored excerpts (`report.cutShort`, reason `wait_budget` when no passage was judged). Only when nothing is ready (the plan was still in recall) does the build show no block and call `abandon`. **Each build records one `memory_retrievals` row under its session id, once its fate is known** (the plan runs with `deferRecord`): `confirm`, when the kickoff carrying the block is sent (a launch, a fresh resume rebuild, a redo's rebuilt kickoff), records it as shown; `abandon` first (no block, a cancel or redo before the kickoff, a failed build or rebuild, the session's end) aborts the plan and records what it would have kept with stage `aborted` (`report.aborted`, `kept = 0`), never as shown. Only confirmed builds count in the stats. The abort signal also fires at shutdown drain; it reaches recall, late interaction, the cross-encoder, the judge and the excerpt embeds (a hung embedder cannot hold the plan). A redo from scratch (§8 "Late input") replans on the corrected trigger and abandons the stale plan. Only a room preview (a build without a session) runs the pipeline inline, without the memory point (`judge: false`); judged filters it meets follow `pending`, but the recency layer it renders may still judge filters, billed and attributed to session type `preview`. Generation builds never retrieve.

**Input** (`buildPlanInput`): the trigger group's text (deleted parts empty), its reply target (stored, else the reply snapshot), the conversation before it (up to 12 messages, hydrated, deleted messages as placeholders), the **participants** (the requesters, the reply target's author, the users mentioned in the trigger; never the agent itself) and the **active people** (participants plus the human senders of the last `auto.query_messages` messages).

**Wide recall** (`auto.candidates` default 60, floor `auto.candidate_min_score` default 0.25 on pre-decay relevance): three hybrid queries (the trigger text, the trigger plus its reply target's text (when a reply), and the conversation window (the last `auto.query_messages` = 6 messages, as one **semantic-only** query)), fused by chunk with the best relevance and decayed score per lane; plus the **user lanes**, which reserve up to `auto.user_lane_candidates` (default 8) slots:
- *presence*: blocks whose provenance tags include a participant ("Participant tags" below);
- *name*: today's lexical lane over each participant's current name plus up to 4 earlier names: Discord usernames from the alias history and, for providers without usernames (Matrix), the distinct `sender_display_name` values that sender id has had in the timeline, newest first (`senderDisplayNameHistory`: a primary-key read of that sender's `memory_sender_names` rows, at most 12, so a build never scans a busy sender's timeline).
- Within the user lanes, hits rank by the request's similarity when it has content words (a rowid-scoped hybrid search), by recency otherwise.

**Person-cued recall.** For each active person, the newest `auto.person_recent` (default 2) provenance-tagged entries they took part in, outside the recency layer, at most `auto.person_recent_max` (default 8) in all. The tagged rows are read newest first in pages (`chunksWithParticipants` with an offset) past the recency layer's blocks, up to 200 rows, so a person active enough to fill the layer still gets their newest older entries; the presence lane pages the same way. No text match is needed (a bare "hey" has nothing to match), and these candidates **skip the re-rank cuts** and go straight to the judge, which decides whether each is worth having in mind. Being active in the window earns no near-tie bonus: only a participant's provenance tag does.

**Exclusions.** Blocks already shown by the recency layer (§9c; a normalized 60-character probe of the cleaned block against the layer's text, which the pipeline renders itself with the same filters; a 60 s memo of each filtered day file lets the build's own diary layer reuse those verdicts instead of judging the same blocks twice) and blocks hidden by memory filters (mechanical, or a cached judged verdict). Judged filters without a fresh verdict ride in the relevance request.

**Re-rank stages** (both optional, default off, "Re-rank stages" below): late interaction scores the pool plus its exhaustive window and cuts to `late.top_n`; the cross-encoder scores the survivors and cuts to `rerank.top_n`. A candidate without late vectors **bypasses** the late cut. Without a cross-encoder, the late top 8 (plus bypassers, up to 12) or the hybrid top 12 go to the judge. Person-cued candidates join after the cuts, and at most `auto.max_judged` (default 12) passages are judged per build, person-cued included: they get a third of the cap when the ranked passages would fill it, more when those are fewer. The passages over the cap go through the fallback rule below, never dropped.

**The final filter** (§8h "Memory"): one request per passage in parallel, at priority `proactive` (below routing, records and the send/ending checks, so they are never delayed by it), one `decisionGroup`, rows of point `memory`. Priority only orders the queue, so memory judging (and the judged filters riding with an unjudged selection) also counts against a capped share of the decision group's slots (`SlotShare` in `src/agent/scheduler.ts`): at most `auto.judge_slot_share` (default 0.5) of `max_in_flight`, at least one slot; a waiter whose share is full is passed over, so the other points always find a free slot in a group of two or more. Kept passages (`keep` and not filter-hidden) are ordered by `relevant`; a participant tie (`about_participant ≥ 0.5`, or a provenance tag of a participant) only breaks **near-ties** (within 0.1: `relevant + 0.0999`) and never outranks a clearly more relevant passage or reserves a slot; then the cross-encoder, late and hybrid scores. **Zero kept means no block.** A passage that got no model verdict (over `max_judged`, group capacity, the point's timeout, a failed chain) is never silently dropped: when only some were judged, the model-kept passages come first and the unjudged ones go through the same fallback rule (at most `auto.fallback_max_results` of them, within `max_results`/`max_tokens`; pending judged filters follow `pending`). The report marks each item `judged` (whether the point answered for it) and, when kept, `selectedBy` (`judge`, `fallback`, or `unjudged` for a selection without a decision model). It counts `unjudged` (passages without a model verdict, whether or not shown) and `fellBack` (shown items the fallback rule chose), and so does the `memory_retrieval` log line; the console marks both (§11 "Memory retrieval in the console"). If none was judged (the whole chain failed, timed out or is budget-blocked) the **fallback** selects every item without a model: the cross-encoder's calibrated cutoff (its provider's `min_score`) when it ran, else the late-interaction cutoff (`late.calibration[<query model>]`), else the hybrid ranking above `auto.fallback_min_score` (0.6); at most `auto.fallback_max_results` (2); pending judged filters follow `pending`. **Without a decision model** (`[decisions]` off, the point disabled, or `auto.judge = false`) the selection is the last re-ranker's calibrated cutoff, else today's behaviour: name-lane hits above `user_lane_min_score` (up to `user_lane_max_results`) then topical hits above `auto.min_score`, up to `auto.max_results`, with the new excerpts; judged filters on what is shown are judged then (bounded) or follow `pending`.

**Packing.** Up to `auto.max_results` (4) items within `auto.max_tokens` (2000): each `- [<citation>] <excerpt>` (angle brackets escaped in the citation's room label and the excerpt so diary text cannot forge the tags, line breaks in the label flattened, continuation lines indented). The excerpts are computed up to four at a time. The note says the items were judged relevant to this conversation and can be opened in full (`JUDGED_NOTE`), or, for an unjudged/fallback block, that they may bear on it (`UNJUDGED_NOTE`).

**Nothing injected counts as work.** The block is part of the harness-built user turn (no synthetic call), and the memory decisions are decision rows, never tool calls: the work gate, records, resume and statistics are unaffected.

### Excerpts (`src/retrieval/excerpt.ts`)

- **Whole blocks by default**: a kept block of up to `auto.excerpt_max_tokens` (400) is shown whole, cleaned.
- **Longer blocks** show the block's own heading text plus a window around its best-matching region: the line (or sentence of a long line) with the most query-term overlap, else (no shared term) the unit closest to the query on the built-in embedder (`QueryVectorIndex.similarity`, used by auto-retrieval and `recall_memory` whenever an embedder is up), expanded over whole units in both directions and marked `…` where cut; a single overlong unit gets a word window around its first matching term.
- **Cleaning**: the diary header line is dropped (its room and date are in the citation), markdown heading markers are stripped, and a heading that only restates the time (`### Evening Events (~7:33 PM)`) is dropped.
- **Compact citation** (`formatCitation`): `memory/<file>.md:<start>-<end>`, then `· <room>` when known, then `· <date>` only when the file name does not already carry it.

### Participant tags from provenance (`src/retrieval/participants.ts`)

Every pipeline-written block comes from one level-1 summary range, and its header names the range to the minute in its own zone. `ParticipantTagger` resolves each block without a provenance row: the level-1 summaries whose earliest/latest timestamps fall in the header's start/end minutes (owned by the block's agent; ties broken by `diary_status = 'done'`, then the diary's room label of the timeline, and mirrors of one donor count as one), then the **human sender ids** of that range's events (user role, not a bot or webhook account; a mirror falls back to its donor's events) with message counts. Results: `memory_block_provenance (agent, content_hash, status tagged|none|ambiguous, summary_id, timeline_key, resolved_at)` and `memory_block_participants (agent, content_hash, provider, sender_id, message_count)`. Ids survive renames. Header-less legacy blocks get `none` and keep relying on name matching; a sub-split oversized block takes its header from the head window. The pass runs after each reconcile (debounced) and at startup, so the **one-off backfill of existing blocks is the same join**, run once (`memory_participants_tagged` logs counts). These are presence tags ("my history with this person"), used by the presence lane, person-cued recall, the near-tie break, and `recall_memory`'s `user` scope.

### Re-rank stages (`src/retrieval/models/`, `src/retrieval/late/`, `src/retrieval/onnx/`)

**Provider chains** (`ProviderChain`): members tried in order with the chat chains' semantics: a failure or a member's own timeout (`timeout_ms`) is a health strike and falls over; an unhealthy member is skipped until its backoff (30 s doubling to 10 min) elapses, then probed by one caller while the others skip it; a member still loading (`ProviderNotReadyError`) is skipped without a strike; `enabled = false` skips a member without waiting for a failure; the caller's abort is neutral. Logs `retrieval_provider_failed` / `retrieval_provider_recovered`.

**Provider kinds** (`[retrieval.rerank.providers.<name>]`, `[retrieval.late.providers.<name>]`):
- `remote`: an HTTP inference server or API. Every remote provider must declare `zdr = true` or `self_hosted = true` (diary text derives from user messages; a config error otherwise). Cross-encoders speak the open `/rerank` shape (`request_format = "documents"`: `{ model, query, documents, top_n }`, the Cohere/Jina/vLLM/Infinity/llama.cpp shape; `"texts"`: `{ query, texts }`, TEI), documents trimmed client-side to the provider's `max_tokens` (about 3 characters per token, the query counted against it), the response size capped while streaming, parsing a bare `[{ index, score }]` or `{ results|data: [{ index, relevance_score|score }] }`. Late encoders speak an embeddings-shaped multi-vector endpoint (`{ model, input, <input_type_field>: "query"|"document" }` → `{ data: [{ index, embedding|embeddings: number[][] }] }`).
- `local`: in process on onnxruntime-node (the runtime the built-in embedder uses) with an HF `tokenizers` tokenizer, from a Hugging Face repo id (`model`, files downloaded once into `<data_dir>/models/<stage>/`, in the background, never on a trigger) or a directory (`model_dir`), `onnx_file` (default `onnx/model.onnx`), `max_tokens` (512), optionally pinned by `revision` (a commit; its own cache directory) and `sha256` (per file; a download, cached file or `model_dir` file that does not match is refused). Concurrent loads of one file share a download. Inference runs in a **child process per model** (`worker-rpc.ts`, `onnx-worker.ts`): onnxruntime-node cannot be loaded in more than one thread of a process (the built-in embedder already runs it on the main thread), so nothing ONNX-based runs in a worker thread. Cross-encoders return the sigmoid of the relevance logit (two-class heads: of the positive margin). No built-in default re-ranker model is shipped: a local provider names its model.

**Cross-encoder** (`[retrieval.rerank]`, default off): query = the request (with its reply target) plus the last three messages, clipped to `query_max_chars`; documents = the cleaned blocks; the survivors are the top `top_n` (8). Each provider's `min_score` is its calibrated cutoff (scores differ across models).

### Late interaction (`[retrieval.late]`, default off)

**Index.** `LateIndexWorker` encodes blocks without token vectors for the index `model` through the document chain (`chain`, background, low priority: batches of `index_batch_size`, a pause between them, local document encoders in their own child process at a lower OS priority), newest first, storing one blob per block in `memory_late_vectors (model, content_hash, dtype, dim, token_count, vectors, scales)`: **fp16** (default; IEEE half, little endian, row-major) or **int8** (one symmetric scale per token in `scales`). Rows are keyed by `lateIndexKey` (`<model>#<digest>`: the model plus every document-side setting that shapes the vectors, i.e. each document-chain member's model, `revision`, `onnx_file`, `sha256`, `document_prefix` and `max_tokens`), so changing one re-indexes instead of mixing spaces. Every document-chain member must serve exactly `model` (family models only encode queries, `query_chain`), and every late provider names its model, a `model_dir` one included. Rows of other keys and of vanished blocks are pruned at start. A failed batch is not blamed on every block in it (`runIsolating`, `src/retrieval/isolate.ts`): a tiny canary request through the chain tells an outage (nothing blamed; the members' health paces the retries) from a bad input, and a bisect (`isolating` chain runs: every member tried, no strike) stores the good blocks in the same pass and records only the blocks that fail on their own. Such a block is retried after a doubling backoff (1 min up to 1 h, `memory_index_failures`); after 5 isolated failures (`INDEX_GIVE_UP_ATTEMPTS`) it is unembeddable for that index key: never retried and left out of the lag (it bypasses the late cut like any block without vectors). Its failure row is cleared once indexed. A local encoder takes a projected ColBERT output (`colbert_vecs`, `token_embeddings`, ..., else any other `[B, T, D]` output) over `last_hidden_state`. **Index lag is a metric**: `late_index_lag { missing, outsideRecency }` at start and hourly, a warning when a block has left the recency layer without vectors.

**Query** (`LateStage.score`, bounded by `timeout_ms`, default 300 ms, for query encode plus MaxSim; past it the stage is skipped for that query and the hybrid lanes carry recall): the trigger plus its reply target, capped at `query_max_tokens` (64) by the **query chain** (`query_chain`, default `chain`): any member serving a model of the index's shared-space family (`model` + `family`), e.g. a large model on a GPU first and a small one on CPU; moving between them never touches the index. Then two branches, one score:
- **Exhaustive window**: the newest `exhaustive_blocks` indexed blocks (or `"all"`) outside the recency layer, resident in the scan scorer (`resident`), updated in the background, never on the query path: index and recency changes are coalesced (2 s debounce, at most 60 s apart during a backfill) and applied incrementally (only blocks that joined or left are read, in small chunks with a yield between them, and passed to the scorer as stored fp16/int8 rows, decoded natively or in the scorer's worker, never on the event loop);
- **beyond the window**, the recall candidates are re-scored exactly from their stored vectors (read in small chunks, decoded in the worker, so `timeout_ms` holds).
Every recall candidate inside the window is re-scored exactly with the shortlist. The scores (MaxSim / query tokens: the mean best-match cosine) merge into one list, cut to `top_n` (20); the window's best `max(rescore, top_n)` blocks join the candidate pool (subject to the same exclusions). With `resident = false` nothing stays resident: the window's stored vectors are read and scored exactly per query (never quantised per query).

**Scan scorers** (`MaxSimScorer`, `src/retrieval/late/scorer.ts`):
- `turboquant` (default `quantization`): TurboQuant codes (`bits` 2–4, a seeded signed permutation plus turbovec's data-oblivious rotation and Lloyd-Max codebook; each block quantised on its own, no training) scanned by a fused SIMD kernel in the native N-API crate (`native/crates/matrix-core/src/turboquant/`, `TurboQuantMaxSim`: FastScan-style 32-token chunks, u8 lookup tables, AVX2 with a bit-identical scalar fallback, a per-block max reduction, threaded, run on the libuv pool so the event loop never waits; copy-on-write block sets so a scan never sees a half-applied update; windows updated in place with `addEncoded` / `removeBlocks`; the codes are reported to V8 as external memory and `free()` releases a replaced or dropped instance at once). The quantised scan returns its top `rescore` (60) blocks, **re-scored exactly** from the stored vectors;
- `exact`: fp32 MaxSim on onnxruntime (a Transpose → MatMul → masked ReduceMax graph built in code, `maxsim-graph.ts`) in a child process, blocks bucketed by length into padded batches; the portable fallback (`late_turboquant_unavailable` is logged once when the native kernel cannot load, or with `quantization = "none"`), and always the rescoring path. A worker that dies (or that the RPC hang watchdog kills: every request has a deadline, an aborted one must be acknowledged within a grace, `close()` has a deadline) is respawned on the next call after a doubling backoff; its windows are rebuilt.
`scripts/bench-late.ts` measures MaxSim throughput on the host and prints the window that fits a target (default 100 ms).

**Coverage gaps never hide memories**: a candidate with no (decodable) vectors bypasses the cut, and only such a candidate (`missingHashes`); a missing or stale index degrades to "no late interaction". `calibration["<query model>"]` is the late cutoff when its score is the last one.

### Two vector indexes (`src/retrieval/embedding/primary.ts`)

Query and document vectors must come from one model, so the embedder cannot fall over per request. The built-in index (`memory_vec`) is **always maintained**; an optional **primary embedder** (`[retrieval.embedding.primary]`: a `[models.*]` chain whose members serve the same model, `dim`, `timeout_ms` default 1000, optional `query_prefix` / `document_prefix`, and `zdr` or `self_hosted` required) keeps its own index `memory_vec_primary` (`VectorStore` with an index slug; `index_meta` keys `active_dim:primary` / `active_model_id:primary`), filled by `PrimaryIndex` in the background (shared embedding cache; the budget claim gate on its chain). A failed batch goes through the same isolation as the late index: an outage (the canary fails too) blames no chunk, and consecutive failed batches slow the worker to at most one request per 5 min; otherwise a bisect stores the good chunks at once and records only the chunks that fail on their own, retried after a doubling backoff of 1 min up to 1 h in `memory_index_failures`. After 5 such failures a chunk is unembeddable for this model (`primary_embed_chunk_unembeddable`): it counts as covered, so it never keeps the primary from serving, and only the built-in index (and the lexical lane) can find it. A model change clears the failures. A query (`dualVectorIndex`) uses the primary index only while it covers every chunk (scores of the two indexes cannot be merged, so this is the rule that never loses a chunk; `primary_embed_index_incomplete` warns while chunks wait for a retry), otherwise the built-in index. The built-in query starts after a 250 ms hedge when the primary has not answered, and the first answer wins; a primary that failed or lost the race is skipped for 30 s, then probed by one query at a time (`primary_embed_query_degraded`, at most once a minute); lexical search is unaffected either way. A primary-model change clears and refills that index only, while the built-in index keeps serving.

**Prompts.** Instruction-trained embedders need a query instruction, and some a document template too; the primary sends `query_prefix` before the query text and `document_prefix` before each document (both default empty, raw text). Examples: Qwen3-Embedding takes `query_prefix = "Instruct: <task description>\nQuery: "` and no document prefix; EmbeddingGemma takes `query_prefix = "task: search result | query: "` and `document_prefix = "title: none | text: "`. Either prefix, when set, is hashed into the primary index's model id (`<wire id>#<hash>`, as the built-in id covers its prefixes), so changing one clears and re-embeds the primary index; an unprefixed primary keeps its plain wire id.

### Observability
