The agent may also attach up to **4 `images`** (workspace paths **or** http(s) URLs) — each loaded to a base64 `data:` URL (URLs via the shared `fetchClient` + `download_size_limit`; local paths confined by `resolveWorkspacePath` + `stat`-capped; MIME sniffed from content-type/magic-bytes→extension) and appended as `image_url` blocks on the user turn, so the user `content` becomes a **multimodal array** (`[{text}, {image_url}…]`; text-only stays a scalar string). This gives Grok **vision over the attached image** so it can recognize and search X/web for a media's subject — a **fallback for sourcing media when `find_source`/SauceNAO comes up empty** (visual recognition + text search, *not* a true reverse-image match). A failed image load is a **hard error** (the model is told its image never reached Grok — no silent degrade); attached image refs partition the short-TTL cache key. Grok returns a prose synthesis + citation URLs (extracted tolerantly from message `annotations` of type `url_citation` **and/or** a top-level `citations` array). The tool then **grounds** that output with miku's own stack: it `parseXStatusUrl`s the citations (keeping real `x.com/.../status/…`, deduped by id), re-fetches the first `hydrate` (default `hydrate_default` 5, cap `hydrate_max`) through the shared **`FxTwitterClient`** (verbatim text + numbered media — §7a), and **inline-captions** the first `caption_top` (default 4) cited **images** via the image caption model — the exact `media`-tool path (`InferenceClient.caption({…, context:"tool"})`); remaining/video media are listed with a one-line "call the `media` tool" hint. A citation that fails to parse or fetch is **dropped and counted** (anti-hallucination signal in the coverage line — no silent truncation). Both Grok's synthesis and every hydrated tweet body are externally-sourced and **wrapped untrusted** (`<untrusted_x_search source="grok-synthesis|tweet" …>`, bodies via `escapeXml`, attrs via `escapeAttr` — a tweet quoting the closing tag can't forge the boundary); structural strings the tool emits (indices, dates, the coverage line, captions we generated) are trusted and unwrapped. Output is a synthesis block + a Sources block (per-citation index, `@handle`, date, canonical URL, windowed verbatim, captioned/listed media) + a coverage line (`Grok cited N posts; hydrated H, D unreachable (dropped); captioned C images`). **Ephemeral, like `x_fetch`** — session rollout only; nothing is written to `media_assets`/`link_previews` (a tweet Grok surfaced was never posted in-channel, so persisting it would fabricate lived context — §5). **Billed as a sub-agent (§8c):** the Grok call (`parseOpenAiUsage`; cost = OpenRouter's reported `usage.cost` when present, which includes the server-side search fees token rates miss, else `[x_search.cost]` rates; `ref:"grok"`) **and** each inline caption (`ref:"caption:<statusId>"`) each append a `tool_invocations` row and feed the per-session cost ceiling (§8d) — this gives tool-context captions a durable home. **Concurrency:** the Grok call goes to OpenRouter (a different provider lane than the agent loop), so it is **not** admitted through `LlmScheduler` — only its per-host `guardedFetch` slot + a wall-clock `timeout_ms` (default 60s, composed with the agent abort signal, and armed until the body is fully read, not just the headers). **Why streamed:** closing the connection cancels a streamed OpenRouter request and stops billing for providers that support cancellation (xAI included), whereas a non-streamed request runs to completion and is billed in full with no usage ever returned — so a timeout or a cancelled turn now actually stops the search. A timed-out search returns an error telling the model the partial search was still charged and not to retry it (or a rewording) in the same turn; captions ride the caption client's own scheduler admission. Every failure path degrades gracefully (Grok error/timeout, no citations, per-item hydration/caption failure) — never throws. A short-TTL in-memory cache (`cache_ttl_minutes`, default 10, keyed on normalized query+filters+model+attached-image-refs) dampens duplicate calls to one Grok synthesis (hydration/captioning always re-run; `details.cached` reports hits). **Per-agent model overrides (spec PER-AGENT-MODEL-OVERRIDES):** the `model`/`deep_model` chains (Grok fast/deep tier) are resolved at session-tool build through the per-agent ladder (`resolveXSearchRef`); `deep_model` keeps its deep→fast fall-through evaluated after per-agent/global shadowing of each key. Inline captions ride the session agent's caption client (same resolution as the `media` tool). Use for **discovery** ("what's X saying about…", "find posts from @… about…"); use `x_fetch` for a known URL. Registered only when `[x_search].enabled` (default true when the block exists). Config: `[x_search]` (§4). Persona docs: TOOLS.md/AGENTS.md/TAIL.md. |

### User profile tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `user_profile_read` | Read a user profile from workspace. Profiles are YAML-frontmatter markdown files under `users/<provider>/` keyed by provider and sender identity hash. Supports reading specific sections or the full document, with configurable excerpt length. Auto-resolves the requesting user's identity via context closure (provider, senderId, displayName). Legacy path discovery migrates profiles from older Matrix-specific paths. |
| `user_profile_edit` | Edit a user profile via patch operations: `set_section` (replace a named section), `append_section` (add content to a section), `delete_section`, `set_frontmatter` (update metadata). Creates profiles on first edit with standardized frontmatter. Validates section names against the canonical set (no `#` or newlines). Writes are serialized per profile via an in-process mutex and committed via temp-file + `rename` for atomicity. `metadata.version` is bumped monotonically on every save. Section bodies containing lines that start with `# ` are escaped (zero-width-space prefix) on write so the heading parser does not partition them on the next read. Config: `[user_profiles]` section. |

**Lookup safety**: profile lookup is scoped to direct children of `users/<provider>/` only. Files in sibling directories (e.g. `users/notes/`) and in deeper subdirectories (e.g. `users/matrix/sub/foo.md`) are ignored even if their frontmatter matches — this prevents workspace-planted markdown from hijacking lookups, and bounds the scan cost to the immediate provider directory. The legacy flat layout (`users/<localpart>__<homeserver>.md`) is still honoured by exact-path probe for the one-time migration.

**Cross-user target policy**: `user_profiles.allow_cross_user_targets` (default `true`) gates explicit targets. When `false`, an explicit target whose (provider, sender_id) doesn't match the trigger sender is rejected. Set to `false` in deployments where the agent should never read or write a profile for a user other than the message-sender currently being responded to.

### Character card tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `character_card_create` | Create a Character Card v2 PNG. Accepts character data fields and an image source (URL or workspace path). Embeds card JSON as PNG tEXt metadata using `character-card-utils`. Image is processed via `sharp` (resize, format conversion). Output path has collision avoidance. Config: `[character_card]` section. |
| `character_card_read` | Read a Character Card with bounded output. Modes: `summary` (character stats, field sizes, book entry index), `field_excerpt` (paginated view of a text field with line numbers), `book_index` (list lorebook entries with sizes), `export_text` (write a full text field to a workspace file), `export_card_json` (write normalized card JSON to workspace). Configurable excerpt window via `default_excerpt_chars`/`max_excerpt_chars`. |
| `character_card_edit` | Edit a Character Card via patch operations on text fields and lorebook entries. Operations: `set` (replace text), `str_replace` (find-and-replace), `append`, `prepend`, `delete_book_entry`, `add_book_entry`, `set_book_entry_keys`, `set_book_entry_enabled`. Re-embeds modified card into the PNG. |

**Path safety**: every card-reading code path (`character_card_read.path`, `character_card_create.imagePath`, edit `*_from_file` / `*SourcePath` operations) is routed through the same `normalizeWorkspaceOutputPath` + `assertPathInsideWorkspace` guards that the write paths already use. Absolute paths and `..` traversal are rejected — these tools cannot read outside the agent workspace.

**Untrusted content labeling**: `character_card_read`'s text-excerpt views (`field_excerpt`, `alternate_greeting_excerpt`, `book_entry_excerpt`) wrap externally-sourced card text in `<untrusted_card_field name="...">…</untrusted_card_field>` blocks (attribute escaped via `escapeAttr`, body via `escapeXml`). This mirrors the rich-XML message pattern in section 9: structural strings the tool emits itself (paths, counts, headings) are trusted; the card text that landed in those fields from external uploads is wrapped so the system prompt can teach the agent to treat content like `system_prompt` / `post_history_instructions` as data, not instructions.

**PNG hardening**: card decode/encode paths run a pre-check (`validatePngChunkSizes`) before invoking `png-chunks-extract`, rejecting any chunk whose declared length exceeds 16 MiB or whose record extends past the buffer. This blocks a DoS where a 100-byte hostile PNG declares a 4 GiB chunk length and triggers the library to allocate against the declaration before the CRC fails. Sharp pipelines apply the same format-aware `limitInputPixels` split as the captioning path (`SVG_MAX_INPUT_PIXELS` for SVG input, `RASTER_MAX_INPUT_PIXELS` for raster) so a legitimate large avatar isn't rejected by the tight SVG decode budget, and `imageUrl` fetches route through `FetchClient`'s shared egress guard to defeat SSRF to RFC1918 / metadata services. Sibling tEXt-chunk decode failures no longer abort `chara` lookups — only the `chara` chunk's own decode failure is fatal.

### Cross-channel messaging tools (`src/tools/cross-channel.ts`)

Five tools that let the agent reach outside the current channel — DM a user, post in another channel, query rosters, or manage DM consent. All five are deferred behind the **contacts** skill (`templates/workspace/skills/contacts/SKILL.md`). `list_members` and `list_channels` are also dual-homed in the **chat-history** skill for roster/enumeration use-cases that do not involve sending. No new immediate-core tools are added.

**Config**: `[messaging]` block, with two boolean flags:

```toml
[messaging]
enabled          = true   # master switch: false disables send_dm + send_to_channel (list tools still work)
dm_initiation    = true   # false: only dm_optout and list tools; no new DM opens; send_to_channel still works
```

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `send_dm` | Open (or reuse) a DM with a user and send a message. Requires `user` (exact stable id or fuzzy display name) and `message` (or `message_ref` to re-use a stashed body). Optional `media` (workspace path or URL; string for single-attachment providers, `string[]` for multi-attachment; schema mirrors `send_message` per `caps.maxAttachmentsPerMessage`) and `as_voice` (where `caps.voiceMessages`). Media refs are resolved via `resolveMedia` (same pipeline as `send_message`) and forwarded as `attachments` to the provider `send()` call; temp files cleaned up on success or failure. Enforces the DM opt-out table before and after id resolution. Exact-id detection (`isLikelyExactId`) is provider-aware: Matrix = `@` prefix, Discord = 15–20 digit snowflake, IRC = `<network>/<nick>` with `/`. Fuzzy input triggers `searchUserIdentities` and returns up to 5 candidate lines (opted-out candidates annotated `[opted out of agent DMs]`; if all are opted out, returns a terminal error). Eligibility check (M3+N2): after exact-id resolution, the user must satisfy at least one of (a) appear in `user_identities` (has ever posted in a shared channel), (b) have an existing DM timeline in `timeline_events`, or (c) appear as a live roster member in any shared channel (checked via `channelClient.memberInfo()` across up to 20 joined channels, short-circuiting on first hit); otherwise the send is refused with a `message_ref` stash. IRC user ids are canonicalized to lowercase before any opt-out read. Calls `IChatProvider.openDm()` to open the channel — errors (closed DMs, offline nick, disabled accounts) are surfaced as actionable messages with a preserved `message_ref`. After a successful `openDm`, writes a `dm_peers` row for the proactive scheduler. Absent `openDm` on the provider → error. `context_note` has `minLength: 1` (enforced at execute time as well as schema). |
| `send_to_channel` | Post a message to another channel by timeline key. Optional `media` and `as_voice` parameters, same schema and resolution pipeline as `send_dm`. Validates the key against `listJoinedChannels()` (provider-provided join registry — reflects currently-joined rooms only). Rejects dm-kind timeline keys — those must go through `send_dm` where consent and eligibility checks apply (C1 guard). Rejects channels outside the session agent's `sessionAgentAccountPrefixes` scope in multi-agent mode (M4). On an unknown key, returns the valid list and stashes a `message_ref`. On a send failure matching the unjoined-room pattern (M_FORBIDDEN / not in room / left), returns an actionable "may no longer be in that room" error with the `message_ref` preserved (N1b). Sends with an embedded cross-channel context note. `[messaging].enabled = false` → error. Visibility gates do not apply to sends (spec principle: visibility gates reads and enumeration, never sends). `context_note` has `minLength: 1`. |
| `list_members` | Roster listing and set operations. `rooms: "current"` / array of keys / `"all"` (requires `query`). Fuzzy `query` searches the identity corpus via `searchUserIdentities`. `op: "intersection"` / `"difference"` for cross-room membership comparisons. Returns stable user ids + display names + last-seen timestamps. Visibility gates: isolated rooms not owned by this session are silently excluded. |
| `list_channels` | Enumerate channels the bot is joined to via `listJoinedChannels()` across all registered providers. `include_dms: true` also lists open DM channels. Returns timeline keys with provider/kind annotations. Respects visibility: isolated channels that the current session is not in are filtered (using `sameChannel()` thread-stripped equality so thread sessions see the parent room as "current"). In multi-agent mode, channels from accounts outside `sessionAgentAccountPrefixes` are filtered (M4). |
| `dm_optout` | Write or clear a `dm_optouts` row for a user (§6b DM opt-out table). Authorization is structural: only the trigger sender of the current session can flip their own bit — proxy requests ("opt out for alice") are returned with a relay-back prompt rather than executed. IRC user ids are canonicalized to lowercase before authorization comparison and storage ops. `action: "opt_out"` sets the row; `action: "opt_in"` clears it. The opt-out persists across sessions and is checked by `send_dm` and the proactive scheduler. |

**Cross-channel context note**: Every message sent via `send_dm` or `send_to_channel` carries an internal `crossChannel?` field on the stored `CanonicalChatEvent` — `{ originTimelineKey, originSenderId, originSessionId, note }` — derived from the caller-supplied `context_note`. This field is stored inside `event_json` alongside `agentSessionId` and is **never transmitted to the chat platform**. The context renderer surfaces it in each format:
- **Rich** (`renderRichMessage`): a `<cross_channel_note origin="…" sender="…" session="…">` element is inserted after the reaction block.
- **Compact** (`renderCompactMessage`): a `[→ from <originTimelineKey>: <note>]` suffix is appended to the message line.
The note tells the agent (in the target channel's session) why it is here and who asked it to come, closing the intent loop across channels.

**Message stash** (`makeMessageStash`): a session-scoped `Map<string, StashEntry>` that stashes message bodies (and their original media refs) under auto-incremented refs (`m1`, `m2`, …). `StashEntry = { body: string; mediaRefs?: string[]; asVoice?: boolean }` — preserving the original media list and voice-message modality so a retry via `message_ref` restores the text body, any attachments, and the `as_voice` flag without the caller re-specifying them (an explicit `as_voice` on the retry overrides the stashed value). The stash is closed over inside the session's tool context and dies with the session. When resolution fails (fuzzy name → candidates; openDm error; channel unknown; media resolution error), the body (and media refs) are stashed and the ref is included in the error so the caller can retry the exact same call with `message_ref` instead of `message`. A long body is sent in chunks: a send failure before any chunk was delivered is an `error:` result as above, but one after a chunk was delivered (a later chunk failed, or storing a delivered chunk failed) is a non-error `partially sent: k of n chunks …` result naming the delivered ids and stashing only the unsent rest under a `message_ref`, so the harness (the output gate's delivery report, late input's effects) treats the call as delivered.

### Session record tools (§8i)

| Tool | Availability | Purpose |
|------|-------------|---------|
| `read_session_record` | Default and proactive sessions; always **immediate** under dynamic loading (forced), also declared by the `sessions` skill | `read_session_record(session_id)`: the session's record (sources, artifacts with paths and message ids, open threads), its `builds_on` chain one hop at a time, and a pointer to the transcript tool. Description situation-first ("where did you get that?", "post the second one"). Throws actionable errors: unknown id, isolated channel, another agent's session, record still being written, no record. Also the call the harness injects at session start (§8i "Injection") |
| `read_session_transcript` | Default and proactive sessions; **deferred**, declared by the `sessions` skill | `read_session_transcript(session_id, query?, range?, offset?)`: the session's raw tool calls in rollout order, arguments and results clipped (match windows around `query`), output bounded and paged by `offset` |
| `session_record_tool` | Default and proactive sessions; **harness-only** (`harnessOnly: true`), executable only during the record turn | `create` / `view` / `str_replace` / `insert` / `finalize` over the run's in-memory record draft, budget-checked per edit. Never immediate, indexed, skill-matched or `tool_search`-findable; the record turn loads it with a synthetic `tool_search` select call (`harness: { kind: "record_load" }`). Outside the record turn the gate makes it throw |

All three are wired by `buildSessionTools` whenever the run has record handles (§8i "Tools"); the two read tools count as work for the work gate when the model calls them (an injected call never does, §8 "The work gate"), `session_record_tool` does not. `harnessOnly` is a module-augmented optional on `AgentTool` (`src/agent/work-gate.ts`), enforced in `DynamicToolRegistry.matchCatalog` (skill patterns, editor backstop), `filterHarnessOnlyFromIndex` (the deferred-tools index), `tool_search` (keyword, `select:`, and the no-match listing), and the factory's and preview's immediate-set computation. `session_record_tool` is the only harness-only tool.

### MCP remote tools

Remote MCP (Model Context Protocol) HTTP servers provide additional tools without requiring custom tool implementations. Servers are defined in TOML config and tools are discovered at startup.

**Config**: `[mcp.servers.<name>]` with `url` (required), optional `enabled` (default true), `transport` (`"streamable-http"` default or `"sse"`), `headers` (key-value pairs, supports env var substitution), and `effects` (bare tool name → effect class, overriding the server's annotations; see **Effect classes** below). The `[mcp]` table itself carries the startup-retry knobs `startup_retry_max_attempts` (default 5; `0` disables), `startup_retry_initial_delay_ms` (default 5000), and `startup_retry_max_delay_ms` (default 60000) — see **Startup retry** below.

**Shipped default — keyless Exa web tools**: `00-defaults.toml` ships `[mcp.servers.exa]` pointing at the public Exa endpoint (`https://mcp.exa.ai/mcp?tools=web_search_exa,web_search_advanced_exa,web_fetch_exa`), so a fresh deploy gets live web search/fetch out-of-box. The Exa public endpoint needs **no API key** (no `headers`/env var), so it never trips the loader's missing-env fail-fast. These Exa tools are the intended replacement for the native `web_search`/`web_fetch`, which remain permitted as deferred basic alternatives — generation sessions select their permitted fetch capability (§ generation sessions). Credentialed MCP servers (with an `Authorization` bearer `headers`) are added only in local config, where the secret lives in `.env`.

**Client pool**: `McpClientPool` in `src/mcp/client-pool.ts`. One `Client` per configured server. The initial connection (and `initialize` handshake) for every server happens at startup and is shared across all sessions. If a server fails to connect, it is logged (`mcp_server_connect_failed`) and skipped — the agent starts without that server's tools — and the pool schedules a bounded background retry for it (next paragraph).

**Startup retry**: a startup connect failure is often a boot-order artifact — the process comes up before its network egress or DNS is ready — so a startup-failed server is retried in the background with exponential backoff: delay `startup_retry_initial_delay_ms · 2^(attempt−1)`, capped at `startup_retry_max_delay_ms`, for at most `startup_retry_max_attempts` retries (`startupRetryDelayMs` is the exported pure helper). Retry timers are `unref`'d (never hold the process open) and cancelled by `stop()`; a handshake that resolves after `stop()` is closed and discarded, never registered. On a late success the pool creates the normal entry, logs `mcp_server_connected` with a `retryAttempt` field, and fires the `onLateConnect` hook. `app.ts` wires that hook to the same registration path startup uses (`registerMcpServerTools`: `adaptMcpTools` + push into the shared `mcpTools` array + `mcpToolServerMap` attribution entries) and additionally clears the console inspector's memoized per-agent/session-type tool blocks (`toolDefsByType`), which were built without the late server's tools. Because every session builds its catalog at `create()` from that shared array, sessions created after the late connect see the new tools through all the normal filters — per-agent `mcp_servers` scoping, the session-type allowlist, and the dynamic-loading immediate/deferred split; **sessions already running keep the frozen tool set they started with**. Each failed retry logs `mcp_server_retry_failed` (warn) and each scheduling `mcp_server_retry_scheduled` (debug); exhaustion logs `mcp_server_startup_retries_exhausted` (error), after which only a process restart brings the server back. `reconnect()` still rejects a server with no entry — until its first successful connect a server has no registered tools, so nothing can invoke it.

**Session recovery**: Streamable HTTP MCP sessions are *stateful* — the server mints an `Mcp-Session-Id` during `initialize` that the SDK replays on every request, and the SDK never re-initializes on its own. A server restart, session timeout, or a non-sticky load balancer routing to a replica that never saw the handshake makes the cached session stale, and every subsequent call returns `Bad Request: Server not initialized` (HTTP 400) or a 404. To keep a transient server blip from permanently disabling a server's tools, the pool supports reconnection:
- `getClient(name)` returns the **live** client; the adapter resolves it per call rather than capturing a reference, so a swapped-in client takes effect immediately.
- `reconnect(name)` closes the dead client and re-runs `connect` + `initialize` + `listTools`, swapping the fresh client and tool list into the entry. Concurrent reconnects for the same server are coalesced to one in-flight attempt. On failure the stale entry is left in place (so the next call retries) and `mcp_server_reconnect_failed` is logged; on success, `mcp_server_reconnected` (with `toolsChanged` if the discovered tool set differs).
- `isSessionTerminatedError()` classifies the lost-session signal narrowly (HTTP 404; HTTP 400 whose body mentions "not initialized"/"session"; or those phrases in a wrapped/SSE error). Generic 4xx/5xx, network blips (`ECONNRESET`), and ordinary tool failures are **not** matched — those leave the server-side session valid, so reconnecting (minting a new session) would be wrong.

**Tool adapter**: `adaptMcpTools()` in `src/mcp/tool-adapter.ts`. Each MCP tool definition is wrapped as an `AgentTool`:
- **Naming**: `mcp_<server>_<tool>` — the server key from TOML config is the namespace prefix. Compatible with the existing session-type `tools` allowlist.
- **Schema**: `Type.Unsafe(inputSchema)` wraps the MCP server's JSON Schema as a TypeBox TSchema. Client-side validation is skipped; the MCP server validates its own inputs.
- **Execution**: resolves the live client via `pool.getClient(server)`, then `client.callTool()` with `AbortSignal` propagation. If the call fails with a lost-session error (and was not aborted), the adapter calls `pool.reconnect(server)` and retries **once**; if reconnect fails it surfaces the original (more informative) session error. MCP `isError` responses are converted to thrown errors — they are not session failures, so they are not retried — which pi-agent-core converts to error tool results.
- **Effect classes**: the adapter registers each tool's class under its exposed name (`registerToolEffect`, §10 "Tool effect classes") from the `annotations` the server returned in `tools/list` (`mcpToolEffect`): `readOnlyHint: true` → `redo_safe`; `idempotentHint: true` with `destructiveHint: false` → `repeatable`; anything else, or no annotations, → `irreversible`. The per-server override `[mcp.servers.<name>].effects = { <bare tool name> = "<class>" }` wins over the annotations, so an operator can correct a server that does not annotate (`app.ts` passes `entry.config.effects` to `adaptMcpTools`). A late-connecting server registers the same way. MCP tools have no compensation, so an `undoable` override still counts as an effect at the fork point.
- **Content mapping**: MCP text and image content blocks map directly to `AgentToolResult` content. Unknown content types (including audio) are serialized as JSON text, since `AgentToolResult` only supports `TextContent | ImageContent`.

**Lifecycle**: Pool starts after factory creation, before provider subscription. Pool stops during shutdown after enrichment pool, before fetch client cleanup.

**Secret registration**: All header values are registered as secrets via `registerSecret()` during pool startup, ensuring auth tokens are redacted in logs regardless of header key name. This explicit registration is load-bearing — the config loader's key-name regex does not match common HTTP header names like `Authorization`.

**No SSRF validation**: MCP server URLs come from TOML config (a trusted source, not user input) and are not validated against internal/metadata IP ranges. This is intentional — unlike `web_fetch` which processes untrusted user-supplied URLs, MCP server URLs are operator-configured infrastructure endpoints.

**Per-agent server scoping**: In agents mode each `[agents.<name>]` block may carry an optional `mcp_servers` key — an array of `[mcp.servers.*]` keys. When absent (the default), the agent sees all configured servers' tools, exactly the legacy behavior. When present, only tools from those servers are exposed to every session type of that agent; `[]` = no MCP tools at all for that agent. The `McpClientPool` is global and unchanged — scoping is a per-session visibility filter applied in `AgentSessionFactory.create()` via `filterMcpToolsByAllowlist()`, immediately before the session-type `tools` allowlist filter (`filterTools`). The two filters compose as an intersection: a session type that allowlists an MCP tool excluded by the agent's `mcp_servers` simply doesn't get it (silent no-op). Attribution is exact: at startup, `app.ts` builds a `Map<string, string>` (tool name → server name) alongside the adapted tools, derived directly from each `adaptMcpTools(entry.name, …)` call. `filterMcpToolsByAllowlist` looks up each tool name in this map (O(1)); a tool absent from the map is not an MCP tool and is never filtered. This is immune to server-key naming collisions — if `foo` and `foo_bar` are both configured, `mcp_foo_bar_action` maps unambiguously to whichever server produced it. The same two-stage filter is applied in the console inspector's `resolveToolDefs` path, keyed per agent+session-type pair, so the displayed tool block matches exactly what the agent can call. Config-time cross-field validation (in `validateAgentConfig`) requires every listed key to name a configured `[mcp.servers.<key>]` block — an unknown key is a startup error. At startup, one `mcp_agent_scoping { agent, servers }` info log is emitted per agent with an explicit `mcp_servers`.

---

## 11. Observability

### Structured logging

All log output is JSON, one object per line. Each record has: `time` (ISO 8601), `level`, `component` (dot-separated hierarchy like `mikuswarm.matrix`), `message` (stable snake_case identifier), plus arbitrary structured fields. Errors are always stringified at the call site.

Log levels: `debug` (10), `info` (20), `warn` (30), `error` (40). Minimum level from config.

All log output passes through the redaction registry — any registered secret is replaced with `[REDACTED]`.

The in-process observability API emits `console_request_completed` at debug level for
every request (`method`, pathname, status, `durationMs`) and promotes requests taking
at least 250 ms to the warning-level `console_request_slow`. The pathname deliberately
excludes the query string so operator search/filter text never lands in timing logs.
The SvelteKit BFF independently emits `agent_api_request_slow` at 250 ms around its
upstream fetch plus Effect Schema decode, which separates agent-side handler time from
the complete BFF hop when diagnosing a slow console view.

### Context dumps

On every model call, the full assembled context is written to a JSON file:

- Filename: `{timelineKey}.{sessionId}.{createdAt}.json`
- Contains: session ID, timeline key, trigger event ID, token estimate, cache boundaries, image blocks, and every message with role, tier, token estimate, and content
- Cache boundaries come from the single exported `CACHE_BOUNDARIES` const (`src/context/dump.ts`); the dump and the `/api/rooms/:key/context` endpoint reference the same const so they cannot drift (the value is an aspirational placeholder until real cache-breakpoint logic exists)
- Secrets are redacted in the serialized output

This makes the "what did the model actually see?" question trivially answerable.

### Observability console (in-process read API + SSE)

An optional HTTP + SSE server (`src/observability/server/`) that exposes the agent's internal state for inspection — the durable session records (frozen context snapshot + transcript), the live context any room would build next, and a live stream of a running session's events. It is the first consumer of the persisted sessions (see §8) and the backend for the console UI. The surface is **read-only except for the operator mutations** — `POST /api/sessions/:id/abort` (the Stop button; §8 "Interrupting a session", §13), `POST /api/sessions/:id/resume` (manual resume-in-place of a parked `failed-resumable` or `interrupted` session; §8 "Session parking & manual resume" / Decision D — long-polls until the resumed run settles; 409 on a re-park, a non-resumable status, a synthetic session type (summarize/condense/diary), a resume already in flight, a busy timeline slot, or nothing to redo; 503 when no resume action is injected), and the pipeline retry actions. Originally **Part B Phase 2** (read API only); the broader admin set (delete/reset/re-run) remains deferred (see "Appendix: Deferred designs" for the admin/pause-resume direction).

**Why in-process** (not a sidecar reading SQLite + dumps): the room view is *hypothetical* ("what the next session would see") and has no stored artifact — it must be produced by the real `ContextBuilder.build()`. Live session streaming needs the in-memory `Agent` (`subscribe`). A sidecar would have to re-implement context assembly (a fidelity risk — the whole point is byte-fidelity) and still couldn't see live state.

**Config** (`[observability.server]`, off by default; bind localhost):

```toml
[observability.server]
enabled = false
bind = "127.0.0.1"
port = 8799
# auth_token = "${MIKUSWARM_CONSOLE_TOKEN}"   # when set, required as a bearer token; must be non-blank (omit the key to disable auth)
```

**Endpoints** (all `GET` except the final `POST`):

| Path | Returns |
|---|---|
| `/api/agents` | **agents meta snapshot**: `{ mode, agents }` — `mode` is `"agents"` or `"legacy"`; in agents mode `agents` is the config-declared list (declaration order), each entry `{ name, accounts: [{ provider, accountId }] }` with Matrix accounts listed before Discord accounts within each agent; in legacy mode `agents` is `[]`. Pure config, built once at startup alongside `agentAccountPrefixesMap` in `app.ts` and injected via `ConsoleServerDeps.agentsSnapshot`; the handler serves it from memory with no DB query. The foundation for all agent chrome in the console BFF (see "Console frontend" below and §4c). Same bearer auth as every other route. |
| `/api/rooms` | **rooms**, reverse-chron: `timelineKey`, `provider`/`accountId` (the key's first two segments, parsed server-side via `parseTimelineKey` so the console can group rooms per account without re-implementing the key grammar; null for a malformed key), display name, lifecycle state, last-activity ts, event/session counts. The display name is the cached human room label from `room_metadata` (resolved by `RoomLabelCache`, see §6 "Room-label resolution"), falling back to the raw `timelineKey` when no label has been resolved yet (an idle room with no recent activity shows its id until its next message or the next startup backfill). The row set is the **union** of timelines with `timeline_events` *or* `agent_sessions` rows, so a timeline whose events were pruned (retention/§13 delete-events) but whose sessions persist still appears (its sessions stay reachable via drill-down). **Thread sub-timelines are folded into their parent room**: a thread (`<roomKey>:thread:<root>`) is a first-class timeline with its own context/summarization, but it resolves to its parent room's label and would otherwise list as an indistinguishable duplicate "room"; so each anchor is mapped to its canonical room key (`:thread:<root>` stripped) and the union is **grouped by room** — one row per room, `event_count`/`session_count` summed and `last_activity_at` maxed across the room and all its threads, with `displayName`/`timelineState` taken from the room key. The room→session drill-down matches the same room+threads set (below), so the aggregated count stays consistent and thread sessions remain reachable. `last_activity_at` per timeline falls back to the latest session activity (`max(created_at, updated_at)`) when no events survive, keeping reverse-chron ordering sensible. This is the console's 5s-poll hot query, and better-sqlite3 runs it on the agent's main thread, so per-timeline counts and the event max are **read from the trigger-maintained `timeline_counts` table** (§ schema) rather than counted: one row per timeline, independent of history size. Only the session-activity fallback remains a correlated seek, coalesce-short-circuited to event-less timelines so `agent_sessions.updated_at` (outside any covering index, behind the fat `trigger_body` payload) is read for those few rows only. **Handler-level TTL cache** (`createCachedRoomsHandler`, 2 500 ms): the handler memoizes the result for 2.5 s — just under the 5 s poll — so no poll sees data older than ~7.5 s at worst. The cache is scoped to the server instance (one closure per `createObservabilityServer` call); `Storage.listConsoleRooms()` direct calls and test databases are unaffected (the cache lives only in the handler). SSE / live sessions read storage directly and are not affected. |
| `/api/rooms/:key/context` | the live `ContextBuilder.build()` for the room in **preview** mode (synthetic trigger = most recent event); the trigger-dependent final user turn is flagged `preview: true`; also carries tier token totals and `cacheBoundaries`. A synthetic `tools` item (the tool-definition block + per-tool breakdown) is prepended **above** the system message when tools resolve (§10a "Tool-definition block"); the `system` message additionally carries `segments` — the per-file/skill system-prompt token breakdown (live-preview-only, never on persisted snapshots; see §10a "System-prompt segment breakdown") |
| `/api/rooms/:key/sessions` | persisted `agent_sessions` for the room, reverse-chron (list/meta shape; no `contextDumpPath`). Both filtered and unfiltered SQL paths project only the metadata consumed by `sessionMeta`; they deliberately do **not** materialize `context_snapshot_json` or `transcript_json` (which live in the `agent_session_payloads` side table, never fetched for list queries) nor `context_dump_path`. Those blobs remain available through the single-session detail endpoint below (`getAgentSession` does a `LEFT JOIN agent_session_payloads`), so clicking a session still renders its complete frozen context and rollout. The match uses a **UNION ALL index-range probe** — an exact match on the room key plus a range scan from `<key>:thread:` to `<key>:thread;` (semicolon = ASCII 59, one above colon = ASCII 58) — so a session that landed on a thread sub-timeline is reachable from its room while both arms hit `idx_agent_sessions_timeline` without a LIKE full-scan. Optional **filters** (§11 "Sessions filter"), AND-combined: `q` (free-text FTS5 search over the session's **user messages** — its trigger message `trigger_body` via `agent_sessions_fts` **OR** any of its interjection bodies via `session_interjections_fts`, OR'd so the "timeline message → session" debug path finds a session by either, returned once regardless of how many interjections match), `status` (one or more lifecycle statuses, repeatable or CSV; values outside the known enum are ignored), `type` (one or more session types, repeatable or CSV). With no params this is byte-identical to the original unfiltered list (`getAgentSessionsByTimeline`); with any param it runs `searchAgentSessionsByTimeline`. A non-empty `q` that tokenizes to nothing usable (pure punctuation) returns `[]` rather than falling back to "all". The `q` text is sanitized by `sanitizeTriggerFtsMatch`, which quotes each term to neutralize FTS5 operators (user input can never inject syntax) and — because this powers a **search-as-you-type** box, unlike the agent-facing `search_messages` where a bare term is an exact-token match — makes **every term an implicit prefix** query, so typing "roc" finds "rocket" (FTS5 prefixes match from the start of a token only) |
| `/api/rooms/:key/session-facets` | `{ types: string[] }` — the distinct `session_type` values present in the room (and its thread sub-timelines, matched by the same UNION ALL index-range probe as the sessions list), sorted, to populate the sessions filter's type menu. Statuses are a fixed enum the client already knows, so only the open-ended types are served |
| `/api/sessions/:id` | the session record + frozen `contextSnapshot` (input context) + persisted `transcript` (rollout) + `rolloutStartIndex` (where the rollout begins inside `transcript`, i.e. past the **leading** run of head final-user-turn `triggerGroup`/`satellite` messages — `rolloutStartIndex` skips only that leading run, so a **resumed** session's appended `triggerGroup` (§8 "Resumable sessions"; built by `buildResumeTurn`) is a *non-leading* final turn that lives **inside** the rollout slice. The rollout renderer therefore renders a `triggerGroup`/`satellite` message it encounters via the same verbatim `MessageBlock` as the head kickoff — tier gutter + XML highlight — rather than the raw-JSON fallback; without that branch a resume turn rendered as a JSON dump of the message object) + `contextDumpPath` (on-disk dump path for parity debugging; detail-only). The `contextSnapshot` is **normalized to the same context wire shape as `/api/rooms/:key/context`** (`renderContextMessage`): the persisted JSON drops optional `ContextMessage` keys (`tier`/`timestamp`) and holds already-externalized image refs under `imageBlocks`, so the handler re-renders each message with present-or-null `tier`/`tokenEstimate`/`timestamp` and refs under `imageRefs` — the one strict `ContextMessageWire` shape the console's BFF schema decodes for both endpoints. A synthetic `tools` item is prepended above the system message when the session's type resolves a tool block (`factory.toolBlockFor`; recomputed for display, its estimate already inside the row's frozen `tokenEstimate` — §10a "Tool-definition block") |
| `/api/sessions/:id/record` | the session's own record (§8i): `{ sessionRecord: { sessionId, timelineKey, agent, text, tokenCount, buildsOn, modelId, createdAt } \| null }` — `null` while the session has no row (no record, or not yet written). `buildsOn` is the stored JSON parsed to a string array (`parseJsonArray`; malformed JSON → `[]`). `404 Unknown session` only when the session id itself is unknown (the same check as `/api/sessions/:id`) |
| `/api/sessions/:id/decisions` | the session's decision evaluations (§8h "Decision visibility"): `{ evaluations: [{ id, ts, decisionGroup, point, agent, timelineKey, agentSessionId, triggerEventId, candidateSessionId, source, reason, verdictJson, answersJson, stateJson, questionsJson, servedModel, servedVersion, latencyMs, inputTokens, costUsd, checkpoint, branchNo, toolCallId, attemptNo, consequence }] }` (the last five are the checks point's anchor, null for other points, §8j) in `ts` order (oldest first; `getDecisionEvaluationsForSession`), `[]` when none. The four JSON columns stay strings on the wire; the console parses them. `404 Unknown session` for an unknown id |
| `/api/sessions/:id/stream` | **SSE** of live `AgentEvent`s for a running session; closes on **run settlement** (`SessionManager.onSettle`), *not* on `agent_end`. A single `run()` drives several agent-loop invocations — the kickoff plus any forced-completion prompts — each emitting its own `agent_end` (with the injected user turn that begins the next turn in between); closing on the first would truncate the live view after one turn. The terminal `completed`/`failed-resumable`/`discarded` markers all evict the agent, which fires `onSettle` once (after the terminal status is persisted, so the client's settle-driven refetch reads the terminal record). A session that is terminal/evicted — *or* still in the manager map but whose run has already settled (the late-subscribe race) — emits one `not_live` event and closes (the console then renders from `/api/sessions/:id`). A live stream opens with one **`rollout_seed`** event — the canonical accumulated `agent.state.messages` (the same array the per-turn transcript flush serializes) plus the session-detail `rolloutStartIndex` — because `Agent.subscribe` delivers only future events: without the seed, a console attaching mid-run rendered an empty rollout until the next turn landed. The handler runs synchronously from subscribe to seed-send, so no live event can interleave before it (the client always folds seed → events, race-free). The seed's **leading final-turn messages** (the slice below `rolloutStartIndex` — the trigger turn) are not part of the rollout: `LiveRollout` hands them to `SessionView` (`onHead`) which renders them in the **verbatim input view** while running. Without this the trigger turn would be missing from the verbatim view until the run completes — the persisted transcript head isn't flushed until the first `turn_end` (§8 "Session capture") and the session query is not refetched mid-run (only on stream end). **Injected user turns** committed mid-run — interjections (`{type:'interjection'}`) and forced-completion prompts (`{role:'user'}`) — surface via the `message_start` events pi-agent-core emits for each (it emits `message_start`/`message_end` carrying the message before pushing it to state; the following `turn_end` carries the *assistant* reply, not the user turn). `LiveRollout` folds those into the rollout (filtered by `isInjectedUserTurn`, excluding the `triggerGroup`/`satellite` head an early attach could surface); without it an interjection injected after attach was invisible until completion. A `message_start` that merely re-delivers a turn the **seed** already carried (a commit landing just before attach, or a re-seed on reconnect) is dropped within the post-seed window via `isDuplicateInjectedTurn`, so it never renders twice. Additionally merges the Layer-0 tap's **tentative** events (spec LLM-FAILURE-HANDLING §4.2): `tentative_event` (a raw per-attempt LLM stream event, not yet committed — this is how tokens stream live now that Layer-0 buffers attempts to the terminal event) and `attempt_discarded` (the console clears the partial and shows "attempt n failed, retrying"). Distinct event kinds so clients can never confuse tentative output with authoritative `message_update`s |
| `/api/media/:ref` | image bytes for an externalized image ref (`:ref` = the media asset id), resolved beneath the workspace root with a path-traversal guard. **In agents mode** the handler looks up the asset's `event_id → getTimelineEventById → timelineKey`, resolves the owning agent's workspace root from it, and expands `local_path` there; unresolvable account → `404`. In legacy mode the global `workspaceRoot` is used. |
| `/api/summaries/:id` | a summary + its lineage (covered events / child summaries) for the detail column |
| `/api/scheduler` | **scheduler snapshot** (spec LLM-FAILURE-HANDLING §9.1): per-group budget state — `active`/`queue` entries with session/type/model/priority/key attribution plus held/waiting times, throttle `backoffUntil`, sticky escalations (the scheduler-wide map is **filtered per group to the keys with an active/queued entry in that group**, so an escalation appears only under the group actually holding it — never duplicated across cards) — beside per-model health (`healthy`/`unhealthy`, consecutive-failure streak, probe-in-flight, `nextProbeAt`, last failure, waiter count). The "who is waiting on what, and which model is down" feed; polled (SSE optional later). `503` when no scheduler is wired |
| `/api/llm-requests` | the in-memory **Layer-0 attempt ring** (spec §9.2; capacity `observability.llm_request_ring_size`, default 500), newest-first: `{ts, sessionId, sessionType, group, model, requestedModel?, servedModel?, priority, attempt, admissionWaitMs, durationMs, outcome, status?, class?, errorMessage?}`. `model` is the wire id of the REQUESTED (head) model (backward-compat). `requestedModel` is the logical id (config block name) of the requested head or per-user selected model; `servedModel` is the logical id of the chain member that actually dispatched the wire call — both absent for non-agent callers and for attempts that never dispatched (budget-violation pre-flight). When `servedModel` differs from `requestedModel`, the attempt ran on a fallback member; the console scheduler table renders it as `requested → served` highlighted in amber. `errorMessage` carries the raw upstream error text (secret-redacted), rendered as the outcome tooltip. Deliberately not durable — the LLM gateway holds the authoritative wire log; this adds what the gateway cannot see (attribution, admission wait, attempt numbering, failures that never reached the wire). `503` when no ring is wired |
| `POST /api/sessions/:id/abort` | **operator Stop button** (§8 "Interrupting a session"): aborts the live run and marks the session `interrupted` via `SessionManager.interrupt()`. `200 { sessionId, status: "interrupted" }` on success; `404` for an unknown id; `409` when the session exists but isn't actively running — idempotent-friendly, so a double-click or a click on an already-finished session is benign. The `409` uses the server's **standard error envelope with structured details**: `{ error: { status: 409, message, sessionId, sessionStatus } }`, where `sessionStatus` is the session's current lifecycle status (e.g. `completed`, `interrupted`) — deliberately named distinctly from the HTTP `error.status` so the two never collide (this was the one route that previously hand-rolled a mixed `{ error, sessionId, status }` shape). The `message` embeds `sessionStatus` too, because the BFF surfaces the raw non-ok 409 body **text** as the operator-facing error message (`console/src/lib/server/api/client.ts` reads `res.text()` into `ApiError.message`), so the message must read sensibly on its own. One of two mutating routes; bearer-auth gates it like every other, **and** it requires the `x-console-request` CSRF-guard header (see below) — without it the request is rejected `403` before dispatch |
| `/api/pipelines` | **pipeline monitor dashboard** (§11 "Pipeline monitor"): one row per pool (`enrichment`/`captioning`/`summarization`/`diary`) — `{ pool, enabled, workerCount, maxRetries, inFlight, counts }`. `counts` are six DB-derived status buckets (`pending`/`processing`/`retrying`/`done`/`failed`/`skipped`); `inFlight` is the one live number (the pool's `activeWorkers.size`). A pool disabled by config reports `enabled: false`, `inFlight: 0` but still surfaces its historical `counts` |
| `/api/pipelines/:pool/items?status=&room=&cursor=&limit=` | keyset-paginated `PipelineItem[]` + `nextCursor`, reverse-chron on `(updatedAt, id)` (diary sorts on `latest_timestamp`). `status`/`room` are indexed filters; `status=pending`/`status=retrying` are pseudo-filters matching the same predicate as the count buckets (retrying = a `pending` row with prior attempts) |
| `/api/pipelines/:pool/items/:id` | the pool-specific detail union: enrichment → produced `mediaAssets`/`linkPreviews`/`replyContext`; captioning → source `media` (bytes via `/api/media/:ref`) + caption/model; summarization → resulting `summary` + lineage + best-effort draft/error + `sessionId`; diary → source `summary` + `sessionId`. For the LLM-backed pools `sessionId` links the latest synthetic `agent_sessions` run so the client reuses `SessionView` |
| `/api/pipelines/stream` | **SSE** firehose of `PipelineActivityEvent`s across all pools (`{ pool, id, kind: claimed\|completed\|failed\|retried\|skipped, status, attempts, room, ts }`, one `event: activity` record each); redacted + heartbeat like the session stream; opens-and-idles when no activity bus is wired |
| `POST /api/pipelines/:pool/items/:id/retry` | **manual retry** (§11 "Pipeline monitor"): resets a terminal *safe* item to `pending` (attempts→0, error cleared) and pokes the pool's wake seam. `200 { pool, id, status: "pending" }`; `404` unknown item/pool; `409` when not retryable — `processing`, or a deferred-unsafe state (summarization `complete`, diary `done`). The `409` uses the standard error envelope with details `{ pool, id, itemStatus }` and a self-describing message. The second mutating route; same CSRF guard |
| `POST /api/pipelines/:pool/retry-failed` | **bulk retry** — reset every `failed` item in a pool to `pending`; `200 { pool, retried }`. Same CSRF guard |
| `/api/usage/summary?window=&agent=` | **Usage & Cost** (§8e/§8f): totals by class + by model over a window (`today`/`24h`/`7d`/`30d`/`month`/`all`), from `getUsageSummary` over `usage_events`. The optional **`agent=`** param — shared by the timeseries/sessions/tool-calls/leaderboard routes — scopes the view to one agent's rows: the handler resolves the name through the static agents snapshot into `provider:accountId` prefixes and the storage queries filter `timeline_key` by them (the same escaped-LIKE prefix convention as `[[limits]]` agent scoping, §8e); an absent or unknown name — or legacy mode — means All, the same rule the `?agent=` URL param follows elsewhere. Also returns `now` (the server clock the window was computed against) and `firstTs` (earliest event *within* the window, or null) — the console divides spend by the **actual elapsed data range** `now − firstTs`, not the nominal window width, so per-period averages don't pretend to data that doesn't exist (a 30d view a week into history averages over ~7d; a month view on the 15th over ~15d not 31). The calendar-aligned `today`/`month` windows snap to the **UTC** boundary (a display convenience — budget *rules* use their own configured tz, §8e) and the console marks them "UTC" so an operator isn't misled when they disagree with a tz'd rule. In agents mode the payload adds **`byAgent`** — the per-agent breakdown, folded in the handler from a per-`timeline_key` rollup (`includeByKey`) through the static agents snapshot (membership is config, never schema; spec CONSOLE-MULTI-AGENT §9), with one residual `agent: null` bucket for null-key spend (background caption/embedding) and accounts no longer in config so the rows always sum to `total` |
| `/api/usage/timeseries?window=&groupBy=class\|model\|agent&agent=` | stacked spend series for the chart, bucketed by range: hourly ≤24h, daily for bounded windows, and **span-scaled** for `all` (day ≤31d → week ≤52w → month ≤36mo → year) so the histogram stays legible as history grows — `all` derives its span from the earliest event (`minUsageTs`). The leaderboard endpoint uses the identical width so the cards' sub-period averages re-bin consistently. `groupBy=agent` (agents mode only; coerced to `class` otherwise) groups by raw `timeline_key` in SQL and folds keys into per-agent series in the handler, with an `unattributed` residual series — same fold rule as `byAgent` above |
| `/api/usage/sessions?limit=&agent=` | recent sessions joined with their per-class `usage_events` rollup (agent-LLM vs tool cost, tokens, `status`, channel, type, trigger). Each row carries `channelLabel` — the human `Name (Space)` room label coalesced from `room_metadata` (else the raw timeline key) — beside the raw `timelineKey` |
| `/api/usage/tool-calls?limit=&agent=` | recent paid `tool`/`caption`/`embedding` events, newest-first; each row left-joins `room_metadata` to add `channel_label` (null only when the event has no `timeline_key`) |
| `/api/usage/leaderboard?window=&limit=&agent=` | **per-actor spend leaderboard** (§7.1 leaderboard tab): a humans-only ranking + a separate system/self block. `users` are real trigger senders (system session types excluded), ranked **contiguously 1..N** by spend with zero-spend dropped — up to `limit` (default 1000) so the console paginates to the lowest non-zero spender — each with totals/events/distinct-sessions, active range, contiguous `rank`, and (top-10 only) its own per-bucket `series`. `systemActors` are the non-human/self workloads (Summarization = summarize+condense, Diary, Proactive), attributed by `session_type`, each with a **`comparisonRank`** = where it would sit among users, and its own series. Also returns `userStats` (count/average/median over the non-zero humans, for the System & self reference cards), `grandTotal` over **every** event (incl. non-attributable null-sender spend) as the share denominator, and `bucketMs`/`now`. Background caption/embedding (null sender + null type) belongs to neither list but counts in `grandTotal`; display names resolve to each sender's most-recent non-null `agent_sessions` name |
| `/api/usage/budgets` | every configured `[[limits]]` rule's live status from `BudgetEngine.ruleStatuses()` (spent/cap/fraction/state/window/resets/scope, plus `components` = per-model spend for a multi-model rule so its bar segments), plus `userSelections` (live per-user model picks, each labeled with the sender's `displayName`/`username` via `Storage.getUserLabels`); each empty when none configured / not wired |
| `/api/usage/user-limits?scope=individuals\|shared&page=` | one hottest-first page of per-user / shared-pool meters from `UserLimitEngine.groupedStatuses()` (grouped by partition, split individuals/shared, non-human senders excluded, 20 groups/page), each meter spent/cap/state/resets/`orderIndex`/scope, user-partition meters additionally labeled with the sender's `displayName`/`username` (`Storage.getUserLabels`: `user_identities` for Discord username + nick, falling back to the latest `agent_sessions.trigger_sender_display_name` — the Matrix name source; nulls when unknown) (ledger-seeded at startup §14) — rendered as scope-tabbed, paginated strips of per-cap health bars; plus `totals` (per-scope group counts). Empty when the feature is off |
| `/api/models/behaviour?window=&groupBy=model\|agent\|site\|task&family=&agent=&site=&task=&selected=&metric=&type=` | **model behaviour** (§8k): scorecard of headline rates per group with previous-window change and low-sample flags, the overview of every rate over time, the chartable metrics with their totals, the chosen metric's series (a rate per group, or a mix family per key), the mix tables per group, model labels, the breakdown (refusals, send contract, style), change markers, the first incident page, facets, `pendingHours` and the audit backlog progress; reads the rollups as they are (never recomputes). `503` when the behaviour service is not wired |
| `/api/models/behaviour/incidents?…&cursor=&limit=` | further incident pages (same filters; `limit` default 25, max 100): one row per session with refusals, nudges, redos, revisions or judged endings, newest first, each with chips, a one-line outcome and a link (session, branch, tool call or attempt) |

The **Usage & Cost** console page (`console/src/routes/usage-cost`, in the TopBar nav) renders these behind the polled remote-function pattern: a window + breakdown (class\|model) selector; a **Total spend** card that also carries the **sub-period averages** (per hour for day-scale windows, per day + per week for larger ones, per day/week/month/year for All time, each shown only while it's coarser than the buckets and the data range covers it) — each an average plus a min/max/σ spread, computed in `$lib/spend-averages` (pure, unit-tested) over the actual elapsed range from `firstTs`/`now` (the spread is across *fully-elapsed* periods, zero-filled; a sub-period longer than the elapsed data is suppressed rather than extrapolated); by-class and top-model cards; a stacked spend-over-time chart (inline SVG stacked-bar — the spec's LayerChart dependency was deferred to avoid the console's first charting lib) with a **real y-axis** (rounded USD gridlines + labels via `niceTicks` in `$lib/spend-chart`) and a **per-column hover tooltip** (each group's value + %, the column total, and the bucket's time span — so the chart reads in absolute terms, not by colour/legend alone); a **Limits** section — now *below* the chart — showing **every** configured rule (fill bar, window, resets-in countdown, scope summary, ok/near/blocked badge — blocked sorted to top, the operator's single source of truth and the `usage_limit_blocked` log join key); and — below Limits — a **tabbed detail area** switching between *Recent sessions*, *Recent paid calls*, and a *User leaderboard*. The active tab, the window, the breakdown, and the agent filter all live in **query params** (`?tab=&window=&group=&agent=`, URL-as-source-of-truth like the rest of the console, read from `page.url` and written via `goto(replaceState)` so a filter toggle doesn't pile up history) — the view is deep-linkable and survives refresh; each tab-bound feed only polls while its tab is visible. The window selector includes an **All time** range alongside the bounded ones. *Recent sessions* and *Recent paid calls* render the channel via a shared `ChannelCell` (the human `Name (Space)` label as a popover trigger; the popover shows the raw timeline id + a copy-to-clipboard button), and *Recent sessions* also surfaces a `status` column so a $0 row — e.g. a coalesced/early-exit session that issued no billable LLM call — is explainable rather than mysterious; its columns run identity-first (session, type, channel, trigger) before the model and token/cost figures.

Under the multi-agent **global gate** (spec CONSOLE-MULTI-AGENT §9) the page grows a **page-wide agent dimension**, all server-side via the routes' shared `agent=` param: a segmented **agent tab row** (All / one tab per configured agent, each with its accent dot and platform tag) that scopes *every* usage view — the cards, the chart, both tables, and the leaderboard — but never the Limits sections (rules carry their own scope); the `?agent=` param combines with the window filter, and an unknown or absent name means All. The breakdown toggle gains **by agent** (per-agent stacked series in each agent's accent color, plus a neutral `unattributed` residual), the card row gains a **By agent** card (from `byAgent`, residual muted), and both tables gain an **agent column** — first column, accent dot + name + the row's provider (accountId appended only under the §3.2 per-provider disambiguation rule), with unresolvable accounts falling back to the muted raw tag. The By-agent card and the agent column render only on the **All** view: pinned to a single agent they would repeat one value down the page, so the filtered view drops them (rows are homogeneous by construction). Below the gate the page renders byte-identically to the single-agent layout — `ChannelCell` keeps its legacy `accountId PROVIDER` tag gated on `distinctAccounts`. The **User leaderboard** is a real-users-only ranking: the top-10 humans rendered as cards (an `auto-fill` grid) above a **client-side-paginated** table (rank, user, spend, share-of-total, events, sessions, first/last seen) that reaches the lowest non-zero spender. Non-human/self actors are pulled out into a distinct **System & self** section — Summarization, Diary, and Proactive cards, each marked (bot icon + violet accent) and showing a *comparison* rank ("would be #N among users") rather than a leaderboard position, beside **Average user** / **Median user** reference cards (over the non-zero humans). The Total card and every actor card are one shared `SpendSummaryCard` component (label + total + range note + the sub-period averages table — leaderboard mode adds a rank badge, share-of-total chip, and event/session counts; `system` mode swaps in the bot icon + comparison-rank chrome), so a card cannot drift from the Total card's presentation. Background polls update data in place with no per-refetch indicator, and window / breakdown / leaderboard switches use TanStack `keepPreviousData` so the cards/chart never blank-flash between cache entries.

**Refusal handling in the read API** (§8j, `src/observability/server/refusal-detail.ts`). `GET /api/sessions/:id` also returns `branches` (the stored branches with their parsed `messages`, fork index, reason, check code, from/to model, cost), `refusalEvents`, `contract` (`{ outcome, nudges, maxNudges, attempts }`; `maxNudges` = the configured `forced_completion_retries`), `checks` (catalogue descriptions, `{ code, kind, remedy, reason, description }`, of every code its branches, events and checks rows name, resolved for the session's agent through `ConsoleServerDeps.checks`) and `audits` (its `session_audits` rows with parsed verdicts, §9i); all empty for a session without them. The session list and detail meta carry `checkChips` (`Storage.getSessionCheckChips`, `null` when all zero): `refused` (every refusal event, observed included), `redone` (rule redos plus contract-redo branches), `nudged` (`contract_nudges`), `revised` and `unjudged` (distinct judged outputs with a `revise` / `sent_unjudged` row). The session SSE forwards `branch_forked` and follows it with a fresh `rollout_seed` of the new live branch (a sibling-edit fork keeps an edited message the client cannot rebuild from the event). **Late input in the read API** (§8 "Late input"): each branch also carries `causeEventId` and `cause` — the message whose arrival caused it (`cause_event_id`), resolved server-side to `{ eventId, senderId, senderName, body, timestamp, editedAt }` from the stored timeline event (its current body, since edits are stored in place, and `last_edit_timestamp` via `Storage.getTimelineEventLastEdit`; `null` without a cause id or once the event is gone). `GET /api/sessions/:id` returns `interjections` (`Storage.listSessionInterjections`: `{ eventId, externalId, senderId, senderName, kind, body, createdAt }` in delivery order), and the list and detail meta carry `redoCount` (`agent_sessions.redo_count`, 0 by default).

**Fidelity guarantee.** `/api/rooms/:key/context` calls `AgentSessionFactory.buildPreview()`, which shares the *single* `ContextBuilder.build()` call site with the live session path (`buildContext`), so the preview cannot drift from what a real session would build. Everything through the rich tier is real and current; only the final user turn is synthetic, and it is labeled `preview: true`.

**Auth & redaction.** When `auth_token` is set it is required as a bearer token on every request and SSE connection — accepted via `Authorization: Bearer <t>` **or** a `?token=<t>` query param (the browser `EventSource` API can't set headers). Fail-fast (issue #5): an **absent** `auth_token` means auth is intentionally disabled (the localhost-operator default — every request is allowed), but a **present-but-blank** token (empty or whitespace-only, e.g. `${MIKUSWARM_CONSOLE_TOKEN}` expanding to "") when the server is enabled is a configuration error rejected at load time rather than silently opening the console. The schema enforces `minLength: 1` on the token; a cross-field check in the config loader catches whitespace-only values. Every JSON body and every SSE payload passes through `redactSecrets`; image blocks are externalized to refs (no base64 over the wire), identical to the persisted transcript, so the live and historical rollout views match.

**CSRF guard (mutating routes are console-BFF-only).** The mutating routes (`POST /api/sessions/:id/abort` and the pipeline-monitor retry routes `POST /api/pipelines/:pool/items/:id/retry` + `POST /api/pipelines/:pool/retry-failed`) are reached **only** by the console BFF's server-side `fetch` (§11 "Console frontend") — nothing browser-facing calls them directly. In production the observability port is **not** exposed to browsers: a reverse proxy fronts the console domain and routes server-to-server to the in-process server. To defend the default localhost-no-token deployment against a CSRF (a page the operator's browser loads firing an auto-submitted form / `no-cors` POST — localhost bind stops network peers but not the operator's own browser), the BFF attaches a constant custom header `x-console-request: 1` to its requests (`console/src/lib/server/api/client.ts`), and the server rejects any mutating request (`POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE`) lacking that header with `403` **before dispatch** (`src/observability/server/index.ts`, the `CONSOLE_REQUEST_HEADER` constant). A *custom* header makes a cross-origin browser request non-"simple", forcing a CORS preflight; this server implements no CORS, so the browser blocks the actual request — and a simple-request CSRF cannot set the header in the first place. The header is a marker, **not** a credential (the bearer token remains the authenticator); the legitimate server-to-server BFF hop is not subject to CORS and passes. `GET` reads (including the SSE `?token=` stream path) need no header and are unaffected.

**Why SSE, not WebSockets.** The only realtime need is *server→client* streaming of a running session's `AgentEvent`s — the console never sends data as the agent (out of scope by design). SSE rides the existing `node:http` server with the same bearer-auth and redaction pipeline and adds **zero dependencies**; the text protocol is trivially consumable by any client (`EventSource`, or the console's `fetch`+`ReadableStream` parser) and matches the "closes on `agent_end`" lifecycle. WebSockets would add an `Upgrade` handshake, a new dependency, binary framing we don't need, and a separate auth path (browsers can't set an `Authorization` header on a WS). WS would only win if the console needed high-rate client→server input (a chat surface), which is explicitly out of scope.

**Liveness & isolation.** `pi-agent-core`'s `Agent.subscribe` delivers only *future* events; the agent is evicted from `SessionManager`'s map only *after* its run settles. So a subscriber can attach while `getAgent(id)` still returns an agent whose run has already ended. The stream handler subscribes to agent events **and registers `SessionManager.onSettle` first** — so a settlement landing between the `getAgent` check and registration still closes the stream — then re-checks `SessionManager.isAgentLive(id)` (session `running` *and* `agent.signal !== undefined`, not mere map presence), self-closing with a `not_live` event if the run already settled (that race fired `onSettle` with no listener attached, so the re-check is the backstop). When the run *is* live, the handler sends the `rollout_seed` catch-up event (see the endpoint table above) so mid-run attaches start from the accumulated state instead of empty, and the stream then stays open across the whole run, closing on `onSettle`. The convention that callers `markRunning` before `attachAgent` is documented on `attachAgent` and defended by `isAgentLive`. Only chat/proactive (`launchSession`) and manual-resume sessions `attachAgent`, and all of them reach a terminal marker → `evict` → `onSettle`; worker-pool sessions (summarize/condense/diary) never attach an agent, so they take the `not_live` path and never reach the spanning logic. The convention that callers `markRunning` before `attachAgent` is documented on `attachAgent` and defended by `isAgentLive`. Separately, the SSE layer is a **read-only observer**: every `res.write` is wrapped best-effort and a write throw (or a `req`/`res` `"error"`) is treated as a client disconnect, so a dead/reset socket can never throw out of the `agent.subscribe` listener and into the live agent loop.

### Pipeline monitor (background-worker observability)

The session views above cover *conversational* agent sessions. The four background worker pools that keep context healthy — **enrichment** (§7a), **captioning** (§7a), **summarization** (§9b), **diary** (§9c) — get their own monitor: a separate console area answering *are they working? what is queued / in-flight / done / failing, and why? what went in and what came out?*

**Unified read model over heterogeneous queues.** The four queues live in different tables (`timeline_events.enrichment_status`, `media_assets.caption_status`, the `summarization_jobs` table, `summaries.diary_status`) with different status vocabularies. The monitor projects them onto one shape. Counts (`getPipelineCounts`) normalize each pool's raw statuses into buckets — `pending`/`processing`/`retrying`/`done`/`failed`/`skipped` plus a captioning-only `deferred` — where `retrying` is a `pending` row with prior attempts and enrichment's never-queued `inactive` rows are excluded. The item list (`listPipelineItems`) projects one row per queue entry into a common `PipelineItem` (`pool`, `id`, raw `status`, `attempts`/`maxRetries`, derived `retrying`, `room`, timestamps, short input/output descriptors, persisted `error`, and `sessionId` for the LLM-backed pools), keyset-paginated reverse-chron on `(updatedAt, id)`.

**Default view hides noise; `deferred` is the captioning "parked" partition.** The raw queues are dominated by rows that are *not actionable signal*: enrichment marks every plain message (nothing to extract) `skipped`, and captioning parks media on non-trigger messages at `pending` indefinitely whenever neither `caption_all` nor `caption_assistant_messages` is set (the pool would never claim them). So the monitor would otherwise read as an all-message timeline. Two mechanisms fix this. (1) **The captioning `deferred` derived status** (`CaptionEligibility`): a fresh (`attempts = 0`) pending asset whose event the pool would never claim — mirroring the `claimPendingCaptions` predicate `trigger_group_id is not null OR caption_all OR (role = 'assistant' AND caption_assistant_messages)` — is surfaced as `deferred` rather than `pending`, both in the projected row's badge and as its own count bucket carved out of `pending` (so the `pending` count/chip is honest backlog). The eligibility booleans ride the pool's `stats()` seam (`PipelineStats.captionEligibility`) and are threaded into `getPipelineCounts`/`listPipelineItems`/`getPipelineItem` for the captioning pool only; absent (no registry, or any other pool) there is no `deferred` partition. The booleans are inlined as SQL literals (trusted config, not user input), so the fragment carries no bind params; captioning's count/list specs join `timeline_events` to evaluate it. (2) **The unfiltered list excludes the noise:** with no status chip selected, the list hides `skipped` (every pool) and `deferred` (captioning). Selecting the explicit `skipped`/`deferred` chip reveals them — the debugging path. Because this default is now the *primary* enrichment view, it is index-backed: the enrichment list spec's `defaultScope` emits the single predicate `enrichment_status not in ('inactive', 'skipped')` (superseding the per-branch `scope`), which matches the partial index `idx_timeline_events_active_updated` (`(updated_at, id) where enrichment_status not in ('inactive','skipped')`) verbatim — so the default view is a bounded keyset walk over the non-noise minority, never a scan past the skipped majority (verified via `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`). The partial index covers only the minority of rows, so it is small and cheap to maintain. Captioning's `deferred` exclusion is config-relative (a `timeline_events` join), so it stays a residual filter over the much smaller `media_assets` table rather than a static index. `deferred` is config-relative: turning a captioning flag on reclassifies those rows back to `pending` live, no migration. (The retry path reads items without eligibility, so a `deferred` row reads as raw `pending` there — not in `PIPELINE_SAFE_RETRY`, so it is correctly not manually retryable; it auto-runs once eligible.) The summarization input descriptor (`L<level> · <input>→<to> tok`) renders the `<to>` side as `actual/target` once the job completes — a correlated subquery joins `result_summary_id` to `summaries.token_count` (the real produced size), falling back to `target_token_count` alone while the job is still pending/running — so target-vs-actual drift (e.g. tuning `leaf_target_tokens`/`condense_target_tokens`) is visible at a glance. The unfiltered list pages on a `(updated_at/latest_timestamp, id)` index; a **status-filtered** list (the monitor's primary "what is failing?" view) pages on the companion `(status, updated_at/latest_timestamp, id)` index as a covering index search, so neither the unfiltered nor the per-status view ever full-scans the large enrichment/captioning tables. All of this is **DB-derived** — the single source of truth that survives restart.

**Count aggregate cost — materialized `pipeline_counts`.** `getPipelineCounts` is polled every 5s by the dashboard (once per pool per poll, per open console tab), and better-sqlite3 runs every query synchronously on the agent's main thread — so a count that *scans* a pool table is paid by message handling and LLM streaming, not just by the console. The counts are therefore not computed on read at all: the schema keeps a **materialized `pipeline_counts` table** — one row per `(pool, raw status, retrying, elig)` bucket (`retrying` = attempts > 0; `elig` = captioning only, the parent event's packed eligibility facts: bit 1 trigger-group, bit 2 backfetched, bit 4 assistant-authored; 0 for the other pools) — kept exact by a set of triggers (`pc_*`) on every insert/update/delete of the four pool tables. The update triggers carry `WHEN` guards so a rewrite that does not move a row between buckets costs nothing; scope entry/exit (`inactive` ↔ active enrichment, a `media_type` change onto/off the captioning track, `diary_status` NULL ↔ set) is handled as leave-old-bucket / enter-new-bucket. Captioning's config-relative `deferred` split is applied at **read** time — `captionEligibleBits` evaluates the current `CaptionEligibility` against each bucket's `elig` bits — so flipping `caption_all` / `caption_assistant_messages` reclassifies the counts live with no rebuild. Two triggers keep the eligibility bits correct as parent events change: `pc_te_au_elig` (`AFTER UPDATE OF trigger_group_id, is_backfetch, role`) moves the event's tracked assets between `elig` buckets, and `pc_te_bd` (`BEFORE DELETE`) settles them before a cascade — SQLite runs FK cascades *after* the parent row is gone, so a child-level delete trigger could no longer read the parent's bits; the child `pc_ma_ad` trigger accordingly acts only when the parent still exists (a direct asset delete). A third edge case is SQLite REPLACE conflict resolution: `insert or replace into media_assets` deletes the conflicting row without firing DELETE triggers (`recursive_triggers` is off and must stay off — it is a global semantic change); the `pc_ma_bi` (`BEFORE INSERT`) trigger closes this gap by reading the old row while it is still present and decrementing its bucket, so the subsequent AFTER INSERT increment leaves the counts exact. For a plain INSERT with no conflict the `WHEN` subquery returns NULL and the trigger body is skipped. The table is a **cache, not a source of truth**: `rebuildPipelineCounts` recomputes it from the base tables inside every `Storage.open()` (one grouped scan per pool, ~0.3s on a 300k-event database; index-only via `idx_timeline_events_enrichment_counts` and `idx_media_assets_counts` + `idx_te_caption_eligibility`, the latter forced with `INDEXED BY` because SQLite otherwise probes the PK autoindex and then walks the fat `event_json` overflow pages to reach the post-`event_json` columns), so any drift — a write that predates the triggers, a hand edit — heals on the next boot, and a unit test asserts trigger-maintained buckets equal a from-scratch rebuild after every write path (transitions, retry counters, scope changes, direct + cascade deletes, trigger-group flips). A read is `select … from pipeline_counts where pool = ?` — a handful of rows, tens of microseconds, independent of table size. The `(status, updated_at)` keyset indexes serve the status-filtered *lists*; they are not involved in the counts.

The offline audit worker (§9i) is not one of the monitored pools: its queue is derived (sessions without a fresh `session_audits` row) rather than a status column, so it has no materialized counts or item list. Its backlog progress (per stage: audited and to go, counted in the background by the worker) shows on the `/models` page (`audit` in `/api/models/behaviour`); per session, in the `session_audited` log and the `audits` field of the session detail.
